## PHASE P13: WAF core engine (T-0239 to T-0262) · milestone M6 · gate G13

Requirement prefix `WAF`. Goal: a pure, I/O-free, deterministic, fuzz-hardened detection engine (`hdd-waf-core`) with vector extraction, three-view normalization, a prefilter plus linear-time signature engine, a rule and pack model, scoring, exclusions, custom rules, bounded parsers, field-kind context, redaction, verdict and event models, fixtures and a benign corpus, performance budgets, mutation testing, and integration into the proxy pipeline and the dry-run inspect API. The structural SQL detectors and the other detector families (P14, P15) plug into this engine.

Engine rules (apply to every task in P13 to P15):
- `hdd-waf-core` has no async, no filesystem, no network, no wall-clock reads; randomness is injected; GeoIP/ASN lookups are traits.
- Every regular expression is compiled with a linear-time engine; no backtracking engine, no lookaround, no backreferences.
- Every loop, buffer and recursion is bounded; every input has a size cap; exceeding a cap sets a flag and follows `over_limit_policy` (never silently passes in `block` mode, R-26).
- Every rule carries examples and counter-examples used as tests; rules without both are rejected by the pack linter.
- Detection changes are measured (R-23): benign corpus zero matches, core set 100%, held-out ≥ 95%, mutation score ≥ 80%.

Gate G13 passes when: unit, property and fuzz-smoke suites pass; coverage ≥ 85% on the crate; `cargo-mutants` score ≥ 80%; benign corpus yields zero matches; the inspect API and the proxy integration work end to end in monitor and block modes on the builder; and the inspection benchmark meets p50 < 1 ms on the reference corpus.

### T-0239 · `hdd-waf-core` skeleton, public API and purity enforcement
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0237 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Define the crate boundary so the engine stays pure, testable and fast.
**Steps.**
1. Define the public API: `Engine::new(Compiled)`, `Engine::inspect(&InspectRequest, &SitePolicy, &mut Scratch) -> Verdict`, `Engine::inspect_response_head/ body_window` hooks for the outbound filter (P21), and `Compiler::compile(RulePacks, SitePolicy) -> Compiled` with deterministic output hashes.
2. Define `InspectRequest` (method, normalized path and raw path, query pairs, headers, cookies, content type, body prefix bytes with `truncated` flag, client context: IP key, country, ASN, browsing context flags from `Sec-Fetch-*`, TLS facts, HTTP version, site/auth-endpoint tags) and `Scratch` (reusable buffers to avoid allocation).
3. Define error and flag types (`InspectFlag`: `Truncated`, `BudgetExceeded`, `OverlongUtf8`, `InvalidUtf8`, `NullByte`, `MultibyteQuote`, `DecodeDepthExceeded`, `ParserLimit`, ...), and `Budget` (max bytes per field, per request, max fields, max decode iterations, max regex scans).
4. Add the purity lint to `xtask verify`: forbid `std::fs`, `std::net`, `std::thread::sleep`, `std::time::SystemTime/Instant` (except in `cfg(test)` and benches), `tokio`, `reqwest` in this crate; check dependency list against an allowlist.
5. Define the stability policy: `Verdict` and `Evidence` are `#[non_exhaustive]` with serde for API use; add a versioned `engine_version` string embedded in events.
6. Create the crate docs with the module map and the invariants above.
7. Create `tests/support` utilities: request builders, hostile string sets, golden verdict snapshots (`insta`).
8. Set up benches skeleton and fuzz target stubs (filled by later tasks).
**Deliverables.**
- `crates/hdd-waf-core` skeleton, lints, docs, test support
**Acceptance.**
- A1: adding `std::fs` or `tokio` to the crate fails `xtask verify`.
- A2: the public API compiles and a trivial inspection returns `Pass` with zero allocations in steady state (alloc counter test).
- A3: `engine_version` changes when compiled rule sets change (hash test).
- A4: docs describe every flag.
- A5: the crate has `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.
**Tests.**
- Unit/compile-fail tests for purity; allocation test with a counting allocator in tests.
**Notes.** The control plane uses the same crate for dry-runs, ensuring identical semantics.

### T-0240 · Request model and vector extraction
`P13` `[DP]` · deps: T-0239, T-0249 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Turn a request into labeled, bounded input strings for every detector.
**Steps.**
1. Implement extraction for each vector of C4.2: path segments (each decoded separately, matrix parameters split), query keys and values, form fields, multipart text parts and part headers and filenames, JSON keys and string leaves, XML text/attributes/CDATA, GraphQL query text and variables, cookies (names and values), selected headers (`User-Agent`, `Referer`, `Origin`, `Accept-Language`, `X-Forwarded-*` when trusted, configured extras, and unlisted custom headers), WebSocket handshake and optional text frames.
2. Label each extracted value with `Vector`, `FieldRef` (name path such as `form:username`, `json:$.user.name[0]`), and `FieldKind` (T-0251), keeping a stable ordering for deterministic verdicts.
3. Implement duplicate handling: inspect each duplicate individually and also the concatenation of duplicates (HTTP parameter pollution), array notations (`a[]`, `a[0]`, `a[b]`).
4. Implement limits: max fields (default 2,000), max total inspected bytes (default `inspect_body_max_bytes` for bodies and 64 KiB for headers+URL), per-field cap (16 KiB; longer values are chunked into overlapping windows of 8 KiB with 256-byte overlap so payloads at boundaries are still seen).
5. Implement content-type handling with confusion defenses: parse by declared type but also sniff (JSON body sent as form, form sent as JSON, XML in `text/plain`), inspecting under both interpretations when ambiguous.
6. Implement the multi-encoding body handling: `Content-Encoding` gzip/deflate/br/zstd decoded with bounded ratio and size via the parsers (T-0249) before extraction.
7. Provide zero-copy views where possible (`Cow`) and reuse of the scratch arena.
8. Add table tests for every vector and hostile inputs (huge numbers of parameters, deep JSON, malformed multipart).
**Deliverables.**
- `extract` module, tests, benches
**Acceptance.**
- A1: payloads placed at chunk boundaries in long fields are detected (boundary test over 10,000 offsets).
- A2: parameter pollution splits are detected via the concatenation view.
- A3: ambiguous content types are inspected under both interpretations.
- A4: extraction respects all caps and flags `Truncated`/`ParserLimit` appropriately.
- A5: extraction never panics (fuzz).
**Tests.**
- Table/proptest/fuzz; benchmark of extraction throughput.
**Notes.** Header allowlists and extras are part of the compiled policy.

### T-0241 · Normalizer: the `decoded` view
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0239 · size: XL · owner: waf
**Objective.** Implement the iterative, idempotent decoding pipeline defeating encoding evasions.
**Steps.**
1. Implement percent decoding iterated to a fixed point (max 3 layers) with strict handling of invalid sequences (leave literal, set flag), `%uXXXX` decoding, `+` to space in query/form contexts, and detection of overlong UTF-8 (`%c0%af`, `%e0%80%af`) with `OverlongUtf8` flag and conversion to the intended character for detection while the original raw view is kept.
2. Implement HTML entity decoding (named entities table, decimal and hexadecimal numeric entities with or without semicolons, with maximum expansion limits) and JSON/JS escape decoding (`\uXXXX`, `\xNN`, `\'`, `\"`, octal) in contexts where such escapes are meaningful (JSON values, script-ish contexts, SQL contexts that treat backslash as escape).
3. Implement Unicode normalization to NFKC and the **quote and operator folding** table (U+02BC, U+2018, U+2019, U+201B, U+FF07, U+00B4, U+2032 to `'`; U+201C, U+201D, U+FF02 to `"`; fullwidth ASCII variants U+FF01 to U+FF5E to ASCII; U+2010 to U+2015, U+FF0D to `-`; U+FF1D to `=`), recording `UnicodeFold` flags.
4. Implement wide-byte (GBK-style) handling: detect sequences like `%bf%27`, `%df%27`, `%a1%27` and decode the quote with flag `MultibyteQuote` (the lead byte consumption modeled by a documented rule).
5. Implement null-byte removal with `NullByte` flag, control character handling (strip or replace per context), and case folding via full Unicode lowercasing for matching (preserving the original for evidence).
6. Implement size bounds (output at most 4x input and hard cap 1 MiB per string), iteration bounds, and invalid UTF-8 handling policy (lossy conversion with replacement plus flag; attackers can exploit decoder differentials so both lossy and raw-byte views are available to byte-level signatures).
7. Provide the `NormalizedString { raw_range, decoded, flags }` type with source-offset mapping so evidence spans can be mapped back to the raw input.
8. Write 300 table cases covering every encoding trick in C4.8 (encoding group), including mixed and nested encodings.
**Deliverables.**
- `normalize::decoded` module, folding tables with provenance comments, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `%252527`, `%u0027`, `&#39;`, `&#x27;`, `'`, `＇`, `ʼ`, `%bf%27` all fold to a detectable `'` (table test).
- A2: output length never exceeds 4x input or 1 MiB (property test).
- A3: the function is idempotent on its own output (proptest, excluding documented non-idempotent flags).
- A4: offset mapping returns valid raw spans for every output position (property test).
- A5: it never panics on arbitrary bytes (fuzz).
**Tests.**
- Table (300) / proptest / fuzz; benchmark ≤ 150 ns per 100-byte string typical.
**Notes.** Idempotence (decoding already-decoded text once more must not change it except through documented layers) is tested explicitly.

### T-0242 · Canonicalizer: the `canonical` view
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0241 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Remove syntactic noise attackers add to hide SQL, expression-language and shell payloads.
**Steps.**
1. Implement SQL-context canonicalization: unwrap MySQL versioned comments (`/*!50000 union*/` becomes ` union `), replace inline comments `/**/` and `/*...*/` (non-versioned) with a single space while recording `CommentSeen` flags and positions, handle nested/unterminated comments conservatively.
2. Implement whitespace canonicalization: collapse tabs, newlines, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return, NBSP and Unicode spaces to a single space; treat `+` as space only in decoded query/form views.
3. Implement concatenation joining in evaluable cases: `'un'+'ion'`, `'un' 'ion'`, `CONCAT('un','ion')`, `'un'||'ion'`, adjacent string literals in SQL context, and `CHAR(39)`, `CHR(39)`, `0x27`, `X'27'`, `UNHEX('27')` to literals when appearing near SQL tokens (bounded evaluation to avoid blowups).
4. Implement lookup unwrapping for `${...}` syntaxes: `${lower:x}`, `${upper:x}`, `${::-x}`, `${env:NAME:-x}`, `${sys:...}`, `${date:...}`, `${j${::-n}di:`, nested up to depth 8, recording `LookupObfuscation` flags (shared with JNDI detection T-0291).
5. Implement shell-context canonicalization helpers: backslash/quote removal inside words (`c'a't`, `c""at`), `${IFS}` and `$IFS$9` expansion to space, brace expansion `{cat,/etc/passwd}`, ANSI-C quotes `$'\x63at'`, environment variable stripping, wildcard globbing hints (`/???/c?t`), recorded with flags (full lexer in T-0289).
6. Implement HTML/JS canonicalization helpers for XSS: attribute value unquoting, tag/attribute case folding, slash/whitespace separators between attributes, comment removal, entity decoding in attribute context (full tokenizer in T-0285).
7. Provide per-context entry points (`canon_sql`, `canon_shell`, `canon_html`, `canon_lookup`) so detectors request only needed views (performance), plus a combined `canonical` view for generic signatures.
8. Write 300 table cases including pathological nesting and ensure bounded runtime (budget 4x input).
**Deliverables.**
- `normalize::canonical` modules, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `/*!50000UnIoN*//**/SeLeCt` becomes `union select` in SQL context.
- A2: `${${::-j}${::-n}di:ldap://x.invalid/a}` becomes `${jndi:ldap://x.invalid/a}`.
- A3: `c'a't /e'tc'/p"a"sswd` canonicalizes to `cat /etc/passwd` in shell context.
- A4: nesting beyond depth limits sets `DecodeDepthExceeded` instead of looping.
- A5: no function exceeds 4x output growth or panics (fuzz).
**Tests.**
- Table (300) / proptest / fuzz; bench.
**Notes.** The `decoded` view keeps comment tokens visible; `canonical` collapses them (C4.3).

**Objective.** Prove the normalizers are safe to run on untrusted input at line rate.

### T-0244 · Prefilter and signature engine (Aho-Corasick plus regex automata)
`P13` `[DP]` · deps: T-0242 · size: XL · owner: waf
**Objective.** Make scanning fast: cheap token prefilter, then linear-time pattern sets.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the compile pipeline: rule definitions to (a) an Aho-Corasick automaton over required literal tokens per rule (extracted by a literal-extraction pass from the regex AST) and (b) per-group `regex-automata` sets (DFA/hybrid with size limits) for verification; groups by category and context so a field scans only relevant sets.
2. Implement size and complexity budgets at compile time: maximum DFA states per group (reject or fall back to the lazy/hybrid engine with a memory cap), maximum pattern length, total compiled memory per site (cap by plan), and reporting of the heaviest rules.
3. Implement the scan API: `scan(field_view, contexts, scratch) -> SmallVec<Match>` with early exit for hard matches when configured, per-request regex-scan budget (maximum bytes scanned across all sets) and `BudgetExceeded` handling.
4. Implement hot swap: compile in a background task off the hot path, validate against the self-test corpus (rule examples and counter-examples), then publish via `ArcSwap`; compile failures keep the last good set.
5. Implement match metadata: rule ID, group, start/end offsets in the scanned view, mapped back to raw offsets via the normalizer map.
6. Implement caching: LRU cache of verdicts keyed by (field hash, context, ruleset hash) for repeated identical values (headers like `User-Agent`) with strict size limits and TTL, safe because the engine is pure.
7. Provide a benchmark suite with realistic traffic corpora and adversarial inputs (long runs of near-matches).
8. Document engine limits and the rationale for linear-time-only.
**Deliverables.**
- `signatures` module, compiler, benches, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: no pattern can cause super-linear scan time (property test with adversarial strings across all shipped rules).
- A2: compile rejects patterns exceeding budgets with precise errors.
- A3: hot swap does not drop requests and applies within 2 s of publication (integration with T-0211).
- A4: p50 scan time for a 200-byte field across all default rules is under 20 µs on the builder.
- A5: matches map back to correct raw offsets for 1,000 randomized encoded inputs.
**Tests.**
- Property/adversarial tests; benchmarks; unit: literal extraction correctness vs regex semantics (differential with plain `regex`).
**Notes.** Backtracking engines (PCRE) are never used.

### T-0245 · Rule model, rule files and packs
`P13` `[DP][API][DOC]` · deps: T-0244 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Define how detections are authored, tested, versioned and shipped.

Define rule files (`crates/hdd-waf-core/rules/<category>/*.toml`): `id` (`HDD-<CAT>-<nnnn>`), `title`, `category`, `subtype`, `atk` references, `severity` (critical, error, warning, notice), `hardness` (hard, soft), `paranoia` (1 to 4), `targets` (vectors and field kinds), `views` (decoded, canonical, raw), `pattern` or `structural` reference, `transforms`, `tags`, `message_key`, `examples` (must match), `counter_examples` (must not match), `references` (CWE/CVE), `since`, `status`.

6. Implement documentation generation: a rules reference page (rule IDs, titles, examples) for the docs site (examples are inert shapes only).

### T-0246 · Scoring engine, thresholds and `docs/SCORING.md`
`P13` `[DP][DOC]` · deps: T-0245 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Decide blocks consistently from hard and soft matches.
**Steps.**
1. Implement severity weights (Critical 5, Error 4, Warning 3, Notice 2), per-category caps (so a single noisy category cannot dominate: default cap 15), and the anomaly score aggregation with deterministic ordering.
2. Implement the decision logic: any **hard** match above the active paranoia level yields `Block` regardless of score; otherwise block when `score >= block_threshold`; paranoia level gates which rules are active (rule `paranoia` ≤ site level); thresholds are per site (default 5) and separate from paranoia.
3. Implement mode handling in the engine output: the engine always computes the full verdict; the **mode** (off/monitor/log/block) is applied by the caller (proxy/dry-run) so `would_block` is always available.
4. Implement per-vector scoring multipliers where defined (for example headers lower weight for generic keywords) documented in rule metadata.
5. Implement score explanation output (list of contributing matches with weights) for the event drawer and dry-run.
6. Write `docs/SCORING.md` precisely (formulas, examples, edge cases, interplay with exceptions and presets).
7. Test with 100 scenario tables (combinations of matches yielding expected decisions), plus property tests (adding a match never decreases the score; hard match always blocks).
8. Benchmark scoring overhead (under 5 µs per request).
**Deliverables.**
- scoring module, docs, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the formulas in `docs/SCORING.md` are executable examples verified by doc-tests.
- A2: hard matches at inactive paranoia levels do not block (explicit tests).
- A3: category caps behave as specified.
- A4: explanations list all contributing matches deterministically.
- A5: scoring overhead meets the benchmark.
**Tests.**
- Table (100) / proptest / doc-tests.
**Notes.** Presets set paranoia and threshold; they do not change rule weights.

### T-0247 · Exceptions engine
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0246, T-0226 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Apply scoped exclusions without weakening rules globally.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the compiled exception structure: per-rule or per-category exceptions with scope matchers (path pattern, methods, vector/field name, CIDR) and expiry timestamps (evaluated against an injected `now`).
2. Implement application order: exceptions remove matching **matches** before scoring; hard matches excepted only if the exception explicitly targets the rule/subtype and scope is narrow (path + field), mirroring the control-plane validation.
3. Record in the verdict which matches were excepted (`excepted_by: exception_id`) so analysts can see what would have happened.
4. Implement performance: exceptions indexed by rule ID and path prefix for O(log n) evaluation; cap per site (200).
5. Implement tests for scoping correctness, expiry edge cases, overlap behavior and the rule that exceptions cannot reduce hard-ban categories on auth endpoints without explicit flag.
6. Implement metrics (`MET-hdd_waf_exceptions_hits_total`).
7. Add property tests: an exception never affects requests outside its scope.
8. Document semantics.
**Deliverables.**
- exceptions module, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: out-of-scope requests are never affected (property test over 100k random requests).
- A2: expired exceptions are ignored using the injected clock.
- A3: excepted matches are visible in the verdict explanation.
- A4: hard-match exceptions require explicit narrow scope.
- A5: lookup cost stays within budget for 200 exceptions.
**Tests.**
- Unit/proptest/bench.
**Notes.** Control-plane validation (T-0226) and engine semantics share the same scope matcher crate.

### T-0248 · Custom rule evaluation
`P13` `[DP][API]` · deps: T-0246 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Evaluate tenant rules safely and predictably.
**Steps.**
1. Define the match tree evaluation: groups (OR between groups, AND within), fields (path, query, parameter name/value, header, cookie, method, client IP/CIDR via radix trie, country, ASN, user agent, body contains, JSON path, request size, TLS/HTTP version), operators (equals, contains, starts/ends with, matches regex, in list, in CIDR, numeric comparisons, exists), negation, case-insensitivity flag.
2. Compile regexes with the restricted syntax (linear-time), plus Aho-Corasick for large `contains any of` lists, and radix trie for IP/CIDR lists; reject at compile with diagnostics (position, code, suggestion).
3. Implement action semantics: `allow` (terminal skip of further detections; recorded), `block`, `ban` (ban intent), `challenge`, `log`; priorities and short-circuit evaluation order documented.
4. Implement resource budgets per rule (maximum scanned bytes) and per request (maximum rules evaluated), with `BudgetExceeded` flagged and handled by policy (fail closed in block mode for deny rules).
5. Implement GeoIP/ASN trait usage with absence handling (`ERR-WAF-003` at compile if country rules are used without a database).
6. Implement evaluation explanations (which condition matched with values redacted).
7. Implement determinism (stable ordering, no randomness), size caps (rule size 16 KB, list entries 1,000).
8. Test with 300 rules (valid/invalid) and hostile regexes (ReDoS shapes) ensuring compile-time rejection or linear behavior.
**Deliverables.**
- `custom` module, compiler diagnostics, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: unsupported constructs are rejected with exact positions.
- A2: hostile regexes complete in bounded time (time-limited test across 200 shapes).
- A3: `allow` rules cannot bypass platform hard bans (platform deny wins by design, tested).
- A4: IP/CIDR lists of 1,000 entries evaluate in under 2 µs.
- A5: explanations never include raw sensitive values.
**Tests.**
- Table (300) / proptest (tree evaluation equals reference interpreter on small domains) / fuzz target on the rule parser.
**Notes.** The control plane rule builder (T-0228) calls the same validation and the same evaluator for dry-runs.

### T-0249 · Bounded parsers: forms, multipart, JSON, XML and decompression
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0239 · size: XL · owner: waf
**Objective.** Parse hostile bodies safely and cheaply for inspection.
**Steps.**
1. Implement `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` parsing (duplicates preserved, nested notations, limits) and `multipart/form-data` parsing (vetted `multer` or own streaming parser; boundary validation, maximum 100 parts, 8 MiB per part inspect cap, header limits, filename extraction including `filename*` RFC 5987 decoding, duplicate `Content-Disposition` tolerance handling by inspecting all variants).
2. Implement JSON parsing with a streaming tokenizer: depth cap 32, key/length caps, big-number handling, duplicate keys preserved as separate occurrences, NaN/Infinity tolerance flags, BOM and encoding detection (UTF-8/16/32 sniffing), and extraction of keys and string leaves with JSON path labels.
3. Implement XML parsing with a tokenizer that **never** resolves entities or DTDs: detect `DOCTYPE`, `ENTITY`, `SYSTEM`, `PUBLIC`, `xi:include`, `xsl:` and report them as signals; extract text, attributes, CDATA with depth cap and size cap; protect against billion-laughs by never expanding entities and by counting entity declarations.
4. Implement bounded decompression for `gzip`, `deflate`, `br`, `zstd` (and stacked encodings up to 2 layers) with output cap 10 MiB, ratio cap 20:1, time budget, and streaming to the extractor; reject invalid combinations (`Content-Encoding` on multipart parts).
5. Implement chunked body reassembly interplay: the engine receives the reassembled prefix; chunk-boundary payload tests verify detection.
6. Implement content sniffing helpers (JSON/XML/form detection) for confusion defense.
7. Implement archive peeking for uploads (zip/tar/gzip headers only: entry names, uncompressed sizes, entry count) with strict caps (used by T-0297).
8. Create fuzz targets per parser and a corpus of malformed and malicious samples (including Class C shapes used only as inert test inputs bounded by limits).
**Deliverables.**
- `parsers` modules, fuzz targets, corpora, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: XML with a billion-laughs DTD is flagged and consumes bounded memory/time (limits asserted).
- A2: zip bombs and gzip bombs are rejected by ratio/size caps without full expansion.
- A3: JSON depth 33 is rejected with `ParserLimit`.
- A4: duplicate and tricky multipart headers are all inspected (table tests).
- A5: parsers are panic-free under fuzz.
**Tests.**
- Table/fuzz/property tests; memory/time bound tests.
**Notes.** Class C resource-exhaustion shapes exist only as small descriptors that trigger limits, never as large real bombs.

### T-0250 · GraphQL light parser and vector extraction
`P13` `[DP]` · deps: T-0240 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Inspect GraphQL requests without a full server-side schema.
**Steps.**
1. Implement a tolerant GraphQL tokenizer/parser sufficient to extract operations, selection depth, field counts, alias counts, fragment spreads, variable definitions, directives, and string literals.
2. Compute metrics: maximum depth, total fields, aliases per operation, batch size (arrays of operations), introspection usage (`__schema`, `__type`), fragment cycle detection, and a cost estimate heuristic.
3. Extract inspectable strings (arguments, variable values from JSON `variables`) as vectors `graphql:variables.*` for the normal detectors.
4. Emit policy-driven signals: depth/alias/batch/introspection thresholds from the site policy (defaults: depth 12, aliases 30, batch 10, introspection blocked on production unless allowed).
5. Handle persisted queries and GET-based queries (`query` parameter), APQ hashes, and content types (`application/graphql`, JSON).
6. Defend the parser (bounded recursion, token limits, no panics).
7. Add tests for depth bombs, alias overloading brute-force patterns, fragment cycles, malformed queries.
8. Document limits and false-positive considerations (large legitimate queries).
**Deliverables.**
- `graphql` module, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: depth and alias thresholds are enforced exactly (boundary tests).
- A2: introspection detection handles aliasing and fragments.
- A3: variables are inspected by the standard detectors.
- A4: the parser is bounded (fuzz, 1 MiB inputs complete within budget).
- A5: persisted query hashes do not crash or bypass inspection of variables.
**Tests.**
- Table/fuzz tests; benchmark.
**Notes.** ATK-056 and ATK-179 to ATK-182 depend on this.

### T-0251 · Field-kind context typing
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0240 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Infer what kind of value each field carries to reduce false positives and tighten hard families.
**Steps.**
1. Implement name-based inference with token matching on normalized parameter names (split on `_`, `-`, camelCase, brackets) mapping to `password`, `username`, `email`, `numeric_id`, `search`, `free_text`, `filename`, `header`, `cookie`, `unknown` per the C4.6 tables, with locale-aware synonyms configurable per site (for example `pwd`, `passwd`, `pass`, `contrasena`).
2. Implement overrides: site-declared mappings (S-057) and auth-endpoint declarations take precedence; learned shapes (opt-in) provide type/charset/length hints (`numeric` fields with digits only produce `numeric_id`).
3. Implement value-based hints when names are unhelpful: all digits and short implies numeric; contains `@` and dots implies email-shaped; long natural language implies free text; used only to relax or tighten **soft** weights, never to relax hard families except in the documented password case.
4. Implement the field-kind policy table API (`policy_for(kind, family) -> Hardness`) used by detectors (P14, P15), including the Balanced/Paranoid differences.
5. Implement deterministic behavior and caching of name inference.
6. Add tests with 200 parameter names across languages and frameworks (WordPress, Laravel, Rails, Django, Spring, ASP.NET naming).
7. Document the heuristics and how to override.
8. Add fuzz/property tests for the tokenizer of names.
**Deliverables.**
- `context` module, tables, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: 200-name corpus classified as expected (table).
- A2: overrides take precedence and are reflected in verdict explanations.
- A3: password-kind handling matches C4.6 exactly.
- A4: unknown kinds are treated as `search` (documented).
- A5: inference is deterministic and allocation-free in the steady state.
**Tests.**
- Table/proptest; alloc test.
**Notes.** Field kinds are metadata only; hard-family coverage for password fields is not relaxed except for H2 (C4.6).

### T-0252 · Verdict and event model, evidence extraction and ban intents
`P13` `[DP][API][SEC]` · deps: T-0246, T-0251 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Produce explainable, privacy-safe results that the proxy, API and UI share.

Implement evidence extraction: from the `decoded` view, a window around the match (up to 512 bytes total after redaction) with the match span marked, mapped back to raw offsets, with truncation markers and escape-safe representation (no control characters; bidi controls replaced by visible markers).

6. Implement size caps and ensure no raw values beyond evidence are retained in the verdict.

8. Add golden tests for verdict JSON and evidence rendering with hostile inputs.

### T-0253 · Redaction library
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0252 · size: M · owner: sec
**Objective.** Ensure stored evidence and logs never contain credentials or tokens.
**Steps.**
1. Implement redaction rules for headers (`Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie`, `X-API-Key`, `X-Auth-Token`, and any header name matching `(token|secret|key|auth|session)`), query/form/JSON fields whose names match password/secret/token patterns, and value-pattern detectors (JWTs `eyJ...`, AWS access key IDs, long hex/base64 secrets, `Bearer ...`, private key headers, credit card numbers with Luhn validation, US SSN-like numbers as optional).
2. Implement replacement with fixed markers (`[redacted:header]`, `[redacted:token]`) preserving length class (short/medium/long) but not content; the evidence span tied to a SQL payload in a password field is shown in redacted form when the field kind is `password` (the payload structure is kept in the *rule metadata*, not the value).
3. Implement streaming-friendly operation with bounded cost and no regex backtracking.
4. Provide a configuration for additional site-specific patterns and sensitive field names (bounded count).
5. Implement a verification scanner reused in logs/tests: given a string, report any unredacted secret-like content.
6. Implement tests with a corpus of real-looking secrets generated at runtime.
7. Document policy and limitations (redaction is heuristic; do not store more than needed).
8. Fuzz the redactor.
**Deliverables.**
- `redact` module, scanner, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: all secret-like samples in the corpus are redacted in evidence and logs.
- A2: password-field evidence never reveals the value (only the matched rule/subtype).
- A3: redaction does not break escaping or offsets (property tests).
- A4: the scanner finds no secrets in 100k generated events.
- A5: the redactor never panics (fuzz) and is linear time.
**Tests.**
- Table/proptest/fuzz; end-to-end event scan test.
**Notes.** Redaction applies before events are queued, not at display time.

### T-0254 · Fixture system, payload classes and held-out sets
`P13` `[QA][SEC]` · deps: T-0245 · size: L · owner: qa
**Objective.** Organize attack and benign fixtures with the safety classes of section 2.2.
**Steps.**
1. Define the fixture file format: UTF-8 text with line-oriented entries and a YAML/TOML front-matter header declaring `class: A|B|C`, `category`, `vector`, `atk`, `source` (original/derived/public corpus with license), `heldout: true|false`, and optional per-entry annotations (`# expect: block subtype=tautology`).

### T-0255 · Benign corpora v1 and the false-positive gate
`P13` `[QA][SEC]` · deps: T-0254 · size: L · owner: qa
**Objective.** Create the corpora that keep detection honest, and gate on zero false positives.

Build `tests/fixtures/benign-general.txt` (500+ entries) covering: names with apostrophes and hyphens (O'Brien, D'Angelo, Nguyen, María-José), addresses (`Apt #4`, `12/B`, `St. John's`), emails (valid edge cases incl. `o'brien@example.com`, plus-addressing), URLs and paths (`/blog/2024/10/my-post`, encoded unicode paths), search queries (everyday and technical), product titles, markdown and code snippets in prose, JSON/XML samples, form values (dates, phone numbers, currencies), user agents of mainstream browsers, referers, cookies (opaque tokens), and password-like strings (random, passphrases, symbols).

6. Add a CI job that fails on any new false positive and prints the minimal reproducer.

### T-0256 · Performance engineering and global inspection budgets
`P13` `[DP]` · deps: T-0244, T-0246 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Meet the latency budgets (inspection p50 < 1 ms) and protect the process from overload.
**Steps.**
1. Build criterion benchmarks for typical requests (GET with 5 params, login POST, JSON API POST 2 KB, multipart 100 KB) and adversarial ones (long near-matches, deep nesting, many parameters), reporting p50/p99 and throughput.
2. Optimize hot paths: avoid allocations (SmallVec, reusable scratch), single-pass normalization where possible, lazy canonical views (only when prefilter hits), early exits for obviously benign fields (alphanumeric-only strings skip heavy scans), and cache identical header values.
3. Implement per-request budgets (CPU time proxy via scanned-bytes and operation counters, since wall-clock is forbidden in the pure crate) and a **global inspection budget** in the proxy (semaphore of concurrent inspections sized from cores; queue limits) with documented shed policy (fail closed in block mode: 503 with Ray ID; monitor mode: pass and mark `skipped_budget`).
4. Measure memory per in-flight inspection and enforce limits (cap scratch size, 1 MiB).
5. Add regression budgets to CI: benchmark results compared with stored baselines (criterion), failing on > 20% regression for key benchmarks.
6. Profile with flamegraphs on the builder and record findings; optimize the top three hotspots.
7. Validate tail latency under concurrency with a load test (functional profile only, builder-local).
8. Document tuning knobs.
**Deliverables.**
- benches, budgets, optimizations, perf report
**Acceptance.**
- A1: inspection p50 under 1 ms and p99 under 5 ms on the reference corpus (builder-class hardware recorded).
- A2: no steady-state heap growth per request (alloc counter).
- A3: overload behavior follows the shed policy (test by saturating the budget).
- A4: CI detects a deliberately slowed function (meta-test).
- A5: scratch memory per request stays under 1 MiB.
**Tests.**
- Criterion benches; load tests; allocation tests.
**Notes.** Hardware used for numbers is recorded; claims in docs cite the AC-24 measurements only.

### T-0257 · Over-limit policy implementation
`P13` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0240, T-0256 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Handle bodies and fields beyond inspection limits explicitly and visibly.
**Steps.**
1. Implement `inspect_prefix` (default): inspect the first N bytes (`inspect_body_max_bytes`, default 128 KiB), tag the verdict `truncated=true`, and record the metric; for streaming bodies the proxy passes the buffered prefix to the engine while continuing to stream the rest after the decision.
2. Implement `block`: requests whose body exceeds the limit (or Content-Length declares more) are blocked with 413 or 403 (configurable) and an event of category `proto`/`upload` subtype `over_limit`.
3. Implement `pass`: no further inspection beyond the prefix; the metric and UI warning make this visible; document risk (attackers can pad payloads beyond the limit; ATK-013 padding variant).
4. Implement the **padding attack mitigation** under `inspect_prefix`: additionally scan the **tail window** (last 16 KiB) of bodies up to a cap (buffered tail for requests below 10 MiB) and sample middle windows for JSON/form bodies where structure allows field-wise inspection (fields beyond the prefix are inspected individually up to the field cap), so adding junk at the start does not hide payloads in later fields.
5. Implement per-field caps and chunked windows (T-0240) for long single values.
6. Implement metrics (`MET-hdd_waf_truncated_total{policy}`) and event tags.
7. Implement tests: payload after 1 MiB of padding in JSON/form/multipart under each policy; boundary conditions at exactly N bytes.
8. Document the residual risk in `SECURITY.md` and S-055 copy.
**Deliverables.**
- policy implementation, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: under `inspect_prefix`, a payload placed in a late JSON field is still detected (field-wise inspection) up to the field cap.
- A2: under `block`, oversize bodies are blocked with the documented status and event.
- A3: under `pass`, the UI warns and metrics increment.
- A4: boundary tests at N-1, N, N+1 behave consistently.
- A5: tail-window scanning detects payloads appended after padding for non-structured bodies.
**Tests.**
- Table/proptest on positions; integration through the proxy harness.
**Notes.** Residual risk is a documented known limitation (C9.5).

### T-0258 · Mutation testing and test-quality gates
`P13` `[QA]` · deps: T-0243, T-0246, T-0247, T-0248, T-0252 · size: M · owner: qa
**Objective.** Make sure the test suite would actually catch bugs in the engine.

6. Add a mutation-regression check: new code must not reduce the score (diff-based mutation on changed files in CI where feasible).
7. Document how to add tests for survivors.
8. Archive reports with SHA-256.
**Deliverables.**
- mutants configuration, reports, new tests, coverage reports
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the mutation score meets the thresholds or the shortfall has a diagnosis document and a plan.
- A2: coverage ≥ 85% for the crate.
- A3: equivalent-mutant exclusions are documented.
- A4: reports are archived and linked in the gate report.
- A5: the sampled mutation job runs in `verify` within 10 minutes.
**Tests.**
- The mutation and coverage jobs themselves.
**Notes.** Mutation testing is repeated after P14 and P15 add detectors.

### T-0260 · Inspect API (`POST /api/v1/waf/inspect`) and dry-run semantics
`P13` `[API][SEC]` · deps: T-0252, T-0237, T-0125 · size: L · owner: api
**Objective.** Provide the dry-run endpoint that the UI, SDK and acceptance runner rely on.
**Steps.**
1. Implement `POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/domains/{dom}/waf/inspect` and the alias `POST /api/v1/waf/inspect` (body includes `site`), accepting a described request (method, URL or path+query, headers, cookies, body as UTF-8 text or base64 up to 64 KB, content type, client context: IP optional, `Sec-Fetch-*` values, field-kind hints) and optionally `mode_override` (`block` for evaluating would-ban semantics).
2. Run the full engine with the site's compiled policy and return: `would_block`, decision details (category, subtype, rule IDs and versions for the owner role, score and threshold, hardness), `would_ban` with the TTL ladder step the IP would receive (read-only computation using offence counters), evidence (redacted), explanation, `config_revision`, `engine_version`, flags (`truncated`, etc.).
3. Guarantee side-effect freedom: never forwards, never bans, never increments offence counters or rate limiter state, never writes events (an audit event with a hash of the sample is written for compliance); enforced by types (the engine invoked with a `DryRun` context that has no mutators).
4. Enforce permissions (`waf.inspect`), rate limits (60 per minute per user, 600 per hour per org), size limits, and idempotency not required.
5. Return the exact `config_revision` so callers (acceptance runner) can verify the policy did not change between inspection and live test.
6. Provide OpenAPI documentation with examples (inert samples only) and SDK method.
7. Implement a batch mode (up to 50 samples per call) for the acceptance matrix with total size limit.
8. Add tests including hostile payloads in all fields and consistency with proxy decisions (differential test: same request through the proxy test harness in monitor mode yields the same verdict).
**Deliverables.**
- endpoints, DTOs, OpenAPI, SDK stubs, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: dry-run calls cause no events, bans or counter changes (store snapshots before/after).
- A2: inspect results equal proxy monitor-mode verdicts for the same inputs (differential test on 500 samples).
- A3: the response includes `config_revision` and `would_ban` details.
- A4: rate limits and size caps are enforced.

**Tests.**
- Integration (API + engine + Redis counters); differential test; security tests for oversize/rate abuse.
**Notes.** Rule IDs are hidden from viewer roles and never shown to visitors.

<!-- PHASE:P14 -->
## PHASE P14: SQL injection shield (T-0263 to T-0284) · milestone M6 · gate G14

Requirement prefix `SQLI`. Goal: deliver the capability at the center of the product: **any SQL injection attempt against any form, login page, URL, header or cookie is detected and blocked, and the attacker's IP is banned, even when the origin application is itself vulnerable.** The phase builds the SQL tokenizer and fingerprint engine, the six hard signature families (H1 to H8 of C4.5) including the six mandated payloads, evasion handling, field-kind context policy, the SQLi ban policy, auth-endpoint behavior, NoSQL/LDAP/XPath/GraphQL injection detectors, write-path hardening for second-order attacks, time-based attack detection, the fixture and benign suites, the sqlmap campaign harness, metrics and UI integration.

This phase implements detection and the ban *decision* (the `BanIntent` and the policy table of C4.10). Ban *storage and enforcement* (Redis, kernel) arrive in P16 and the end-to-end lab proof (AC-38, AC-39) is completed there; here the proof is at the engine, inspect-API and proxy-verdict level plus a sqlmap campaign in `monitor` mode through the walking-skeleton proxy.

Doctrine reminders (C4): hard hits ban on first occurrence outside cross-site subresource context; password-field H2 is the one documented relaxation (soft 4 in Balanced); benign names such as `O'Brien` must pass; the mandated set is the six payloads supplied by the operator plus the variant families.

Gate G14 passes when: the mandated set and all variant fixtures are 100% `would_block` with category `sqli` in every vector of C4.2; held-out detection ≥ 95%; benign corpora produce zero false positives; the sqlmap monitor-mode campaign coverage ≥ 95% of injection-bearing requests (exact figure and unflagged classes reported); mutation score on SQLi modules ≥ 80%; fuzz smoke is clean.

### T-0263 · SQL tokenizer with dialect awareness
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0242, T-0262 · size: XL · owner: waf
**Objective.** Tokenize attacker-controlled text as SQL would see it, in several starting contexts, without depending on a database.
**Steps.**
1. Define token classes: `Keyword`, `Function`, `Operator`, `Number`, `String` (single, double, backtick, `$$`, `N'...'`, `E'...'`, `X'...'`), `Identifier`, `Comment` (`--`, `#`, `/* */`, `/*! */` unwrapped by the canonical view), `Punct` (`;`, `,`, `(`, `)`), `Variable` (`@x`, `@@x`, `$1`, `:name`), `Whitespace`, `Unknown`, plus a synthetic `BreakoutQuote` token representing a quote that closes an assumed enclosing string.
2. Implement the tokenizer as a hand-written, allocation-light lexer over `&str`/bytes with bounded steps (maximum tokens 2,048 per field; beyond that flag `ParserLimit`), handling dialect differences: MySQL/MariaDB (backslash escapes, `#`, `--` requiring whitespace, `/*!`), PostgreSQL (`$$`, `E''`, `::`, `||`), MSSQL (`[ident]`, `--`, `;`, `+` concat, `@@`, `0x`), Oracle (`||`, `q'[...]'`, `dual`), SQLite (`[ident]`, double-quote identifiers, `||`), ANSI baseline.
3. Evaluate three **starting contexts** per input: `none` (as if in an unquoted numeric position), `single_quote` (as if the value is inside `'...'`), `double_quote` (inside `"..."`), plus `backtick` for MySQL identifiers; for the quote contexts, the first matching closing quote becomes a `BreakoutQuote` and tokenization continues in normal mode, which is how `' OR 1=1--` is understood.
4. Provide keyword/function tables per dialect with a compact perfect-hash lookup, categorized (boolean connectors, set operators, DML/DDL, time/delay functions, metadata names, string/hex functions).
5. Provide token stream helpers: reduced token codes (a short alphabet used by fingerprints), position mapping back to the `decoded` view for evidence spans, and a streaming iterator to avoid allocating vectors on hot paths.
6. Document the design with a table of sample inputs and resulting token sequences for each mandated payload in each context.
7. Write 400 table tests across dialect features and 200 adversarial inputs (unterminated strings/comments, nested quotes, huge numbers).
8. Fuzz the tokenizer for panics and quadratic behavior.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-waf-core::sql::tokenizer`, tables, docs, tests, fuzz target
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `' OR 1=1--` tokenizes in `single_quote` context as BreakoutQuote, OR, Number, Operator, Number, Comment.
- A2: `admin' --`, `admin' #`, `admin'/*` produce Identifier, BreakoutQuote-or-Quote, Comment tokens in the relevant contexts.
- A3: tokenization is linear time on adversarial inputs (property test with measured scaling).
- A4: token and step caps produce `ParserLimit` flags instead of panics or long loops.
- A5: tables cover all five dialects with at least 60 cases each.
**Tests.**
- Table (400) / adversarial (200) / proptest (scaling) / fuzz.
**Notes.** The tokenizer is an original implementation; no third-party SQLi library code is copied.

### T-0264 · Fingerprint engine and fingerprint database tooling
`P14` `[DP][QA]` · deps: T-0263, T-0254 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Recognize SQL injection by token-sequence shape, learning from labeled corpora without overfitting.
**Steps.**
1. Define fingerprints as short strings of reduced token codes (for example `q o n o n c`) computed from the first N significant tokens after the breakout point, in each starting context, with rules for collapsing repeated tokens.
2. Build the fingerprint database tooling (`xtask sqli-fingerprints build`): input labeled corpora (attack-labeled fixtures from `tests/fixtures/sqli`, benign corpora), output sets `attack_fp`, `benign_fp` with counts; fingerprints observed in both are flagged for manual review and excluded from automatic blocking.
3. Implement the runtime matcher: a perfect hash set lookup of fingerprints (embedded in the binary, versioned) used as a *soft* signal (score 3) unless the fingerprint is on the curated `hard` list (derived from H-families) ; unknown fingerprints with SQL-like token composition get a low soft score.
4. Enforce the **license and provenance discipline**: only original fixtures and permissively licensed or explicitly allowed public corpora (recorded in the fixture headers) feed the database; held-out sets are excluded from training (lint on the build tool).
5. Implement cross-validation tooling reporting precision/recall on held-out data and per-subtype confusion; produce a report included in gate documentation.
6. Implement database update safety: the generated set is checked in as a data file with a hash, regenerated deterministically, and reviewed as a diff (counts added/removed).
7. Implement size and performance constraints (set size under 1 MB, lookup under 100 ns).
8. Test with the mandated payloads and variants to ensure they map to hard fingerprints.
**Deliverables.**
- fingerprint builder, runtime matcher, generated data, reports, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the builder refuses held-out fixtures and unlicensed corpora (tests).
- A2: fingerprints present in both attack and benign sets are never auto-hard.
- A3: the mandated payloads map to fingerprints marked hard.
- A4: held-out recall report is generated (≥ 95% target at the gate).
- A5: the database file is deterministic (hash stable across two builds).
**Tests.**
- Unit: reduction and collapsing rules; integration: build and cross-validate; benchmark lookup.
**Notes.** The fingerprint layer supplements, never replaces, the explicit hard families.

### T-0265 · Hard family H1: tautologies and always-true predicates
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0264 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Detect boolean-condition injections regardless of operands, quoting and spacing.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the semantic evaluator over token streams: after a boolean connector (`or`, `and`, `xor`, `||`, `&&`, possibly preceded by closing parentheses `)` sequences or a breakout quote), parse a bounded expression (comparison of operands, `like`, `rlike`, `regexp`, `in (...)`, `between`, `is [not] null`, `not`, `true/false`, bare literals) and evaluate it over literals: numbers, strings (quote-normalized so `'1'` equals `1`), booleans, NULL, identical identifiers (`a=a`), with MySQL-style loose comparisons (string to number) and case-insensitive string compare.
2. Classify as tautology when the expression evaluates to true (including trivially true shapes `1`, `true`, `'x'`, `1<2`, `2>1`, `'a'='a'`, `'a' like 'a'`, `1 in (1)`, `1 between 0 and 2`, `not 0`, `1=1`, `1 is not null`), with variants wrapped in parentheses `((...))` and quote/paren mixtures (`') or ('1'='1`, `")) or (("1"="1`).
3. Define subtype `tautology`; hardness rules: **hard** when a boolean connector appears together with either a breakout quote/paren in the preceding tokens or a SQL-ish token (keyword, comment, `limit`) around, or when the field kind is numeric; **soft 4** for a bare `or 1=1` in prose-like text without breakout (e.g., "x or 1=1 is true").
4. Cover all the mandated forms: `' OR 1=1--`, `' OR '1'='1`, `' or 1=1 LIMIT 1 --`, plus `1' or '1'='1`, `' || '1'='1`, `' OR 'x'='x`, `" or ""="`, `' or 1 --`, `' OR TRUE--`, `' or 'a' like 'a`, `' or 1 in (1)--`.
5. Implement operand evaluation limits (maximum expression length 64 tokens) and timeouts via token counters.
6. Write rule metadata (`HDD-SQLI-0001..`) with examples and counter-examples (`O'Brien`, `rock 'n' roll`, `1=1 is a tautology in math`, `select your plan or save`, `what is 2>1 ?`) and link ATK-001.
7. Test across the vector/field-kind matrix.
8. Measure false positives against the benign corpora (must be zero).
**Deliverables.**
- H1 evaluator and rule files, fixtures (≥ 80 variants), tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: every H1 fixture variant is hard and categorized `sqli/tautology`.
- A2: counter-examples produce no hard match.
- A3: M1, M2 and M6 are hard hits in every vector.
- A4: evaluation never exceeds its token cap; adversarial long expressions are flagged not looped.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora for H1.
**Tests.**
- Table (200) / proptest (spacing, case, encoding permutations of M1 to M6 stay detected) / fuzz.
**Notes.** The proptest generator applies the evasion catalog (C4.8) transformations to the mandated set.

### T-0266 · Hard family H2: quote breakout followed by comment or terminator
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0264 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Catch authentication-bypass idioms such as `admin' --`, `admin' #` and `admin'/*` without flagging ordinary apostrophes.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the H2 rule over token streams: a quote (single, double, backtick, or `)` after a closing quote) that immediately (ignoring whitespace) precedes a comment starter (`--`, `#`, `/*`) or a statement terminator sequence (`;--`, `;#`), where the token before the quote is an Identifier, String-like, Number or `)` (so it plausibly closes a SQL value).
2. Handle dialect specifics: MySQL `-- ` needs trailing whitespace or end of input (still flag `--` at end or before newline), `#` as comment, `/*` unterminated; PostgreSQL/Oracle/MSSQL `--` immediately after quote; also `-- -`, `--+`, `%23` encoded hash after decoding.
3. Define subtype `comment_termination` (with alias `auth_bypass` when the surrounding field kind is username/email/password or on an auth endpoint) and hardness rules from C4.5: **hard** in all kinds except `password`, where it is **soft 4** under Balanced and **hard** under Paranoid; on declared auth endpoints in the `strict` profile it is hard everywhere except password-kind in Balanced.
4. Cover the mandated forms `admin' --`, `admin' #`, `admin'/*`, and variants `admin'--`, `admin')--`, `admin"--`, `' --`, `'--`, `') --`, `'; --`, `1'#`, `admin' -- -`, `admin'%23`, `admin'/**/--`, `admin'/*!`.
5. Define counter-examples that must not match: `O'Brien`, `D'Angelo`, `it's -- fine` (quote not directly followed by the comment), `l'#1` and `I'#1 fan` (**soft 2** only in `free_text` and `search` field kinds, where `'#<digit>` is numbering in prose; hard in `username`, `email`, `numeric_id`, unknown kinds and on auth endpoints, and `'#` followed by a letter is hard in every kind but `password`; boundary cases are listed in E1.11 and read from `h2-boundary.txt`), `5'10" tall`, `rock 'n' roll`, `'Hello' -- he said` (quote closes a quoted word; flagged soft not hard unless the preceding token pattern is an identifier directly adjacent to the quote with no space and the quote is unbalanced).
6. Implement the **balance heuristic**: if quotes in the field are balanced and the comment follows a closing quote of a complete quoted word separated by spaces, downgrade to soft; if the quote count is odd and the quote touches an identifier/number, treat as breakout (hard).
7. Write rule metadata with examples/counter-examples and link ATK-002, ATK-011.
8. Test across vectors and field kinds, including password-kind behavior in both strictness modes.
**Deliverables.**
- H2 rule logic, rule files, fixtures (≥ 80 variants), tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: M3, M4, M5 are hard hits in username, email, search, free-text, header and cookie vectors.
- A2: in password-kind fields under Balanced they are soft 4 (blocked only if the threshold is reached or on Paranoid) and the verdict explains why.
- A3: all counter-examples produce no hard match.
- A4: encoded forms (`%27%20--`, `%27%23`, `%2527--`) are detected.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora for H2 (names with apostrophes are covered).
**Tests.**
- Table (200) / proptest (evasion permutations) / fuzz; benign gate.
**Notes.** The password-kind relaxation is `DEV-V5-003`-adjacent policy documented in C4.6 and visible in S-057.

### T-0267 · Hard family H3: UNION-based extraction and column probing
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0264 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Detect result-set injection attempts.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the `UNION [ALL|DISTINCT] SELECT` detector over the canonical view and token stream (comments/whitespace/versioned comments between tokens are already normalized), including `UNION` split by comments (`UN/**/ION` is not valid SQL, so ignore) and `UNION` with `(SELECT ...)` parentheses.
2. Implement column-count probing detection: `ORDER BY <n>` / `GROUP BY <n>` where `n` is a small integer immediately following a breakout quote/closing paren or in a numeric-context field; `NULL,NULL,...` padding in a select list; `SELECT 1,2,3...` literal lists.
3. Implement the **select-after-breakout** rule: after a breakout quote/paren, a `SELECT ... FROM|,|--` shape is hard (subquery injection) even without UNION (`' AND (SELECT ...)`, `' OR EXISTS(SELECT ...)`).
4. Define subtype `union` and `probe`, hardness hard; soft-only for isolated `ORDER BY 5` without breakout in free text (2).
5. Add metadata functions that appear in union payloads (`@@version`, `version()`, `user()`, `database()`, `current_user`, `schema()`, `concat(`, `group_concat(`) to strengthen confidence (bonus soft weight, not required for hard).
6. Write rule metadata and fixtures (≥ 60) including obfuscated forms, case variations, versioned comments, whitespace variants, JSON-escaped, double-encoded.
7. Define counter-examples: "union station", "selection of items from our store", "order by 5 pm" (prose), SQL tutorial text with `UNION` in a sentence without `SELECT` adjacent.
8. Link ATK-003, ATK-004 and test benign.
**Deliverables.**
- H3 detector, rules, fixtures, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL--`, `1 UNION ALL SELECT username,password FROM users`, `-1 union/**/select 1,@@version,3`, `' ORDER BY 5--` are hard.
- A2: counter-examples do not match.
- A3: encoded and obfuscated forms (double URL encoding, comment-as-space, case mix) match.
- A4: sentences containing both words far apart (more than 3 tokens) do not hard-match.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table (150) / proptest / benign gate.
**Notes.** Prose heuristics only affect soft signals; hard shapes require grammatical adjacency.

### T-0268 · Hard family H4: stacked queries and dangerous statements
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0264 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Detect statement chaining and administrative procedure abuse.
**Steps.**
1. Implement detection of `;` (statement terminator) followed (ignoring whitespace/comments) by DDL/DML/administrative keywords: `drop`, `alter`, `create`, `truncate`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `exec`, `execute`, `declare`, `shutdown`, `grant`, `revoke`, `merge`, `call`, `copy`, `load`, `attach`, `pragma`, `vacuum`, `set`, `use`, `begin`, `commit`, `rollback`, `waitfor`, `backup`, `restore`.

4. Handle `;` encoded as `%3b`, `&#59;`, fullwidth `；` (folded), and splitting by comments.
5. Handle Class B payload fixtures (e.g., `'; DROP TABLE users--`) strictly as inert strings in tests and the inspect API (never live to non-sandbox targets).
6. Write rule metadata; counter-examples: CSS or JS code in free-text fields with semicolons and words like "update" or "set" ("Please update; set up later"), semicolon-separated lists in prose.
7. Link ATK-005, ATK-022; create fixtures (≥ 60).
8. Validate against benign corpora.
**Deliverables.**
- H4 detector, rules, fixtures, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `'; DROP TABLE users--`, `1; UPDATE users SET admin=1`, `; EXEC xp_cmdshell('...')`, `'; shutdown --` are hard.
- A2: prose with semicolons and verbs ("Please update; set it later") is not hard.
- A3: encoded semicolons are detected.
- A4: `INTO OUTFILE` and `COPY ... TO PROGRAM` shapes are hard.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table (120) / proptest / benign gate.

**Objective.** Detect inference and exfiltration payloads based on SQL function usage.

Implement function-call detection (token `Function` followed by `(`, case-insensitive, whitespace/comment tolerant) for: `sleep`, `benchmark`, `pg_sleep`, `waitfor delay|time`, `dbms_pipe.receive_message`, `dbms_lock.sleep`, `randomblob` (with large argument), `generate_series` (large), `extractvalue`, `updatexml`, `exp(~`, `floor(rand(`, `utl_inaddr.get_host_address`, `utl_http.request`, `xp_dirtree`, `xp_fileexist`, `load_file`, `lo_import`, `pg_read_file`, `openrowset`, `opendatasource`, `dbms_xmlgen`, `ctxsys.drithsx.sn`, plus clause forms `into outfile`, `into dumpfile`.

**Notes.** Developer-oriented sites need the `code_friendly` option documented in S-057.

### T-0271 · Authentication-bypass idioms (H7) and evasion constructs (H8)
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0265, T-0266 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Close the remaining classic idioms and the encoding/obfuscation tricks that attackers use against signature filters.
**Steps.**
1. H7 explicit idioms: `' or ''='`, `'='`, `' or 1 --`, `admin' or '1'='1'--`, `' or username like '%admin%'--`, `' having 1=1--`, `' group by x having 1=1--`, `admin' and 1=1--`, `') or true--`, `' or 'a'='a`; implement as semantic checks reusing H1/H2 evaluators with subtype `auth_bypass`.
2. H8 evasion: version-comment keywords (`/*!50000select*/`), hex/CHAR/CHR construction of quotes or keywords near SQL tokens (`concat(0x27,...)`, `char(39)`), scientific-notation glue (`1e0union`, `1.e(`), `%00` inside keywords, concatenation of keyword parts, mixed-case keywords with comment-as-space, nested comments, `+`/`%0b` whitespace variants, and unusual separators (`/*!*/`, `\N`, `+-` sign noise before numbers).
3. Implement **normalization-bypass resilience**: for every H-family detection, run the detector on `decoded`, `canonical` and a third *aggressive* view (strip all non-alphanumeric/space noise characters from candidate keyword runs) used only for keyword adjacency checks; flag `evasion.*` subtypes when detection occurs only in the aggressive view (soft 4, upgraded to hard when combined with breakout).
4. Implement double-parse differentials: detect inputs where `decoded` and `raw` yield different SQL interpretations (one benign, one malicious) and treat as hard (`evasion.differential`).
5. Handle parameter pollution splits: concatenated duplicates view is analyzed with the same detectors (T-0240).
6. Write rule metadata and fixtures (≥ 100) covering the full C4.8 catalog items 1 to 12, 14, 15, 17 to 20 (transport-level ones are tested at the proxy layer).
7. Counter-examples for evasion rules: legitimate uses of fullwidth characters in Asian text, scientific notation in numeric fields ("1e5" as a number), legitimate hex strings (colors `#ff00aa`, hashes).
8. Validate against benign corpora; add tests for the `aggressive` view limits.
**Deliverables.**
- H7/H8 logic, aggressive view, fixtures, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: each C4.8 evasion item has at least 5 fixtures that are detected as hard (or soft with explicit documented reason).
- A2: legitimate CJK, hex colors, hashes and scientific notation do not trigger.
- A3: differential interpretations are flagged.
- A4: detection results are stable under 3 levels of re-encoding.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table (250) / proptest (transformations of the mandated set) / fuzz.
**Notes.** The proptest transformation set is the executable form of C4.8.

### T-0272 · Field-kind context policy and learned parameter shapes
`P14` `[DP][API][SEC]` · deps: T-0251, T-0265, T-0266 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Apply the C4.6 policy table and add optional positive-security learning.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the policy table lookups for SQLi families by field kind and strictness (Balanced/Paranoid), including `code_friendly` and `shared` options, and expose them through the verdict explanation.
2. Implement benign-name safeguards: apostrophes inside names/addresses never contribute to hard families unless followed by SQL syntax; `#` as number sign is only a comment signal after a quote.
3. Implement **learning mode** (opt-in): observe legitimate traffic (requests that returned 2xx/3xx and had no matches) per (path pattern, method, parameter name) and record shape statistics: character class histogram, min/max length, numeric-only ratio, enum cardinality; store only aggregates (no values) in `param_schemas.observed` with sample counts, requiring a minimum of 500 samples and 7 days before suggestions.
4. Implement enforcement modes for learned shapes: `log` (record deviations as soft signals), `enforce` (deviations score as soft 3; hard families remain independent); exceptions allowed; never enforce on parameters with high variance.
5. Implement UI hooks for S-057 (suggestions list, accept/reject, enforce toggle) and APIs.
6. Implement privacy safeguards: the learner never stores values, only aggregate histograms with k-anonymity thresholds (do not store categories with fewer than 20 distinct observations); reset and delete controls.
7. Write tests with synthetic traffic generated through the real proxy harness.
8. Document the privacy model in the privacy page and S-057.
**Deliverables.**
- policy lookup, learner, APIs, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: policy outcomes match the C4.6 table for all kind x family combinations (table test).
- A2: the learner stores no raw values (schema and database inspection test).
- A3: deviations from learned numeric-only parameters add soft score only in enforce mode.
- A4: learned shapes can be reset and deleted.
- A5: `code_friendly` lowers soft weights but not hard detections.
**Tests.**
- Table tests; integration with the proxy harness; privacy inspection test.
**Notes.** V4 of the shield (C3.3).

### T-0273 · SQLi ban policy: from hard hit to `BanIntent`
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0252, T-0265, T-0266 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Encode C4.10 as an explicit, testable decision table inside the engine and policy layer.
**Steps.**
1. Implement `sqli_ban_intent(verdict_matches, request_ctx, site_policy) -> Option<BanIntent>` that applies the decision table of C4.10 (mode, hardness, cross-site context, soft score blocks, allowlists, never-ban hints) and returns the intent with `PolicyBranch` identifiers (`hard_hit`, `hard_hit_cross_site`, `soft_score_repeat`, `password_h2_soft`, `paranoid_hard`, `monitor_would_ban`).
2. Implement cross-site context extraction from the request context: `Sec-Fetch-Site` (`cross-site`, `same-site`), `Sec-Fetch-Dest` (subresource destinations), `Sec-Fetch-Mode`, `Referer`/`Origin` mismatch heuristics (documented), treating missing headers as no browser context.
3. Implement the soft-score repeat rule (three score-blocks from the same key within 10 minutes → ban intent in Balanced; first in Paranoid), reading the recent-activity counters through an injected trait (the real store arrives in P16/P17).
4. Implement attack-diversity input (distinct categories within 10 minutes) as an injected counter query (V15).
5. Implement the TTL ladder hint (`ttl_step_hint`) from offence counts (injected) and scope selection (site vs org) from policy.
6. Write a decision-table test with ≥ 120 rows covering all combinations (mode x hardness x context x allowlist x kind x strictness) and property tests (a cross-site request never yields a ban intent; a hard hit in block mode outside cross-site context always yields one unless never-ban).
7. Document the table in `docs/BAN-POLICY.md` with the same IDs as test rows.
8. Surface `would_ban` in monitor/log modes for the UI.
**Deliverables.**
- policy module, docs, decision-table tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: all 120 rows pass; the table in docs is generated from the test data (no drift).
- A2: no ban intent arises from cross-site subresource requests (property test).
- A3: monitor mode yields `would_ban` without bans.
- A4: password H2 behavior matches C4.6 under both strictness levels.
- A5: the soft-score repeat rule behaves per specification with an injected clock.
**Tests.**
- Table/proptest; doc-generation test.
**Notes.** The ban storage/enforcement and TTL ladder are P16 (T-0315 to T-0332); this task is the decision logic.

### T-0274 · Auth-endpoint SQLi mode and the success-after-attack tripwire
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0225, T-0273 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Treat login and similar endpoints with extra strictness and detect actual bypasses in monitor mode.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the strict profile for declared/detected auth endpoints: every parameter is inspected (no prefix shortcuts), password-kind soft relaxations apply per strictness, hard families unchanged, and thresholds tightened by 1 (min 3) for soft scores.
2. Implement response-based learning per auth endpoint: record the distribution of response status classes and `Location` patterns (status 302 to dashboard vs 200 login page with errors, 401/403) as aggregates, and classify outcomes into `success_like`, `failure_like`, `unknown` (confidence tracked); owner can correct via UI.
3. Implement the **V13 tripwire** in `monitor`/`log` modes: if a request matching a hard SQLi family to an auth endpoint is followed by a `success_like` response from the origin, emit a **critical** event `possible_auth_bypass` with Ray ID, endpoint and subtype, create an attention item, and notify owners immediately; in `block` mode such requests are blocked so the tripwire cannot fire (the event type `blocked_auth_bypass_attempt` is used instead).
4. Implement per-account/IP interplay hooks: attempts with hard SQLi against auth endpoints also count toward credential-stuffing detection (P17).
5. Ensure that error responses for blocked auth requests are identical to other blocks (no hint of special treatment).
6. Test with the Vuln-Lab login endpoint in lab mode later; now with a controllable local origin that implements a vulnerable-like login (test fixture inside tests only, not shipped).
7. Add metrics (`MET-hdd_auth_endpoint_attacks_total{kind}`).
8. Document how the tripwire helps owners discover that their site was exploitable.
**Deliverables.**
- strict profile, response learner, tripwire, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: in monitor mode, a hard SQLi login request that the (test) origin accepts triggers the critical `possible_auth_bypass` event once.
- A2: in block mode, the same request is blocked and no tripwire fires.
- A3: the response learner classifies success/failure patterns after N samples with confidence.
- A4: block responses on auth endpoints are indistinguishable from other blocks.
- A5: metrics increment correctly.
**Tests.**
- Integration with a test-only vulnerable-like origin and the proxy harness; unit: classifier; browser: attention item display.
**Notes.** The test origin lives under `tests/` and is never shipped; the shipped lab app is `hdd-vulnlab` (P28).

### T-0275 · NoSQL, LDAP, XPath and GraphQL injection detectors
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0250, T-0264 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Cover non-SQL query-language injections that target the same forms.
**Steps.**
1. NoSQL: detect operator keys in JSON and bracket notation in forms/queries (`$ne`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$in`, `$nin`, `$regex`, `$where`, `$or`, `$and`, `$not`, `$exists`, `$expr`, `$function`), JavaScript injection in `$where` and string contexts (`';sleep(5000);'`, `||1==1`, `this.password.match`, `return true`), and Mongo-style auth bypass (`{"username":{"$ne":null},"password":{"$ne":null}}`).
2. LDAP: filter metacharacters and structures in contexts expecting values (`*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*`, `)(|(`, `*)(objectClass=*`, `\2a` escapes), with hardness hard when parentheses and boolean operators `&|!` form a filter shape.
3. XPath: predicates and functions in value contexts (`' or '1'='1` is covered by SQL; add `//*`, `/*[1]`, `count(/*)`, `string-length(`, `substring(name(`, `text()=`, `contains(`, `] | //`), hard when XPath axes/functions are used after a breakout.
4. GraphQL injection: injection of query fragments into variable strings (`" }) { __schema`), unusual braces in `variables`, and use of aliases to brute force (counts), integrating with T-0250 metrics.
5. Define subtypes (`nosql_operator`, `nosql_js`, `ldap_filter`, `xpath`, `graphql`) and categories (`nosqli`, `ldapi`, `xpathi`) with ATK links (ATK-025 to ATK-028, ATK-056).
6. Write rule metadata, fixtures (≥ 120) and counter-examples (JSON containing `$` in legitimate keys like currency fields with field kind awareness: keys beginning with `$` are rare; allowlist for known frameworks like MongoDB drivers is not needed because operator keys from untrusted clients are exactly the attack).
7. Handle content types: JSON bodies and bracket-notation arrays in form/query (`user[$ne]=`).
8. Validate against benign corpora.
**Deliverables.**
- detectors, rules, fixtures, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: Mongo operator injection in JSON and bracket forms is hard.
- A2: LDAP filter breakouts are hard; ordinary parentheses in names are not.
- A3: XPath function/axis injection is hard after breakout; prose with slashes is not.
- A4: GraphQL variable injection is flagged with correct subtype.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table (200) / proptest / benign gate.
**Notes.** Applications using `$`-prefixed keys legitimately can add scoped exceptions (documented).

### T-0276 · Write-path hardening and second-order injection mitigation
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0272 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Reduce stored-payload risks (stored SQL, XSS, template payloads) at the point where data enters the origin.
**Steps.**
1. Define "write requests": POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE bodies and query parameters on those methods; apply stricter policy on **storage-likely fields** (free text, names, titles, bios, comments, addresses) with lowered soft thresholds (-1) and hard-family strictness (no `code_friendly` relaxation for names/titles).
2. Implement the **no-prefix-skip** rule: write requests under the shield are always inspected fully up to the field cap (no early exit on benign-looking prefixes).
3. Implement second-order indicators: payloads that are harmless in the first request but contain SQL control sequences destined for later concatenation (quote + comment markers in stored fields like display names) are flagged soft 3 with subtype `second_order_write` and event tags for analysts.
4. Implement outbound cross-check (links to P21): responses that echo previously stored suspicious content (DB error strings or script payloads) raise `data_leak`/`xss_stored_response` signals.
5. Implement policy options: `reject_suspicious_writes` (block soft second-order indicators) default off in Balanced and on in Paranoid.
6. Add UI controls (S-057) and explanations of residual risk.
7. Write tests with write-path fixtures (profile updates, comments).
8. Link ATK-019, ATK-071, ATK-282/283 heuristics.
**Deliverables.**
- write-path logic, options, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: suspicious stored-field payloads in write requests are flagged with subtype `second_order_write`.
- A2: Paranoid rejects them; Balanced records them.
- A3: GET requests are unaffected by the stricter write rules.
- A4: the UI states the residual risk (second-order attacks may still pass).
- A5: legitimate names with apostrophes and hyphens are unaffected.
**Tests.**
- Table tests; benign gate; integration with the proxy harness for write flows.
**Notes.** This is mitigation, not a guarantee; documented as a known limitation.

### T-0277 · Time-based attack behavioral detector
`P14` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0269, T-0261 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Catch blind time-based injection even when the payload evades static signatures.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the latency-correlation detector in the proxy: for each (site, path pattern, method), maintain a baseline of origin response time (EWMA and p95 over a rolling window); record per-request latency and the request's parameter shape signature (names only).
2. Flag anomalies: requests from one client key that produce origin latency exceeding baseline p99 by more than 3 s repeatedly (≥ 3 within 60 s) and whose parameters contain any SQL-punctuation soft signal; emit event `time_based_suspected` with a soft score and an attention item.
3. Implement the optional **tarpit-on-suspicion** action: when the same client key sends repeated suspicious time-delay-shaped requests, respond to subsequent suspicious requests with a bounded delay (≤ 2 s, concurrency capped) to waste attacker time without consuming unbounded resources; off by default and only in Paranoid.
4. Ensure the detector does not fire on legitimately slow endpoints (baseline learning, minimum sample counts, per-path learned slowness).
5. Implement metrics and events; integrate with the ban policy as a soft intent.
6. Test with a local origin implementing controllable `sleep` endpoints and a script that produces blind-style request patterns.
7. Add configuration and UI explanation.
8. Document limitations (requires traffic; thresholds).
**Deliverables.**
- detector, optional tarpit, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a blind time-based probing pattern against a slow-on-demand local endpoint is flagged within 3 probes.
- A2: legitimately slow endpoints (baseline-slow) are not flagged.
- A3: the tarpit respects caps (duration, concurrency) and is off by default.
- A4: events carry subtype `time_based_suspected` with no payload values.
- A5: the detector adds under 10 µs to the hot path.
**Tests.**
- Integration with the proxy harness; unit: baseline math; benchmark.
**Notes.** Static detection (H5) remains the primary defense.

### T-0280 · sqlmap campaign harness (lab-only) and coverage measurement
`P14` `[QA][LAB][SEC]` · deps: T-0261, T-0278 · size: L · owner: qa
**Objective.** Measure how well the shield withstands a real automated SQL injection tool, safely.
**Steps.**
1. Define the lab scope: the harness runs only in `lab` mode against Vuln-Lab addresses or a builder-local deliberately vulnerable test origin, through HDD in `monitor` mode (coverage measurement) and `block` mode (containment), never against live profile hosts (TargetGuard enforced; oracle tools are invoked only via `hdd-acceptance` lab mode).
2. Implement the campaign runner that drives sqlmap with documented parameters: levels 1 to 3, risk 1 to 2, techniques `BEUSTQ` as lab allows, `--batch`, threads 1, delay set to respect the lab profile (500 req/s cap, 10 minutes), user agent default and `--random-agent`, `--tamper` lists (a published set: `space2comment`, `randomcase`, `charencode`, `charunicodeencode`, `between`, `equaltolike`, `apostrophemask`, `apostrophenullencode`, `base64encode`, `percentage`, `space2plus`, `space2randomblank`, `versionedkeywords`, `versionedmorekeywords`), and separate runs per tamper and one combined.
3. Capture every request sqlmap sends via HDD's event stream in `monitor` mode (`would_block` flags) and the origin-side log (the lab app records requests), then compute: total requests, injection-bearing requests (heuristic: contains the injection marker or payload shape per sqlmap's payload files as understood from request logs, labeled by the lab origin), flagged vs unflagged counts, unflagged classes with examples, per-tamper coverage, time to first hard hit.
4. In `block` mode run the same campaigns and measure: whether any data extraction succeeded (the lab app logs canary extraction events), time until the IP ban (once P16 lands; before that, until first 403), and the number of requests that reached the origin.
5. Record results in `acceptance-lab/sqlmap/*.json` with raw logs and SHA-256; produce a Markdown summary with the target thresholds: coverage ≥ 95% of injection-bearing requests in monitor mode; zero extraction in block mode.
6. Analyze unflagged request classes, create new fixtures (not tuned on held-out) and rule improvements; rerun until thresholds are met or document the residual with a diagnosis (failure budget R-14).
7. Add similar harness stubs for other oracles (nikto, wapiti, nuclei, ZAP baseline, ffuf) used in later phases.
8. Document how to reproduce and the safety constraints (lab only).
**Deliverables.**
- campaign runner in `hdd-acceptance` lab mode, reports, new fixtures
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the harness refuses non-lab targets (guard test).
- A2: monitor-mode coverage report is produced with the exact figure and unflagged classes.
- A3: block-mode runs show zero successful extraction (lab canary log).
- A4: results are reproducible with the same seeds and recorded tool versions.
- A5: improvements are fed back as fixtures without using held-out data.
**Tests.**
- Harness self-tests with a recorded local fixture of sqlmap-like requests (inert); the real campaign is a lab run (`UNVERIFIED(capability_not_supplied)` without a lab).
**Notes.** The harness is the source for the claim wording in S-003 (tested claim with exact figures and limits).
