Implement the matrix runner in `hdd-acceptance`: cross product of the six mandated payloads and the core variants against every vector (path, query, form, JSON, XML, multipart text, multipart filename, cookie, header) and each field kind (password, username, email, numeric id, search, free text), using the inspect API; assert `would_block=true`, category `sqli`, expected subtype, and `would_ban=true` where policy requires (except documented password H2 and cross-site cases).
2. Implement the proxy-level path: through the walking-skeleton proxy on the builder or pilot **sandbox hostname** (live) using the inspect-first gate, GET/query vectors only on `test_hostname`, body vectors only on `sandbox_hostname`; one payload at a time with unban between (until ban storage lands, rely on 60 s TTL once available), recording 403 + Ray ID + event.
3. Implement the benign suite run through the same paths: zero blocks.
4. Implement cross-site tests (`Sec-Fetch-*` headers) expecting blocks without bans once bans exist (AC-34 hooks).
5. Implement reporting: matrix tables with PASS/FAIL per cell, counts, failure details (minimal reproducers), and evidence hashes.
6. Add failure budget handling: failing cells open diagnoses.
7. Integrate with `cargo xtask acceptance --only AC-39` and record the lab-dependent portion (AC-38/AC-39 lab proof) as `UNVERIFIED(stage_not_reached)` until P16/P28.
8. Document the safety gating (Class A/B rules).
**Deliverables.**
- check implementation, reports
**Acceptance.**
- A1: matrix cells for the six mandated payloads are 100% PASS at the engine and inspect API level.
- A2: benign suite yields zero false positives in every context.
- A3: live sandbox runs respect the inspect-first gate (an altered revision fails the test).
- A4: body vectors never target `test_hostname`.
- A5: the report lists cell counts and the status taxonomy.
**Tests.**
- The matrix suite; meta-test with a deliberately disabled rule confirming failure detection.
**Notes.** Full proof with bans and a vulnerable origin completes in P16 (T-0330) and P28.

## PHASE P15: All other attack detectors (T-0285 to T-0314) · milestone M6 · gate G15

Requirement prefix `DET`. Goal: implement the detector families of the attack coverage matrix (Part C, C5) beyond SQL injection, using the same engine rules: pure functions, linear-time patterns, structural tokenizers where syntax matters, rule files with examples and counter-examples, fixtures in Class A/B/C form, benign gates, and ATK traceability enforced by `xtask attack-matrix check` (T-0313).

For each detector task the common deliverables are: rule files under `crates/hdd-waf-core/rules/<category>/`, a detector module where logic is structural, fixtures under `tests/fixtures/<group>/` (Class A for live-safe GET shapes, Class B/C inert strings), held-out sets under `heldout/`, benign counter-examples added to the corpora, proptest permutations of the evasion catalog applicable to the family, fuzz coverage through `inspect_request`, metrics and event subtypes, docs for the rules reference, and ATK links.

Every detector defines its hard/soft split explicitly, its field-kind behavior (C4.6 equivalents), and the ban policy branch (hard hits ban outside cross-site context unless the matrix row says `B`).

Gate G15 passes when: every ATK row marked as detected has fixtures and tests; held-out detection ≥ 95% per group; the benign gate stays at zero false positives; the mutation score for new modules ≥ 80%; fuzz smoke is clean; and inspection latency budgets still hold with all detectors enabled.

### T-0285 · XSS: HTML and JavaScript-context tokenizer and vector library
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0262 · size: XL · owner: waf
**Objective.** Detect script injection by understanding HTML/JS context rather than only matching strings.
**Steps.**
1. Implement an HTML tokenizer (`html5gum` or equivalent, wrapped for bounded memory) over the `decoded` and html-canonical views producing tag open/close, attribute name/value, comment, doctype, and text tokens, with tolerant parsing for broken markup.
2. Implement detectors on tokens: `<script>` start tags; event-handler attributes (`on*` for the full HTML event list, case-folded, with whitespace/slash separators); URL-valued attributes (`href`, `src`, `action`, `formaction`, `data`, `poster`, `srcset`, `xlink:href`, `background`) carrying `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `data:text/html`, `data:image/svg+xml`; dangerous tags (`iframe`, `object`, `embed`, `base`, `meta http-equiv=refresh`, `link rel=import`, `svg` with scripts, `math`, `template` with events); `srcdoc`; `style` with `expression(`/`url(javascript:`/`-moz-binding`.
3. Implement JS-context detectors for reflected payloads in script/attribute contexts: `</script>` breakouts, quote breakouts into handlers (`" onmouseover="`, `'-alert(1)-'`), template literal injection, `eval(`, `Function(`, `setTimeout("string"`, `document.cookie`, `document.write`, `innerHTML`, `location=`, `window.name` with suspicious patterns.
4. Define categories/subtypes (`xss`: `script_tag`, `event_handler`, `uri_scheme`, `dangerous_tag`, `css`, `dom_sink`, `breakout`) with hardness rules: hard when a complete executable construct is present (tag + handler, scheme URL in a URL attribute, `<script` start tag), soft for lone keywords (`alert`, `onerror` without tag context), field-kind relaxations for code-friendly sites (docs, blogs) limited to soft weights.
5. Provide the XSS fixture vectors (Class A: `<script>alert(1)</script>`, `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>`, `<svg/onload=alert(1)>`, `javascript:alert(1)`, `"><script>`, etc.) and counter-examples (legitimate text about HTML, code samples in markdown fields with explicit code fences are still hard in non-code-friendly sites but soft in `code_friendly`).
6. Write rule metadata linked to ATK-061 to ATK-066, ATK-073, ATK-075.
7. Test across vectors including headers (`Referer`, `User-Agent`) and cookies.
8. Benchmark the tokenizer (p50 under 30 µs for 200-byte strings that pass the prefilter; strings without `<`, `>`, quotes, `javascript:` skip tokenization).
**Deliverables.**
- `xss` module, rules, fixtures (≥ 150), tests, bench
**Acceptance.**
- A1: all Class A XSS fixtures are hard in query, form, JSON, header and cookie vectors.
- A2: counter-examples are not hard.
- A3: the tokenizer is bounded (fuzz and adversarial nesting tests).
- A4: strings without relevant characters skip tokenization (performance test).
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora (including HTML-rich comment samples marked benign soft-only where code-friendly).
**Tests.**
- Table (250) / proptest / fuzz; benign gate.
**Notes.** CSP and response sanitization are complementary and covered in T-0287 and the outbound phase.

6. Define subtypes (`metachar_binary`, `substitution`, `pipe_shell`, `reverse_shell`, `powershell`, `obfuscated`, `arg_injection`) and hardness rules; field-kind relaxations (search/free text: semicolon-binary pairs hard only if grammar-valid).

Implement host classification via a WHATWG-like URL parser with alternative IP representations: decimal (`2130706433`), hex (`0x7f000001`), octal (`0177.0.0.1`), dotted-mixed, IPv6 (`[::1]`, `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`), zero-compression forms, `0.0.0.0`, `localhost` and subdomains, DNS-rebinding services (`nip.io`, `sslip.io`, `xip.io`, `lvh.me`, `localtest.me`, `*.localhost`), userinfo tricks (`http://good.example@127.0.0.1/`), fragments/backslash confusion, and unicode dots.
3. Classify targets: loopback, private (RFC 1918, CGNAT), link-local (including `169.254.169.254`, `fd00:ec2::254`), metadata hostnames (`metadata.google.internal`, `metadata.azure.com`? use `169.254.169.254` and named hosts list, `100.100.100.200`), cloud-internal suffixes (`.internal`, `.local`, `.svc`, `.cluster.local`), unspecified, multicast.
4. Detect dangerous schemes: `gopher`, `dict`, `ftp`, `file`, `ldap(s)`, `jar`, `netdoc`, `tftp`, `sftp`, `smb`, `php`, `data` in URL-typed fields.
5. Detect OAST/callback domains (`oast.*`, `interact.sh`, `burpcollaborator.net`, `canarytokens.com`, `requestbin`, `webhook.site`, `pipedream`, `.invalid` fixtures) as soft 3 (benign usage exists) rising to hard when combined with internal targets or in fields not expected to be URLs.
6. Hardness: internal/metadata/scheme-abuse targets are hard in URL-typed fields and soft 4 elsewhere; define subtypes (`loopback`, `private`, `metadata`, `scheme`, `encoded_ip`, `rebinding_name`, `oast`).
7. Fixtures for ATK-091 to ATK-097 (all textual) and counter-examples (legitimate external URLs, links in comments, `example.com` references).
8. Benign gate and fuzz on URL parsing.
**Deliverables.**
- URL canonicalizer, SSRF detector, rules, fixtures (≥ 150), tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: all alternative IP encodings of loopback and metadata addresses are classified correctly (table of 80).
- A2: userinfo/fragment/backslash tricks are resolved to the true host before classification.
- A3: external legitimate URLs in URL-typed fields pass.
- A4: the shared URL classifier is the same code used by the egress SSRF guard tests (property test equivalence on the host classification subset).
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table (200) / proptest on IP representations / fuzz URL parser.
**Notes.** ATK-091 to ATK-097; same classification table as T-0009 to avoid drift.

### T-0294 · CRLF, header and email-header injection
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0241 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Block newline-based injection into headers, logs and mail.
**Steps.**
1. Detect CR (`%0d`), LF (`%0a`), CRLF, Unicode line separators (U+2028/9, U+0085) in parameters, path, headers and cookies after decoding, particularly when followed by header-like text (`Set-Cookie:`, `Location:`, `Content-Type:`, `Content-Length:`, `HTTP/1.1 200`, `Bcc:`, `To:`, `Cc:`, `Subject:`, `MIME-Version`).
2. Hardness: CRLF followed by a header name pattern is hard (`crlf`, `response_splitting`, `email_header`); lone newlines in multi-line fields (textarea) are normal and not flagged except in single-line field kinds (`email`, `username`, `subject`, `name`, `url`, `redirect`); headers containing CR/LF/NUL are rejected at the protocol layer (R) before inspection.
3. Detect HTTP response splitting payloads (`%0d%0aContent-Length:0%0d%0a%0d%0aHTTP/1.1 200`), log forging shapes (`\n[ERROR]`, fake log lines) as soft 2.
4. Detect SMTP command injection (`\r\nMAIL FROM:`, `RCPT TO:`, `DATA`) and IMAP/POP injection tokens in mail-related fields.
5. Provide field-kind sensitivity: `subject`, `from`, `to`, `reply-to`, `email`, `name` fields (name-based inference) treat any newline as hard.
6. Fixtures for ATK-042 to ATK-045 and counter-examples (multi-line comments, addresses with newlines in textarea fields).
7. Add tests for header/URL contexts and multipart part names.
8. Benign gate and fuzz.
**Deliverables.**
- detector, rules, fixtures (≥ 80), tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: CRLF plus header-name injections are hard.
- A2: newlines in textarea fields are not flagged.
- A3: single-line field kinds with newlines are hard.
- A4: SMTP/IMAP command injections are detected.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora (multi-line text included).
**Tests.**
- Table (120) / fuzz.
**Notes.** Protocol-layer rejection of CR/LF/NUL in raw header values is in T-0356.

- A5: relative paths never match.
**Tests.**
- Table (120) / integration with proxy harness / browser (allowlist UI).

### T-0296 · Deserialization signatures
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0262 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Block serialized-object payloads for common runtimes.
**Steps.**
1. Implement format detectors on parameters, cookies, headers and bodies after base64/URL decoding attempts (bounded: up to two decode layers when the string looks like base64): Java (`aced0005`, `rO0AB`, `H4sIAAAAAAAA` gzip+base64 of Java streams), PHP (`O:\d+:"`, `a:\d+:{`, `s:\d+:"`, `C:\d+:"`, phar metadata signatures), Python pickle (protocol opcodes, `gASV`, `cos\nsystem`, `c__builtin__`, `!!python/object`), .NET (BinaryFormatter `AAEAAAD/////`, ViewState `/wEP`, `TypeNameHandling` `$type`), Ruby (`\x04\x08` Marshal header, `!ruby/object`), Node (`_$$ND_FUNC$$_`), YAML (`!!` tags), Jackson/Fastjson polymorphism (`@type`, `autoType`, `["java.lang.`, `com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl`, `ldap://` within JSON).
2. Add gadget-name indicators (`ysoserial` common gadget class names: `CommonsCollections`, `Transformer`, `InvokerTransformer`, `TemplatesImpl`, `JdbcRowSetImpl`, `BadAttributeValueExpException`, `Spring`, `Groovy`) as hard when seen decoded.
3. Hardness: hard for magic bytes in places where binary serialization is not expected (cookies, query, form fields typed unknown), soft for protocols declared by the owner (an app legitimately using ViewState with MAC: ViewState structure detection is soft unless it fails typical shapes or includes gadget names).
4. Implement detection of padding/oracle probing patterns (repeated ViewState mutations) as repetition soft signals.
5. Define subtypes (`java_serialized`, `php_object`, `pickle`, `dotnet`, `ruby_marshal`, `node_serialize`, `yaml_tag`, `json_polymorphic`) and ATK links (ATK-105 to ATK-111).
6. Fixtures (inert strings, Class A for GET-safe shapes like `O:8:"stdClass":0:{}`), counter-examples (legitimate base64 images, JWTs, long tokens, ASP.NET ViewState with MAC on declared sites).
7. Benign gate and fuzz on decode attempts (bounded).
8. Document owner options for apps that legitimately use serialization.
**Deliverables.**
- detector, rules, fixtures (≥ 100), tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: serialized object magic in cookies and parameters is hard.
- A2: JWTs and image base64 are not flagged.
- A3: gadget names are hard when decoded.
- A4: declared legitimate ViewState sites get soft handling only.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table (150) / fuzz / benign gate.
**Notes.** Bounded decoding prevents decode-bomb issues.

### T-0297 · File upload defenses
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0249, T-0262 · size: XL · owner: waf
**Objective.** Block malicious uploads (webshells, polyglots, bombs) at the edge.
**Steps.**
1. Inspect multipart filenames: normalize (decode, strip path components, handle `filename*`, null bytes, trailing dots/spaces, Unicode RTL override tricks (U+202E) flagged), extension analysis (all extensions in double/multiple extension names: `shell.php.jpg`, `shell.jpg.php`, `shell.php;.jpg`, `shell.pHp`, `.phtml`, `.php5`, `.phar`, `.jsp`, `.jspx`, `.asp`, `.aspx`, `.ashx`, `.cgi`, `.pl`, `.py`, `.sh`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.exe`, `.dll`, `.msi`, `.jar`, `.war`, `.htaccess`, `.user.ini`, `web.config`, `.config`), with a deny list and per-site allow list of permitted extensions for upload endpoints.
2. Inspect content: magic-byte sniffing (`infer`) vs declared type vs extension (mismatch soft 3 or hard when executable types hide behind image extensions), polyglot detection (valid image header plus embedded `<?php`, `<script`, `<%`), webshell signatures (`eval(`, `base64_decode(`, `system(`, `passthru(`, `shell_exec(`, `assert(`, `$_POST[`, `$_REQUEST[`, `c99`, `r57`, `b374k`, `ASPXSpy`, `cmd.exe /c`), SVG/HTML scripts, archives (entry names with traversal, absolute paths, excessive entries, ratio bombs; nested archives depth cap), Office documents with macros indicators (`vbaProject.bin`), EXIF fields with script content (bounded EXIF parser).
3. Enforce size/dimension caps: per-file limits by endpoint policy, image dimension headers (PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP) checked for pixel-flood (width*height cap 100 MP), animated GIF frame counts.
4. Implement per-site upload endpoint declarations (path patterns where uploads are expected, allowed extensions/types/size) and treatment of unexpected multipart on other endpoints (soft 3, ATK-134).
5. Hardness: executable extensions, webshell signatures and polyglots are hard (`upload` category); size/bomb violations are `R` (reject 413/422 with event) not bans unless repeated.
6. Streaming design: inspect headers and the first 64 KB of each part plus filename immediately; for larger parts scan sliding windows up to the part cap, discarding after scan to bound memory; the proxy streams the remainder to the origin only after a pass decision on the prefix with an abort path (connection reset) if later windows match (documented: partial data may have reached the origin in streaming mode; configurable `buffer_uploads_before_forward` for stricter sites).
7. Fixtures (inert byte strings generated at runtime in tests; no real malware), counter-examples (legitimate images with EXIF, PDFs, zip files with normal entries).
8. Benign gate, fuzz (multipart + archive peeking), bounded-memory tests.
**Deliverables.**
- upload inspector, endpoint declarations, rules, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: double-extension and polyglot test files are blocked (generated at runtime).
- A2: archive bombs (descriptor-based) and zip slip names are rejected without extraction.
- A3: image pixel-flood headers are rejected without decoding pixels.
- A4: memory usage per upload inspection stays below 1 MiB beyond streaming buffers (measured).
- A5: legitimate images/PDFs/zips pass.
**Tests.**
- Table (200 generated files) / fuzz / memory tests.
**Notes.** ClamAV-style AV scanning is an optional Tier 2 integration (documented).

### T-0298 · HTTP method policy and request-semantics anomalies
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0262 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Constrain unusual methods and header-based semantics tampering.
**Steps.**
1. Implement method policy: allow `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS` by default; block `TRACE`, `TRACK`, `CONNECT` (protocol-level), `DEBUG`, and unusual WebDAV methods unless the site declares WebDAV; per-path method allowlists configurable (V8).
2. Detect method override headers (`X-HTTP-Method-Override`, `X-HTTP-Method`, `X-Method-Override`, `_method` parameter) and apply policy: ignore-with-log or block when attempting to turn `GET`/`POST` into `DELETE`/`PUT` unless declared.
3. Detect semantic-tampering headers: `X-Original-URL`, `X-Rewrite-URL`, `X-Forwarded-Path`, `X-Custom-IP-Authorization`, `X-Forwarded-For` with internal values when the peer is untrusted (informational because we strip), `X-Host`, `Forwarded` abuse; these are stripped/blocked per C9.3 and counted.
4. Enforce content-type policy: methods with bodies must declare `Content-Type` for declared API endpoints; reject `multipart/form-data` on JSON-only API paths (V8), and reject unusual combos (JSON with `Content-Length: 0`).
5. Detect unusual request-line shapes at the WAF layer that survived the protocol layer: very long paths (policy cap 8 KiB), repeated slashes patterns, `..;` segments, encoded NULs, non-printable characters.
6. Define categories (`method`, `proto`) and ATK links (ATK-150, ATK-151, ATK-057).
7. Fixtures: GET-safe shapes; counter-examples (OPTIONS for CORS preflight, legitimate `PUT` APIs).
8. Benign gate.
**Deliverables.**
- rules, config options, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `TRACE` is blocked by default; CORS preflight `OPTIONS` passes.
- A2: method override headers are handled per policy.
- A3: per-path method allowlists work and are enforced.
- A4: stripped headers are counted and never forwarded.
- A5: zero false positives on benign corpora.
**Tests.**
- Table / integration with proxy harness.
**Notes.** Protocol-level rejections are P18.

### T-0299 · Host header and virtual-host confusion

- rules, router checks, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: SNI/Host mismatch yields 421 and event.
- A2: duplicate and malformed hosts are rejected.

- Table / integration with TLS clients.

### T-0300 · Request-smuggling detection at the WAF layer

6. Link ATK-135 to ATK-141, ATK-146, ATK-155.
7. Fixtures at the byte level (raw socket tests used in P18).
8. Metrics and events.

- detection rules, differential harness, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: embedded request-line-in-body is flagged.
- A2: obfuscated TE headers are rejected.
- A3: differential harness finds zero parsing disagreements on the ambiguity corpus (HDD rejects them).
- A4: events are emitted with subtype and the connection is closed.
- A5: legitimate chunked requests pass.
**Tests.**
- Raw-socket table tests; differential tests; fuzz of the HTTP parser path.
**Notes.** Comprehensive raw-socket testing is AC-14 (T-0373).

**Objective.** Secure upgrade handshakes and bound WebSocket abuse.
**Steps.**
1. Inspect the upgrade handshake as a normal request (all detectors on query, cookies, headers) and enforce `Origin` policy: require `Origin` header to match site hosts or allowlist (CSWSH defense, ATK-184), configurable per path (default on when cookies are present).
2. Enforce limits: maximum concurrent WebSockets per IP and per site, message size (default 1 MiB), message rate (default 100/s per connection), idle timeout, ping/pong requirements, compression settings (disable permessage-deflate by default or cap ratio).
3. Implement optional text-frame inspection (opt-in): inspect text frames with the normal detectors up to a per-frame cap (64 KB) and rate cap; binary frames are not inspected; on a hard hit close the connection with code 1008 and emit events; bans per policy.
4. Implement connection-level fairness (per-tenant caps) and metrics.
5. Handle subprotocols (GraphQL over WS, STOMP, MQTT over WS) without breaking: inspection only for text frames when enabled; protocol-specific parsers are out of scope (documented).
6. UI in S-056 (WebSocket panel).
7. Fixtures: handshake payloads, cross-site handshake attempts; counter-examples (legitimate chat messages with apostrophes).
8. Test with the harness (browser WebSocket clients, hostile frame sequences).
**Deliverables.**
- handshake and frame policy, UI, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: cross-origin handshakes are rejected when policy requires origin match.
- A2: oversized or too-fast messages close the connection with the expected code.
- A3: frame inspection (when enabled) blocks hard hits in text frames.
- A4: per-IP and per-site caps work under load.
- A5: legitimate chat traffic passes (benign corpus).
**Tests.**
- Integration with real sockets and browser clients; fuzz on frame handling.
**Notes.** WebSocket passthrough plumbing is T-0367.

### T-0306 · Scanner and attack-tool fingerprints
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0262 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Identify automated attack tools and ban them on first contact.
**Steps.**
1. Build the tool signature set from original research notes (user agents and request shapes), covering at least: sqlmap, nikto, nmap scripting engine, masscan, zgrab, acunetix, nessus, openvas, wpscan, w3af, zap, burp (default markers), gobuster, dirb, dirbuster, ffuf, feroxbuster, wfuzz, nuclei, whatweb, wapiti, arachni, havij, jaeles, skipfish, httprobe, httpx scanners, `python-requests` default UA (policy: soft), `Go-http-client` (soft), `curl`/`wget` (policy only), empty UA, UA strings with known attack markers.
2. Add payload-marker signatures: sqlmap's characteristic `AND 1=1` patterns with random identifiers, nuclei's `{{interactsh-url}}` residue, scanner header markers (`X-Scan-Memo`, `Acunetix-*`), OAST callback domains in parameters, canary strings (`testing_wvs`, `acunetix`, `nessus`).
3. Define classes: `scanner` (known offensive tool: hard, ban) vs `automation` (generic libraries: soft score + challenge) and allow the owner to exempt their own scanner IPs or a signed header token (`HDD-Scan-Allow: <hmac>` generated per site, short-lived, for the owner's authorized scans; validated in the pipeline; documented).
4. Detect header-set anomalies typical for tools (missing `Accept`, constant `Accept: */*`, header order fingerprint vs UA), feeding bot scoring (P17).
5. Implement update mechanism through signed rule packs (platform rollout) so new tool signatures ship without code releases.
6. Fixtures for ATK-189, ATK-190, ATK-024; counter-examples (legitimate monitoring agents declared by owner, search engines, `curl` used by developers: not hard).
7. Test false positives with a corpus of real browser UAs (500+ strings) and API client UAs.
8. Document how owners authorize their own security scans.
**Deliverables.**
- signature set, owner exemption mechanism, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: known tool UAs are hard and produce bans in block mode.
- A2: browser UA corpus (500+) has zero matches.
- A3: owner exemption token works and expires.
- A4: generic libraries are soft/challenge, not hard.
- A5: signature updates ship via packs without redeploy.
**Tests.**
- Table / corpus tests; integration for exemption tokens.
**Notes.** UA matching alone is weak (spoofable); combined signals appear in T-0340.

### T-0307 · Directory and file enumeration (forced browsing) detector
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0262 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Detect wordlist-driven path brute forcing.
**Steps.**
1. Maintain per (site, client key) sliding counters of responses with status 404 (and 403) for distinct paths, extension diversity (many extensions on one stem), and similarity of sequential paths, using bounded sketches (HyperLogLog for distinct count, small Bloom filter for recent paths).
2. Define thresholds (defaults): ≥ 20 distinct 404 paths in 60 s → challenge; ≥ 60 → ban (`directory_enumeration`); ≥ 10 distinct sensitive-extension probes (`.bak`, `.old`, `.zip`, `.sql`, `.tar.gz`, `.swp`, `~`, `.env`, `.git`) → ban.
3. Account for legitimate crawlers (verified bots) and broken sites with many 404s (learn per-site baseline 404 rate; adjust thresholds; exempt known asset 404 patterns).
4. Detect known wordlist ordering fingerprints (alphabetical or common wordlist sequences) as an additional soft signal.
5. Link with honeypot hits (T-0309) and scanner fingerprints (T-0306) in a unified `recon_score` per client key.
6. Implement events with aggregated counts rather than per-request events to bound storage.
7. Link ATK-191, ATK-192, ATK-088, ATK-087.
8. Test with scripted enumeration (a wordlist of 5,000 paths) in lab/builder against a local origin, and legitimate browsing with broken links.
**Deliverables.**
- detector, thresholds, UI wiring, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a 5,000-path wordlist scan is challenged within 20 requests and banned by 60.
- A2: a legitimate user clicking 5 broken links is unaffected.
- A3: verified bots are exempt.
- A4: memory per client key stays under 2 KB (measured).
- A5: events are aggregated.
**Tests.**
- Simulation tests; proptest on sketches; memory bound tests.
**Notes.** Thresholds are configurable per site (S-062).

### T-0309 · Sensitive-file honeypots, decoys and the tarpit option
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0233, T-0308 · size: M · owner: waf
**Objective.** Implement tripwires that expose recon traffic with minimal risk to real users.

- A3: honeypot conflicts with real routes prevent activation.

### T-0311 · Information-disclosure controls: debug endpoints and error masking
`P15` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0308 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Reduce what a vulnerable origin reveals to attackers.
**Steps.**
1. Implement header stripping/replacement policy (response phase, applied in the pipeline): remove `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, `X-AspNet-Version`, `X-AspNetMvc-Version`, `X-Generator`, `X-Drupal-Cache`, `X-Pingback` (WordPress), `Via` details when requested; set `Server: Hack-Dev-Defence` (override allowed).

Implement error page masking: origin 5xx responses with HTML bodies matching debug/stack-trace patterns (Django/Flask debug pages, Laravel Ignition, Spring Whitelabel with stack traces, ASP.NET yellow screen, PHP errors/warnings with file paths) are replaced with the branded generic error page (`block` outbound mode) or only recorded (`monitor`); detection patterns shared with the outbound filter (T-0408).
3. Block direct access to common debug endpoints (`/debug`, `/_debug`, `/console`, `/__debug__/`, `/_profiler`, `/telescope`, `/horizon`, `/elmah.axd`, `/trace.axd`, `/server-status`, `/server-info`, `/status` for Apache) unless declared in use (these are also in the honeypot catalog with distinct policy: a hit on a debug endpoint that returned 200 raises a critical exposure event in monitor mode).
4. 5. Implement settings in S-097 with explanations.
6. Link ATK-258, ATK-266, ATK-274 to ATK-280.
7. Fixtures with local origins serving fake sensitive content (test-only), plus benign pages.

- header policy, error masking hooks, exposure detector, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: stack-trace pages are masked in outbound block mode and recorded in monitor mode.
- A2: a scanner hit that receives a real `.env` response triggers a critical exposure event.
- A3: headers are stripped/replaced per policy and do not break the origin's own cache headers.
- A4: declared debug endpoints are not blocked.
- A5: zero false positives on benign pages.
**Tests.**
- Integration with test origins; unit: patterns.
**Notes.** The exposure event is one of the most valuable signals for owners of vulnerable sites.

<!-- PHASE:P16 -->
## PHASE P16: Bans, jail, appeals and end-to-end proof (T-0315 to T-0332) · milestone M7 · gate G16

Requirement prefix `BAN`. Goal: turn detection into containment. Every hard detection in `block` mode (outside cross-site subresource context) bans the attacker's IP key; the ban is enforced in the proxy within 100 ms on the creating node and within 2 s everywhere, mirrored to the kernel for proxied ports, visible and reversible in the UI and API, resistant to poisoning and self-lockout, appealable by legitimate visitors, and explainable. This phase also adds platform-wide promotion, evasion defenses, collateral-damage controls and a builder-local end-to-end proof that an exploitable test origin is protected: exploit succeeds directly, fails through HDD, and the source is banned.

Design invariants (C6): bans are by IP key (IPv4 /32, IPv6 /64 by default); the hot path never awaits the database; Postgres is the durable source of truth, Redis the fast shared store, local memory the enforcement copy; unban effect ≤ 2 s; the runner IP is bannable; bans apply to proxied ports only (80/443, UDP 443) so SSH and DNS remain available; every ban stores its reason and evidence (R-24).

Gate G16 passes when: AC-08 (ban persistence and unban), AC-34 (ban-poisoning resistance), AC-22 (IP resolution) subsets, the builder-local vulnerable-origin proof, loom/shuttle concurrency tests and all P16 UI checks pass; AC-38/AC-39 full lab proofs remain scheduled for P28 with the minimal local equivalent passing now.

### T-0315 · Client IP resolution and IP keys
`P16` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0208, T-0262 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Determine the true client address safely, and derive stable ban keys.
**Steps.**
1. Implement `resolve_client_ip(peer, headers, trusted_cidrs) -> ClientIp`: the TCP peer unless the peer is in the site/platform trusted proxy list (`upstream_cdn.trusted_cidrs`, `HDD_TRUSTED_PROXIES`), in which case parse `X-Forwarded-For` from right to left to the first untrusted entry, validate each entry (IP syntax, no ports or garbage), cap chain length (20), and ignore `Forwarded`/`X-Real-IP` unless the peer is trusted and the header is configured; default trusts nothing.
2. Strip inbound `X-Forwarded-*`, `Forwarded`, `X-Real-IP`, `HDD-*` headers from untrusted peers before setting HDD's own (also for h2).
3. Implement IP key derivation: IPv4 `/32`; IPv6 to configurable prefix (default `/64`, options `/56`, `/48`, `/128`), IPv4-mapped IPv6 collapsed to IPv4, zone IDs rejected, canonical text and compact binary forms.
4. Provide `ClientIp` with both the address (for display and kernel enforcement) and key (for lookups), plus `source: Peer | Xff(depth)` for audit.
5. Handle PROXY protocol (v1/v2) as an opt-in listener mode for operators behind L4 load balancers, with an allowlist of sender addresses; reject unsolicited PROXY headers otherwise.
6. Write spoofing tests: untrusted peers sending `X-Forwarded-For`, `Forwarded`, `X-Real-IP`, `HDD-Connecting-IP`; chained headers with mixed trusted/untrusted hops; IPv6 forms; malformed lists.
7. Add property tests: resolved IP is never an entry to the right of the first untrusted hop; keys are stable under textual variations.
8. Document operational guidance for CDNs and load balancers.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-common::clientip`, listener support for PROXY protocol, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: spoofed headers from untrusted peers never influence the resolved IP.
- A2: with a trusted CDN peer, the right-to-left rule yields the expected client in 30 table cases.
- A3: IPv6 addresses within the same /64 map to one key; different /64s do not.
- A4: unsolicited PROXY protocol headers are rejected.
- A5: resolution is allocation-free in the common case (alloc test).
**Tests.**
- Table (80) / proptest / fuzz on header parsing / alloc test.
**Notes.** AC-22 verifies this live with spoofed headers from the runner.

### T-0316 · Ban store: local enforcement copy, Redis, Postgres and resync
`P16` `[DP][DB]` · deps: T-0315, T-0211 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Make bans fast to check, durable, and consistent across nodes.
**Steps.**
1. Write migration for `ip_bans`, `ban_offences`, `ban_appeals` (if not yet present), and `campaign_clusters` per B5.7 with RLS (platform bans have `org_id` null and use platform-owned access paths).
2. Implement the local enforcement structure in each proxy node: three sharded maps (platform, org, site) keyed by `IpKey` with `expires_at` and a compact `BanInfo`, wrapped for lock-free reads (`ArcSwap` snapshots for bulk resync plus a sharded concurrent map for incremental updates), size cap 100,000 entries with oldest-expiry eviction that never evicts manual or platform bans, and a background reaper for expired entries.
3. Implement the **hot path check**: O(1) local lookup (platform, org, site in order) with no network I/O; a miss means not banned; Redis is not consulted on the request path.
4. Implement creation: write local immediately, then asynchronously (a) Redis (`hdd:banned_ips` zset score=expiry plus `hdd:ban:{scope}:{key}` hash with TTL), (b) publish `hdd:events:ban` with a monotonic revision, (c) enqueue the durable Postgres insert through the event pipeline with an idempotency key; failures retry with backoff and surface in metrics.
5. Implement subscribers: on `ban`/`unban` messages apply to the local structure; on a revision gap or reconnect, resync the full active set from Redis and verify against Postgres periodically (every 30 s incremental check, every 5 minutes full reconciliation) to heal divergence.
6. Implement unban: remove locally, Redis, publish, mark Postgres `released_at` with actor; ensure unban beats stale create messages (tombstones with revision ordering).
7. Implement Redis-down behavior: local bans continue to work; creation continues locally and queues Redis writes (bounded); node restarts rebuild from Postgres.
8. Add loom/shuttle tests for the concurrent structure and chaos tests (drop messages, restart nodes, partition Redis).
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-common::banstore`, migration, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the hot-path check performs no I/O (verified by a test harness that panics on socket use) and costs under 200 ns p99 for 100k entries.
- A2: a ban created on node A is enforced on node B within 2 s p95 (integration with two proxy instances).
- A3: dropped pub/sub messages heal via gap resync or reconciliation.
- A4: unban wins over delayed create messages (ordering test).
- A5: eviction never removes manual or platform bans (property test).
**Tests.**
- loom/shuttle model tests; chaos integration (Redis/Postgres restarts); benchmark.
**Notes.** The store implements the "never await the DB on the hot path" rule (C2).

### T-0317 · Ban policy engine: intent to ban, TTL ladder, scopes and attack diversity
`P16` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0316, T-0273 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Implement C6.4 so all ban sources share one decision point.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the `BanPolicy` service in `hdd-proxy` consuming `BanIntent`s from detection (hard hits, honeypots, scanners, rate limiter, credential stuffing, campaigns, shield) and producing `Ban`/`NoBan` with reasons, following the C6.4 decision order: never-ban check, tenant allowlist, mode check, cross-site rule, scope selection, ladder TTL.
2. Implement offence counters (`hdd:offence:{org}:{ip_key}` with TTL = decay window, default 30 days) updated atomically (Redis Lua) with local fallback; TTL ladder step = min(offence count, ladder length) using the site's `ban_ttl_ladder` (default 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 7 d), test bans 60 s (acceptance flag via signed header or runner token), rate-limit bans 10 min first then ladder.
3. Implement the **attack-diversity rule** (V15): maintain per-key set of distinct categories in a 10-minute window (small bitset in Redis/local); three or more categories → ban intent `attack_diversity` even if each was soft.
4. Implement cross-site counter: cross-site hard hits increment a separate counter and convert to a rate-limit ban at 3 per 60 s (C6.5).
5. Implement scope selection: site-level default; org-level propagation when `propagate_to_org` is on and the reason is a hard hit; platform-level only via promotion (T-0323).
6. Implement idempotency: repeated intents for an already banned key extend or keep the existing ban per rule (do not increment offences for requests rejected by the jail).
7. Implement explainability: `PolicyBranch` identifiers, evidence references (Ray ID, rule), config revision.
8. Write the decision table tests (reuse T-0273 rows plus ladder, scope, diversity and cross-site conversions), property tests, and an end-to-end test with real Redis.
**Deliverables.**
- `BanPolicy` service, Lua scripts, tests, docs `docs/BAN-POLICY.md` additions
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the ladder yields 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 7 d for repeated hard hits, with decay after the quiet window (test clock).
- A2: three distinct categories within 10 minutes produce an attack-diversity ban.
- A3: cross-site hits never ban until the 3-in-60-s conversion.
- A4: jail-rejected requests do not increment offence counters.
- A5: policy decisions carry branch IDs present in the docs table.
**Tests.**
- Table (150) / proptest / integration with Redis; chaos with Redis down (local fallback).
**Notes.** Platform-wide promotion is T-0323.

### T-0318 · Never-ban list and tenant allowlist semantics
`P16` `[DP][SEC][API]` · deps: T-0317 · size: M · owner: sec
**Objective.** Make it hard to ban the wrong addresses and clear what allowlisting means.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the platform never-ban list: loopback, `admin_cidrs`, platform public IPs, origin IPs of managed sites, provider health-probe ranges from the profile, DNS secondary addresses, and operator-added entries (`HDD_NEVER_BAN_CIDRS`, platform admin UI); **excluded by design:** the acceptance runner IP (preflight enforces).
2. Implement tenant allowlist entries (`access_entries` with action allow): behavior defined as (a) bypass jail and rate limiter, (b) inspection still runs and records `would_block` in monitor-style (no enforcement), unless `skip_inspection=true` (explicit risk acknowledgment), (c) never create bans for these keys.
3. Implement precedence rules: platform deny/global jail > tenant allow? Decision: **platform never-ban beats everything** (they can't be banned by anyone), tenant allow beats tenant deny at equal specificity, platform global bans override tenant allowlists only for abusive hard hits across tenants (documented; the key is also protected if in never-ban).
4. Implement the safety event: a hard hit from a never-ban key emits a critical `never_ban_attack_attempt` (possible compromise of a trusted host) and alerts owners/platform admins once per hour per key.
5. Implement matcher structures (radix tries) for fast lookup, compiled into the snapshot, with the same matcher crate used by the control-plane "Test an IP" tool (T-0232).
6. Implement API/UI hooks for platform never-ban management (T-0424) with runner-IP guard.
7. Add tests for precedence matrices (60 cases) and for IPv4/IPv6 CIDR edge cases.
8. Document semantics and risks of `skip_inspection`.
**Deliverables.**
- matchers, policy integration, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: never-ban keys are never banned by any path (property test over random intents).
- A2: tenant allowlisted keys with inspection on record `would_block` and are not blocked.
- A3: `skip_inspection=true` entries require the acknowledgment and are shown prominently.
- A4: hard hits from never-ban keys raise the critical event with rate limiting.
- A5: the runner IP is rejected from the never-ban list by validation.
**Tests.**
- Table/proptest; integration; unit: radix trie correctness against a naive implementation.
**Notes.** Anti-self-harm baseline (C9.2).

### T-0319 · IP Jail pipeline stage and branded 403
`P16` `[DP]` · deps: T-0316, T-0318 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Reject banned clients at the earliest possible point with a consistent response.
**Steps.**
1. Implement pipeline stage 6: resolve client key, check never-ban/allowlist, then jail lookup (platform → org → site); on hit return the branded 403 immediately (HTML or JSON by `Accept`, `HDD-Ray-ID` header, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Retry-After` not set, no hint of remaining time), connection `close` for HTTP/1.1 after the response to discourage keep-alive abuse.
2. Count jail hits per key in memory with aggregation (flush every 10 s to `event_aggregates` and metrics) instead of one event per hit; sample 1 in N full events for forensics (configurable) to avoid write amplification during floods.
3. Implement cheap early rejection at connection level for floods: if a key accumulates more than M jail hits per second (default 50), drop the TCP connection without a response (RST/close) and count it, reducing per-request work; the kernel/XDP layer takes over via P25.
4. Ensure the jail stage runs before body reading (no request body buffering for banned clients) and before TLS session resumption leaks (TLS handshake still occurs because SNI is needed; plan to drop pre-handshake via kernel when available).
5. Implement the block page rendering with the shared visitor template (S-140), Ray ID, appeals link when enabled.
6. Implement response uniformity: identical for all banned reasons (no reason leakage).
7. Add metrics (`MET-hdd_jail_hits_total`) and latency tests (jail hit path under 50 µs).
8. Test HTTP/2 behavior (RST_STREAM vs response), HEAD requests, and websocket upgrade attempts from banned clients.
**Deliverables.**
- pipeline stage, aggregation, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a banned client's request receives 403 with Ray ID and never reaches inspection or origin (origin counter zero).
- A2: jail-hit flood of 100k requests generates bounded events (aggregation test).
- A3: the response is identical regardless of ban reason.
- A4: jail hit path latency p99 under 50 µs.
- A5: banned WebSocket upgrades are refused before upgrade.
**Tests.**
- Integration with load generator (functional profile), unit: aggregation; h2 tests.
**Notes.** Jail hits do not extend the ban or increment offences.

### T-0322 · Ban stream contract for the host agent and enforcement acknowledgments
`P16` `[DP][OPS]` · deps: T-0316 · size: M · owner: infra
**Objective.** Define the protocol the kernel firewall agent consumes, so P25 only implements enforcement.
**Steps.**
1. Define the `BanStream` contract: Redis stream/pubsub messages (`ban`, `unban`, `snapshot_begin/end`, `reconcile_request`) with fields (key, family, expiry, scope, reason class, revision), signed with an internal HMAC key so a compromised Redis writer cannot inject arbitrary kernel rules; message size caps and rate limits.
2. Define acknowledgments: the agent writes back `hdd:fw:ack:{revision}` with status and timing so the control plane can display propagation per layer; define missing-ack timeouts and states (`pending`, `applied`, `failed`, `unsupported`).
3. Define reconcile semantics: the agent every 30 s requests/derives the authoritative active set (from Postgres via a read-only role or Redis snapshot) and diffs against the kernel set; failures are metrics and alerts.
4. Implement a `NoopEnforcer` reference consumer in the repository that acknowledges messages (used in tests and when no kernel backend is available) and a contract test suite that any real enforcer must pass.
5. Define restricted addressing: kernel enforcement applies to destination ports 80/443 and UDP 443 only; never to 22, 53; never to keys in the never-ban list (agent double-checks against the list).
6. Define capacity limits: maximum kernel set size (default 100k), eviction rules consistent with L7 (agent reports overflow).
7. Document the contract and security model (signing, least privilege, no shell).
8. Write chaos tests for message loss, duplication, reordering, and replay (replay protection via revision monotonicity and expiry).
**Deliverables.**
- contract docs, message types in `hdd-common`, `NoopEnforcer`, contract tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: forged (unsigned) messages are rejected by the reference consumer.
- A2: duplicated and reordered messages converge to the right state (property test).
- A3: acknowledgments appear in the control plane propagation view.
- A4: never-ban keys are refused by the agent logic even if present in a message.
- A5: the contract suite is runnable against any `Enforcer` implementation.
**Tests.**
- Property/chaos tests; contract suite.
**Notes.** The nftables implementation and XDP loader land in P25 (T-0463 to T-0467).

### T-0323 · Org-wide propagation and platform-wide global jail promotion
`P16` `[DP][API][SEC]` · deps: T-0317, T-0320 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Share intelligence about clearly malicious sources across domains and tenants responsibly.

8. Document the policy and tenant disclosures in the privacy page (T-0101).

- A2: tenants cannot discover other tenants' identities from global bans (API/UI inspection test).
- A3: CGNAT-class keys require manual review.
- A4: promotion respects never-ban and excludes same-owner orgs.

### T-0324 · Appeals: visitor flow, workflow and owner inbox (S-145, S-146, S-069)
`P16` `[UI][API][SEC]` · deps: T-0320, T-0065 · size: XL · owner: ui

Verify the Ray ID: exists, belongs to the same site, and the submitter's IP key equals the event's key or the request is from a trusted flow (e.g., a different IP with proof) — the default rule is **IP key must match**; if it does not match, still accept but flag `ip_mismatch`; responses are identical regardless of verification result (no oracle); rate limits: 3 per hour per IP key, 10 per day per site, 100 per day per site globally.

### T-0325 · Ban evasion defenses: campaign detector and fingerprint-linked escalation
`P16` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0317, T-0306 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Defend against attackers who rotate IPs.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the campaign detector: for each (site, endpoint pattern, signature id) maintain a bounded set (HyperLogLog) of distinct IP keys producing hard or soft matches in a 10-minute window; when distinct keys ≥ N (default 20) open a `campaign_cluster` row, mark the (site, endpoint) as **elevated**, alert owners and platform, and apply the campaign policy.
2. Define campaign policies: challenge all *new* clients (no clearance cookie, no prior good sessions) on that endpoint; tighten rate limits for that endpoint; optionally block the signature entirely for new keys; auto-expire after 30 minutes of calm.
3. Implement fingerprint-linked escalation: after a hard-hit ban, remember a salted hash of (header order, selected header values, UA, accept-language) and the TLS fingerprint if available for the ban duration; new IP keys presenting the same fingerprint **and** the same attack signature are challenged first and banned on the second hit; fingerprints alone never ban.
4. Implement IPv6 rotation defense: when ≥ 5 distinct /64s inside the same /48 (or /56) are banned within 60 minutes, escalate to a ban of the covering prefix (/56 or /48) for a short TTL with owner notification, never above the prefix of a known ISP aggregate without review (ASN-based allowlist of broad prefixes).
5. Implement residential-proxy handling: no per-IP bans for low-evidence cases; rely on challenge and endpoint hardening.
6. Provide UI: campaign view in the security overview (active campaigns, endpoints, counts, actions, end), and events grouped into incidents.
7. Add tests simulating rotating-IP attacks (builder-local multi-source via loopback aliases/netns) and measuring detection time.
8. Document limitations.
**Deliverables.**
- campaign detector, escalation logic, UI, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: 30 rotating sources hitting one endpoint with the same payload shape open a campaign within the window and trigger challenge for new clients.
- A2: legitimate users with clearance cookies are unaffected during a campaign.
- A3: fingerprint-only matches never ban.
- A4: IPv6 prefix escalation respects ASN safeguards.
- A5: campaigns auto-close after calm and restore normal policy.
**Tests.**
- Simulation tests (netns/aliases); unit: HLL thresholds and window logic; UI tests.
**Notes.** Implements V16 and ATK-208.

### T-0326 · Shared-address (CGNAT) collateral mitigation
`P16` `[DP][SEC][UI]` · deps: T-0317, T-0325 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Reduce harm to innocent users behind shared addresses.
**Steps.**

Implement shared-address indicators: ASN class lists (mobile carriers, universities, large ISPs with CGNAT, corporate egress, Tor exits, public proxies/VPNs — from `hdd-intel` data when available), observed behavior (many distinct user agents and session cookies per key with legitimate traffic in the last 24 h), reverse DNS hints.
2. Implement the site option `shared_address_policy`: `ban` (default for keys without indicators), `challenge_first` (soft-score blocks challenge instead of ban for flagged keys), `short_ban` (hard-hit bans for flagged keys limited to 5 minutes and logged), `review` (queue for owner review).

7. Document tradeoffs openly (an attacker behind CGNAT may get softer treatment; hard hits still block each request).
8. Add metrics for shared-address decisions.
**Deliverables.**
- indicators, policy options, UI hooks, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: with `challenge_first`, soft-score blocks on shared keys produce challenges, not bans.
- A2: hard hits from shared keys still get blocked (403) and banned for the short TTL when `short_ban`.
- A3: indicators come from data sources (no hand-wired lists in logic) and unknown ASNs default to normal policy.
- A4: collateral hints appear in the UI.
- A5: policy is documented with the tradeoffs.
**Tests.**
- Scenario tests; unit: indicator computation; browser: hints.
**Notes.** Requires GeoIP/ASN data for ASN-class indicators; otherwise only behavioral indicators apply.

### T-0330 · Ban end-to-end tests with a builder-local vulnerable test origin
`P16` `[QA][SEC]` · deps: T-0319, T-0324, T-0327 · size: XL · owner: qa
**Objective.** Prove the product promise in a controlled local environment before the lab and pilot runs.
**Steps.**
1. Build a **test-only vulnerable origin** under `tests/support/vuln_origin/` (never shipped, loopback-bound, disposable SQLite or Postgres container): endpoints with intentionally unsafe string-built SQL for login (`/login`), search (`/search?q=`), numeric ID (`/item?id=`), plus reflection for XSS and a file read for traversal; includes canary rows and an admin account for non-destructive proofs.
2. Start HDD (proxy, API, Redis, Postgres) on the builder with the origin behind it in `monitor` and `block` modes.
3. Execute the proof matrix: (a) **direct** exploit proofs against the origin (Class A only: auth bypass as canary admin, UNION extraction of a canary table, sleep ≤ 2 s) succeed — demonstrating vulnerability; (b) the same through HDD in `block` mode with the Vulnerable-Origin Shield: 403 with Ray ID, **client IP banned**, subsequent benign requests from the IP get 403, origin access counter unchanged by the exploit attempts; (c) legitimate login/search/ID requests from another IP succeed; (d) the six mandated payloads against the login form via POST body and via query string each ban a fresh source address (using loopback aliases 127.0.0.2+ as distinct clients); (e) cross-site subresource requests with attack-shaped URLs are blocked without ban; (f) unban restores access within 2 s.
4. Include IPv6 sources (loopback aliases `::1`-range /64 members) to prove /64 keys.
5. Include resilience: Redis stopped mid-test (local bans persist), proxy restarted (bans reload from Postgres), second proxy node receives bans.
6. Capture timing: time from payload to enforcement on the same node and on the second node.
7. Produce a report with evidence: origin logs, proxy events, ban records, timings; assert numbers against thresholds (≤ 100 ms same node, ≤ 2 s other node).
8. Wire the suite into `cargo xtask acceptance --only AC-38-local` and mark the Vuln-Lab version for P28.
**Deliverables.**
- `tests/support/vuln_origin`, e2e suite, report
**Acceptance.**
- A1: direct exploits succeed against the test origin (proof of vulnerability) and fail through HDD with a ban.
- A2: each of the six mandated payloads bans a fresh source in POST and GET forms.
- A3: cross-site subresource attack URLs do not ban.
- A4: enforcement latency thresholds are met.
- A5: the suite survives Redis stop/start and proxy restart without losing bans.
**Tests.**
- The suite itself, run 5 times for stability.
**Notes.** The test origin is intentionally insecure; it binds loopback only, refuses to start otherwise, and is excluded from release builds (guard test).

## PHASE P17: Rate limits, bots, challenge and reputation (T-0333 to T-0352) · milestone M7 · gate G17

Requirement prefix `BOT`. Goal: behavioral defenses that work even when no signature matches: sliding-window rate limiting with Redis and a local fallback, per-path and auth-endpoint limits, automatic bans for violators, slow-attack mitigation, the proof-of-work challenge and clearance system, under-attack mode, bot scoring, verified bots, TLS fingerprint spike, credential-stuffing and password-spraying detection, form-abuse defenses, local reputation and external lists, GeoIP/ASN enrichment, feed ingestion, adaptive thresholds and anti-scraping. No third-party CAPTCHA, no tracking, no cognitive puzzles.

Principles: challenge is preferred over ban for ambiguous evidence; bans require hard evidence or repeated violations; shared-address risk is considered (P16); every action is explainable with metrics and events; defaults are conservative and tuned by measurement on the benign traffic corpora and by the operator.

Gate G17 passes when: AC-11 (rate limiting), AC-44 (challenge and bots), credential-stuffing lab tests, and AC-48 (scanner/bot detection) subsets pass; challenge pass rates and solve times meet targets on a reference device matrix; false-positive tests on benign traffic replays show zero blocks and bounded challenge rates; and all UI screens meet the UI definition of done.

### T-0333 · Rate limiter core: Redis sliding window with local fallback
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0316, T-0261 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Provide accurate, fast, shared rate limiting that keeps working when Redis does not.
**Steps.**
1. Decide key structure and algorithm in an ADR: sliding window log vs sliding window counter vs GCRA. Default for ordinary limits: **sliding window counter with two sub-windows** (documented error bound: the estimate can differ from the exact count by at most the weight of the previous window's tail, which is at most one limit per boundary; tests measure it). **Authentication endpoints and ban-triggering limits use an exact algorithm** (sliding window log capped at the limit, or GCRA) so their counts are never approximate. Redis Lua scripts give atomicity with keys `hdd:rl:{site}:{scope}:{key}`; scopes: `ip`, `ip_path`, `session`, `asn`, `fingerprint`, `api_key`, `global_ip`.
2. Implement the Lua script returning (allowed, remaining, reset_ms, violation_count) in a single round trip with `EVALSHA`, script loading on startup and recovery from `NOSCRIPT`, pipelining multiple scopes per request (cap 4 scopes) to keep p99 under 1 ms in-datacenter.
3. Implement the local fallback with `governor`-style in-memory limiters (sharded, bounded memory with TTL eviction) used when Redis is unreachable (circuit breaker with half-open probes), logging the degraded mode and exposing `MET-hdd_rate_limiter_fallback_total`.
4. Implement limit definitions in the snapshot: default (60 requests / 10 s per IP per site), per-rule overrides (T-0334), allowlist bypass (T-0318), verified bot exemptions, challenge clearance modifiers (cleared clients get 2x limits).
5. Implement the stage 9 pipeline integration (after jail, before body acquisition): compute keys, call limiter asynchronously with a 5 ms timeout; on timeout use local fallback decision (fail-open for ordinary limits but fail-closed for auth endpoints under Paranoid).
6. Implement response headers (`RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset`, `Retry-After`) for 429 responses only (avoid leaking limits to attackers on normal responses unless the owner enables).
7. Add benchmarks (limiter overhead) and chaos tests (Redis kill, latency injection).
8. Document semantics, accuracy bounds and memory use.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-proxy::ratelimit`, Lua scripts, ADR, tests, benches
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a burst of 100 requests with limit 60/10 s yields 60 allowed (±5% for the counter algorithm, exactly 60 for the exact algorithm used on auth endpoints) and the rest 429, measured against a reference implementation.
- A2: Redis outage switches to local limiting within 100 ms and recovers automatically.
- A3: limiter overhead p99 under 1 ms with Redis and 5 µs local.
- A4: memory of the local limiter is bounded (cap and eviction tested).
- A5: auth endpoints fail closed under Paranoid when both limiters are unavailable.
**Tests.**
- Integration with real Redis; chaos; proptest of window arithmetic; benchmark.
**Notes.** Counters are never written to Postgres on the hot path.

### T-0334 · Per-path and auth-endpoint rate rules (engine side)
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0333, T-0230 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Apply the owner's rate rules and the auth-endpoint presets accurately.
**Steps.**
1. Compile `rate_limit_rules` into an indexed structure: exact paths and prefixes in a radix tree, glob patterns, method sets, scope/limit/window/action, ordered by specificity then priority, with caching of match results per route key.
2. Implement the **auth-endpoint presets**: for declared/detected auth endpoints apply Balanced 10/min per IP per path, Paranoid 5/min, with an additional per-account-HMAC counter (T-0343) and burst allowance 3; apply session-scoped limits for authenticated APIs when configured.
3. Implement conflict resolution (most specific rule wins; if equal, lowest limit) and explain the effective rule in the verdict/event.
4. Implement action semantics: `429` (default), `challenge` (serve challenge instead), `ban after N violations` (default 5 violations in 10 minutes with the rate-limit ladder first step 10 min).
5. Implement dry-run simulation support: compute from the traffic sample what would have been limited (used by S-061).
6. Implement special exemptions: ACME challenge paths, `/__hdd/*`, health checks, allowlisted keys.

### T-0335 · Rate-limit actions: 429 page, auto-ban and progressive penalties
`P17` `[DP][SEC][UI]` · deps: T-0334, T-0317 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Make limiting actions safe, consistent and escalating.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the 429 response: branded page/JSON (`ERR-VISITOR-429`), `Retry-After` seconds, `HDD-Ray-ID`, no rule names, `Cache-Control: no-store`.
2. Implement violation counting: each 429 increments a violation counter (Redis, local fallback) per key per rule; reaching N violations in the window yields a `rate_limit` `BanIntent` (first TTL 10 minutes, then the ladder), with cross-site rule not applicable (rate limiting is about volume).
3. Implement progressive penalties for repeat offenders across rules: second ban step increases limits strictness for that key for 24 h (halved limits) before ban.
4. Implement protections against self-DoS: do not count 429s toward limits again; ensure rejected requests are cheap (no body reading, immediate close for abusive keys).
5. Implement challenge as an action alternative (serve clearance challenge; cleared clients continue under the 2x limits).
6. Implement metrics and events (aggregated) and attention items for sustained limiting.
7. Provide UI copy for S-142 and S-061 consequences, including shared-IP hints.
8. Test with scripted bursts and legitimate bursty clients (page loads with many assets).
**Deliverables.**
- response handlers, violation logic, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: sustained abuse leads from 429 to ban per configuration (AC-11 scenario).
- A2: legitimate page loads (50 assets in 2 s) do not trigger limits at defaults (asset paths are excluded or weighted lower via asset classification).
- A3: 429 responses never reveal limit values beyond `Retry-After`.
- A4: banned keys recover after TTL (test clock).
- A5: rejected requests do not read bodies.
**Tests.**
- Integration burst tests (functional profile); benign page-load replay; unit: violation counters.
**Notes.** Asset classification (extension and path based) reduces false positives.

### T-0336 · Slow-attack mitigation at application layer
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0208 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Protect against Slowloris, slow POST (RUDY) and slow-read attacks beyond protocol timeouts.
**Steps.**
1. Implement header-read timeout (10 s) enforcement with per-IP concurrency of half-open connections (default 30 per IP, 10,000 per node) and drop policy for stragglers.
2. Implement minimum body throughput enforcement: after the first 5 s, require a sustained minimum rate (default 100 bytes/s measured over 10 s windows) for request bodies; exceeding violations closes the connection and counts toward a `slow_attack` intent; allow exceptions for declared upload endpoints (lower minimums with total time caps).
3. Implement slow-read protection: write timeouts and bounded response buffering per connection; connections that do not read within 30 s are closed; h2 flow-control window checks.
4. Implement per-IP/connection caps with a fairness scheduler so slow clients cannot starve others (bounded accept queue, shed policy documented).
5. Implement metrics (`MET-hdd_proxy_shed_total{reason}`), events (aggregated), and ban policy hooks (repeat offenders get rate-limit bans).
6. Test with a controllable slow client generator in the `protocol-abuse` profile against the sandbox hostname and builder-local stacks (5 connections, capped).
7. Validate that legitimate slow mobile clients on weak networks are not cut off (lower bounds, grace).
8. Document tuning.
**Deliverables.**
- timeouts and throughput enforcement, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: Slowloris-style header dribbling is cut off at 10 s and counted.
- A2: RUDY-style slow bodies are closed after the grace period at the default minimum rate.
- A3: slow-read connections are closed after 30 s.
- A4: 5 slow connections cannot degrade fast clients (latency test).
- A5: legitimate clients at 5 KB/s uploading small forms succeed.
**Tests.**
- Raw-socket attack generators (builder-local and sandbox profile); fairness tests.
**Notes.** Raw protocol tests (AC-14) cover HTTP/2-specific attacks in P18.

### T-0337 · Challenge engine: proof-of-work tokens, clearance cookies and replay protection
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0108, T-0333 · size: L · owner: sec
**Objective.** Implement the data-plane challenge from C7.2.
**Steps.**
1. Write the ADR for challenge cryptography (HMAC-SHA-256 signing, nonce store, difficulty semantics, key rotation with overlap) and calibrate difficulty: build a device benchmark page and measure solve times on desktop, mid-range phone and low-end phone (via browser harness CPU throttling); define difficulty tiers (baseline 14 bits, elevated 18, suspected automation 20 to 22) with a cap such that the median mid-range phone solves within 3 s.
2. Implement endpoints on customer domains: `GET /__hdd/challenge` (serves S-141 for interstitial display), `POST /__hdd/challenge/verify` (verifies token and solution), and the transparent interstitial flow: a challenged request receives a 403/429-like interstitial (status 403 with `HDD-Challenge: 1`? choose 403 with the challenge page; for XHR/fetch expectations an `application/json` variant with `challenge_url`), then after verification redirects (303) to the original URL (validated same-origin, preserving method only for GET/HEAD; non-GET requests ask the user to retry the action).
3. Implement token issuance (bound to site, route class, IP bucket, UA hash, expiry 60 s, one-time nonce in Redis with local fallback) and verification (constant-time compare, replay prevention, difficulty check, clock skew tolerance).
4. Implement the **clearance cookie** `__Host-hdd_cl` (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/): payload `{v, site_id, ip_bucket, ua_hash, exp, level}` with HMAC; validity default 30 minutes (5 min to 24 h per site setting); cookie does not bypass inspection, bans or rate limiter (it modifies challenge decisions and grants 2x rate limits).
5. Implement IP bucket tolerance (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /56) for mobile networks and fail-safe when UA changes (re-challenge).
6. Implement abuse resistance: limit challenge issuance per key (10 per minute), cap outstanding nonces per key, protect verify endpoint against brute force, and ensure the challenge endpoints cannot be used as an oracle for site existence (neutral on unknown hosts).
7. Implement metrics (`MET-hdd_challenge_issued_total`, `solved`, `failed`, solve-time histogram) and events.
8. Test replay, cross-site token reuse, tampering, expired tokens, UA/IP changes, and key rotation overlap.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-challenge` data-plane module, endpoints, ADR, tests, calibration report
**Acceptance.**
- A1: tokens cannot be replayed, transferred across sites or IP buckets, or used after expiry (test suite of 30 cases).
- A2: median solve time on the reference mid-range phone profile ≤ 3 s at baseline difficulty (CDP throttling profile recorded).
- A3: clearance does not bypass inspection or bans (tests).
- A4: key rotation with overlap does not invalidate valid in-flight challenges.
- A5: verify endpoint brute force is rate limited.
**Tests.**
- Unit/integration; browser tests with throttled CPU; fuzz on token parsing.
**Notes.** Accessibility: automatic solve, no puzzle (WCAG 3.3.8).

### T-0341 · Verified bots: forward-confirmed reverse DNS and published ranges
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0340, T-0009 · size: M · owner: dns
**Objective.** Let legitimate crawlers pass and fake crawlers fail.
**Steps.**

2. Implement optional IP-range validation using the vendors' published ranges when the operator allowlists their fetch locations (egress); store ranges as signed/checksummed data with expiry.
3. Implement asynchronous verification so the request path does not block: first request from an unknown claimant is treated per policy (default: allow-with-log for 1 request while queueing verification, then challenge on repeat if unverified); verification workers rate-limited (50 lookups/s) with a bounded queue and timeouts (2 s).
4. Implement failure handling: DNS errors → treat as unverified (fail closed for the claim) but do not ban; fake crawlers (claim + failed FCrDNS) are class `automation_suspected` and are challenged.
5. Provide the owner test tool (S-062): input IP/UA → shows verification steps and result (DNS only; the tool never sends requests to the IP).
6. Provide metrics and cache stats.
7. Test with local DNS servers simulating PTR/A records for good and bad crawlers and spoofers.
8. Document supported crawlers and extension.
**Deliverables.**
- verification module, caches, tool endpoint, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a spoofed Googlebot UA from a random IP is challenged after failing FCrDNS.
- A2: a valid crawler (simulated PTR chain) passes and is cached.
- A3: DNS failures do not ban and are retried later.
- A4: the verification queue is bounded and rate limited.
- A5: the owner tool performs no HTTP to the tested IP.
**Tests.**
- Integration with local DNS; unit: suffix matching; load test of the queue.
**Notes.** ATK-201.

### T-0342 · TLS fingerprint spike (JA3/JA4) and ADR
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0208 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Decide whether and how to capture TLS ClientHello fingerprints for bot detection.
**Steps.**
1. Spike `tls-parser` (or equivalent) to peek the ClientHello from the TCP stream before handing it to rustls: design a peeking acceptor that buffers the first TLS record (bounded 16 KB), parses cipher suites, extensions, curves, point formats, ALPN, SNI, supported versions, signature algorithms, then replays the buffered bytes into rustls.
2. Compute JA3 (MD5 of fields) and JA4-style fingerprints (sorted, truncated hashes, more stable against extension randomization) using our own implementation (document formats and license considerations; no copying of third-party code), store as short hashes.
3. Measure overhead (latency and CPU), robustness against malformed ClientHellos (fuzz), TLS 1.3 ECH/encrypted ClientHello considerations (fingerprint limited), and compatibility with session resumption and early data.
4. Evaluate usefulness: collect fingerprints from the browser harness (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit versions), common HTTP libraries (curl, Python requests, Go, Java) and scanners (sqlmap via Python, nikto), measuring separability; document the limits (Chromium extension randomization, spoofing by uTLS).
5. Decide the integration: fingerprints as one bot-score feature and as a ban-evasion linking signal (T-0325), never a sole blocking basis; store only hashes (no raw ClientHello).
6. Write the ADR (accept/defer), including privacy analysis (fingerprints as quasi-identifiers; retention limits).
7. If accepted, implement the peeking acceptor behind a feature flag and wire into bot scoring; if deferred, record the effort estimate and defer to P32 with reasons (R-08 spike-first).
8. Add fuzz targets and perf benchmarks.
**Deliverables.**
- spike code (or implementation), ADR, evaluation report
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the ADR states a decision with measurements.
- A2: if implemented, the acceptor never loses or reorders bytes (differential test vs direct rustls handshake) and passes fuzzing.
- A3: overhead under 100 µs per new connection (measured).
- A4: separability results are documented with honest caveats.
- A5: only hashes are stored.
**Tests.**
- Fuzz; differential handshake tests; benchmark.
**Notes.** HTTP/2 SETTINGS fingerprinting (Tier 3) is deferred to P32.

### T-0343 · Credential-stuffing and brute-force detector
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0334, T-0274, T-0340 · size: L · owner: sec
**Objective.** Detect and slow account-takeover attacks against the protected site's login.
**Steps.**
1. Implement username observation on declared auth endpoints: extract the username/email field (by field-kind inference and declared field names) and compute `HMAC(site_key, normalized_username)` immediately; never store or log the plaintext username; keys per site rotate on demand.
2. Track per client key: distinct username HMACs attempted in sliding 10-minute windows (HyperLogLog), failure counts, and attempt rate; thresholds: > 5 distinct usernames with failures → challenge, > 15 → ban (`credential_stuffing`), > 30 attempts/min → rate action.
3. Track per username HMAC across IPs: failures in 10 minutes from ≥ 3 distinct IP keys (distributed brute force) → step-up challenge for logins to that username and an owner alert; HDD cannot lock the origin's account but can challenge and slow attempts.
4. Implement response-pattern learning (success-like vs failure-like) per endpoint (shared with T-0274) with owner correction and confidence; when unknown, rely on request volume only.
5. Detect password spraying: one client key or small key set trying many usernames with few attempts each, same password hint (cannot see passwords, so approximate with identical request body length/shape hashes) → challenge.
6. Integrate with breached-credential signals when the origin is HDD itself (platform dogfood): use the results of the app's own breach checker; for tenants this is not available.
7. Implement dashboards and events: `credential_stuffing` incidents with counts of distinct usernames (HMAC counts only), top sources, success-like outcomes after attack (critical alert when a spray is followed by many success-like responses).
8. Test with lab-style generators (10,000 synthetic usernames, distributed sources) and benign login traffic (shared offices, password managers retries).
**Deliverables.**
- detector, learning, events, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: stuffing from one IP with 100 usernames is challenged within 6 usernames and banned by 16.
- A2: distributed attack on one username triggers step-up for that username and an alert.
- A3: no plaintext usernames are stored or logged (inspection test).
- A4: benign shared-office logins (20 users, 5 failures each) do not ban.
- A5: success-like spikes after sprays create a critical alert.
**Tests.**
- Simulation (builder-local multi-source); privacy inspection; benign replay.
**Notes.** ATK-157 to ATK-160, ATK-285.

### T-0344 · Account-enumeration and user-differential signals
`P17` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0343 · size: S · owner: sec
**Objective.** Alert owners when their login/reset endpoints reveal account existence.
**Steps.**
1. Implement passive differential analysis on declared auth/reset endpoints: cluster responses by (status, redirect target, size class, selected header set) and correlate with attempted username HMACs; if responses for different usernames differ systematically (e.g., "user not found" vs "wrong password" size patterns) with statistical confidence, raise `account_enumeration_possible` (low severity) with remediation text.
2. Detect enumeration behavior from clients: many requests varying only the username with response-differential harvesting patterns (sequential or dictionary-like usernames); treat as `credential_stuffing`-adjacent soft signal.
3. Implement timing differential signal (response time differences across usernames beyond noise) as a weaker hint with minimum samples.
4. Surface in the Security overview and readiness ("Authentication responses are uniform: Unknown/Pass/Fail with confidence").
5. Respect privacy: only aggregates and HMACs.
6. Provide guidance in docs for fixing enumeration in the origin.
7. Test with controllable origin endpoints returning different responses.
8. Link ATK-161, ATK-287.
**Deliverables.**
- analyzer, UI hooks, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a test origin with differing responses triggers the finding; a uniform origin does not.
- A2: the finding includes confidence and sample counts.
- A3: no plaintext identifiers are stored.
- A4: false positives are minimized by minimum sample thresholds.
- A5: remediation text is present.
**Tests.**
- Simulation tests with two test origins; statistical unit tests.
**Notes.** This is an advisory finding, not a blocking rule.

### T-0346 · IP reputation: local scores, Tor/VPN/datacenter lists and feed ingestion
`P17` `[DP][SEC][OPS]` · deps: T-0009, T-0317 · size: L · owner: sec
**Objective.** Build the reputation data layer used by bot scoring and policy.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the `hdd-intel` reputation store: local reputation score per IP key built from events (hard hits, bans, honeypots, challenge failures) with exponential decay (half-life default 7 days), bounded size (500k keys, LRU by low score), and exposure as a feature for scoring and an optional policy (challenge above threshold).
2. Implement list ingestion: Tor exit lists, public proxy/VPN/datacenter ranges, and operator-enabled threat feeds from `threat_feeds` (format adapters: plain CIDR list, CSV, JSON), downloaded by the worker through the egress client with size caps, checksum or signature verification, scheduled refresh, validation (CIDR parsing, count limits), expiry per entry, and atomic swap into compiled radix tries.
3. Implement feed provenance and licensing metadata; refuse unknown-license feeds unless the operator accepts explicitly; record `UNVERIFIED(capability_not_supplied)` when no feeds are configured.
4. Implement policies per site and per list (allow, log, challenge, block) with defaults: Tor/VPN allow, datacenter challenge only on auth endpoints and signup, threat feeds log (block opt-in), local reputation challenge above 80.
5. Implement explainability: events show which list matched (name, age).
6. Implement staleness handling (stale lists beyond max age are ignored with alert).
7. Test ingestion with fixtures and with a local feed server serving good, malformed and oversized data.
8. Link ATK-202 to ATK-204.

- reputation store, ingestion pipeline, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: malformed or oversized feeds are rejected without replacing the current list.
- A2: list lookups cost under 200 ns p99 for 1M CIDRs.

### T-0349 · Adaptive thresholds and baselines
`P17` `[DP][API]` · deps: T-0333, T-0140 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Detect abnormal traffic relative to each site's own normal.
**Steps.**
1. Maintain per-site baselines (EWMA and robust percentile estimates) for request rate, error rate, 404 ratio, unique client keys per minute, origin latency and bytes, by hour-of-week seasonality (168 buckets) learned over time with minimum history before use.
2. Compute anomaly scores (z-score with MAD scaling) and define states: normal, elevated (> 3), severe (> 5); require sustained duration (≥ 2 minutes) to avoid flapping; expose through metrics and the shield input (P26).
3. Use baselines to adapt actions: per-site automatic tightening of rate limits (temporary multipliers 0.5) during severe states, triggering under-attack mode (T-0339) per configuration, and campaign thresholds scaling with traffic volume.
4. Provide owner visibility: baseline charts with bands in S-070, explanations for adaptive actions, opt-out per site.
5. Ensure learning excludes known attack periods (do not learn from bans/under-attack intervals) to avoid poisoning baselines.
6. Implement storage (compact rollups in Postgres) and warm start after restarts.
7. Test with synthetic seasonality and attack injections.
8. Document limits and guidance for small sites with sparse traffic.
**Deliverables.**
- baseline engine, adaptive hooks, UI bands, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a 10x request spike for 3 minutes on a stable site produces `severe` and triggers configured actions.
- A2: daily seasonality does not trigger false alarms across a simulated week.
- A3: attack periods are excluded from learning.
- A4: sparse sites do not trigger spurious adaptation (minimum history rule).
- A5: owners can disable adaptation.
**Tests.**
- Simulation tests (time series generators); unit: MAD/EWMA math; property tests.
