## PHASE P32: Backlog, Tier 2 to Tier 6 (T-0541 to T-0560) · after milestone M12 · gate G32

Requirement prefix `BKL`. Goal: a prioritized, fully specified backlog of capabilities that extend the product after the Tier 1 minimums are proven. Tasks in this phase begin only after gate G31 passes (or earlier on explicit operator request for a named task) and follow every rule of the constitution: ADR first for anything with an architectural choice, honest claims, acceptance evidence, and the same gate discipline.

**Tier map.**

| Tier | Theme | Tasks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tier 2 | Customer-value extensions on the existing architecture | T-0541 to T-0546 |
| Tier 3 | Protocol and DNS depth | T-0548 to T-0550 |
| Tier 4 | Scale-out and resilience | T-0552 to T-0555 |
| Tier 5 | Extensibility | T-0547 |
| Tier 6 | Ecosystem and enterprise | T-0551, T-0556 to T-0559 |
| Governance | Backlog management | T-0560 |

Non-negotiables: no Tier 2 to 6 feature may weaken a Tier 1 guarantee (inspection never fails open in `block` mode, hot path never awaits the database, tenant isolation, claims policy); each task states its operator-dependent inputs; features that add attack surface (plugins, SSO, caches, provider adapters) require a STRIDE delta and a lab pentest note before merge; any new outbound call goes through the central egress client and the allowlist; cost and complexity are weighed against the single-VPS-first philosophy and recorded in the ADR.

Gate G32 is the per-task closing review used each time a backlog item completes (the gate report format is the same, appended to `docs/gates/G32-<task>.md`).

### T-0541 · Tier 2: DNS provider import adapters (read-only) for common providers
`P32` `[API][UI][SEC]` · deps: T-0157, T-0184, T-0413 · size: L · owner: dns
**Objective.** Let owners import their existing zone by connecting a provider API token with read-only scope, reducing onboarding friction and errors.
**Steps.**
1. Write a short **ADR** selecting the first adapters by user demand and API stability (candidates: Cloudflare, AWS Route 53, DigitalOcean, Google Cloud DNS, Azure DNS, Namecheap, GoDaddy, Hetzner DNS, deSEC); record scopes needed (read-only), rate limits, record-type coverage and proprietary features per provider.
2. Extend the `ImportAdapter` trait (T-0157) with `authenticate`, `list_zones`, `export_zone` (normalized records plus provider-specific metadata such as proxied/orange-cloud flags and ALIAS/ANAME/redirect rules mapped to the HDD unsupported-type report); tokens are held encrypted for the import session only (default) and deleted after the import completes unless the owner opts into "re-sync later".
3. Implement each adapter against the provider API through the egress client with pinned hosts; pagination, rate-limit backoff, error mapping to owner-readable messages; no write operations exist in the adapter code (a static check forbids non-GET methods in the adapter modules).
4. Map provider semantics: Cloudflare proxied → HDD proxied with explicit confirmation, page rules/redirects reported as unsupported, Route 53 alias records → flatten/ALIAS handling or unsupported report, health-check-based routing → unsupported with explanation, geo/weighted routing → unsupported with explanation.
5. Present the import results in the existing parity UI (S-047) with a provider-specific section and the instructions for the NS change at the provider (human step) — HDD never changes anything at the provider.
6. Add **scoped token guidance**: step-by-step creation of minimal read-only tokens per provider (documented and screenshot-tested in docs tests where possible), token validation that rejects tokens with write scopes when the provider API exposes scopes (warn strongly otherwise).
7. Write tests against recorded provider API fixtures (VCR-style, sanitized) and against local fake servers for error conditions; no live provider calls in CI (live smoke tests optional with operator-provided read-only tokens).
8. Update docs and the capability matrix.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, adapters, UI sections, docs, fixture-based tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: for each adapter the fixture zones import with the documented mapping and unsupported-type report.
- A2: adapters cannot perform non-GET calls (static gate).
- A3: tokens are deleted after import by default (test).
- A4: provider hosts are pinned in the egress allowlist and nothing else is contacted.
- A5: tokens with write scopes trigger the documented warning/rejection where detectable.
**Tests.**
- Fixture replay, fake-server error tests, static gates.
**Notes.** Live smoke tests need operator tokens: UNVERIFIED(`capability_not_supplied`) otherwise.

### T-0542 · Tier 2: origin pools, load balancing and active health-based failover between origins
`P32` `[DP][API][UI]` · deps: T-0365, T-0369, T-0405 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Support multiple origins per site with health-aware distribution, preserving all security guarantees.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on the model: pools with weighted round robin, least-connections, consistent hashing by cookie/header (sticky sessions), priority tiers (primary/secondary), health-check definitions (path, interval, thresholds, expected status/body hash), and failover semantics; per-origin TLS settings and lockdown state; interaction with the SSRF guard (every origin validated independently).
2. Extend the data model (`origin_pools`, `origins`, memberships), snapshot representation (immutable per-site pool structures with precomputed weights), and API/UI (S-052 gains a pool editor; S-053 shows per-origin health).
3. Implement the **selector** in the proxy: lock-free per-request choice honoring weights and health, retry-on-another-origin for idempotent requests on connection failure (once), outlier ejection (passive health: consecutive 5xx/timeouts), slow-start for recovered origins, and connection pools per origin with bounded size.
4. Implement **active health checks** (T-0369 extension) with jitter, per-origin state machine (healthy, degraded, unhealthy, draining), hysteresis, and event/alert integration; maintenance mode ("drain") for planned changes.
5. Implement **sticky sessions** options safely: cookie-based affinity (`__Host-hdd_aff`, signed, no origin data), IP-hash affinity, header-hash; documented limitations with CGNAT.
6. Implement **security invariants:** a pool never mixes origins with different TLS verification modes without explicit per-origin settings; the secret origin header/mTLS is applied per origin; failover never sends traffic to origins failing lockdown verification when `strict_lockdown` is enabled; the WAF decision is made before pool selection (so failover cannot bypass inspection).
7. Implement metrics, events, and S-053 visualizations (table alternatives), plus bulk operations and API.
8. Write tests: distribution accuracy (chi-square tests for weights), failover timing, outlier ejection, retry rules, sticky behavior, drain, invariants, performance overhead (≤ 50 µs per request), chaos tests (origin flapping).
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, data model, selector, health logic, UI, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: weighted distribution within 2% of configured weights over 100k requests.
- A2: unhealthy origins are ejected within the configured threshold and re-admitted with slow start.
- A3: no request bypasses inspection through failover (test).
- A4: draining stops new connections without dropping in-flight requests.
- A5: overhead target met.
**Tests.**
- Unit/statistical, integration with multiple fake origins, chaos.
**Notes.** Tier 4 multi-region origin steering is out of scope.

### T-0543 · Tier 2: tenant-pinned rule-pack versions and staged tenant rollouts
`P32` `[API][UI][DP]` · deps: T-0425, T-0237 · size: M · owner: web
**Objective.** Give cautious tenants control over when platform rule updates apply to their sites.
**Steps.**
1. Extend policy documents with `rule_packs.pin` (pack → version or `latest-stable`/`latest`), constraints (security-critical hotfix packs may override pins for `critical` CVE-class patches only, with notice), and update windows (apply updates only during a chosen window or manually).
2. Implement the **tenant update flow**: a new platform version appears as "available update" with release notes and dry-run results on the tenant's own recent traffic (baseline replay); one-click "apply to monitor first" (shadow mode: rules log `would_block` without enforcing) for N days; then promote to enforce; rollback available at any time.
3. Implement **shadow evaluation** in the data plane: dual evaluation of old and new pack with only the old affecting verdicts while new results are recorded; bounded overhead (≤ 20% inspection CPU while active; automatically disabled under load); results aggregated for the diff report.
4. Add UI (S-058 pack section, S-092 revisions integration) and API; the platform admin console (S-107) shows pin distribution and lagging tenants; security-critical packs have a maximum pin lag (30 days) after which the platform forces the update with notice.
5. Implement compatibility rules: pins cannot reference versions older than N-2 or retired for security reasons; the engine keeps multiple compiled pack versions in memory bounded by the number of distinct pins in use.
6. Write tests: pin resolution, forced-update policy, shadow evaluation accuracy (verdicts identical to single evaluation of the pinned version), memory bounds with many pins, rollback, audit events, permissions.
7. Document trade-offs (older pins lack new protections) in the UI with plain language and in claims-lint terms.
8. Update the capability matrix and the owner docs.
**Deliverables.**
- policy extensions, shadow evaluator, UI/API, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: pinned tenants receive only their pinned version's verdicts (differential test).
- A2: shadow mode records `would_block` without affecting responses.
- A3: forced updates for critical packs occur at the policy deadline with notification.
- A4: memory use is bounded by distinct pins (test with 50 pins).
- A5: UI explains the security trade-off of pinning.
**Tests.**
- Differential, statistical, integration.
**Notes.** Pinning is opt-in; the default remains platform-managed rollout.

### T-0544 · Tier 2: opt-in static content cache with purge API
`P32` `[DP][API][UI][SEC]` · deps: T-0365, T-0410 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Reduce origin load and improve resilience during attacks for static assets, without risking cache poisoning or leaking private content.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on scope and risk: cache only explicitly enabled path patterns/extensions, `GET`/`HEAD`, 200/301/404 within limits, honoring `Cache-Control`/`Expires`/`Vary` conservatively, never caching responses with `Set-Cookie`, `Authorization` requests, `Cache-Control: private/no-store`, or non-idempotent methods; cache key = (site, normalized host, path, normalized allowlisted query params, `Accept-Encoding` variant, `Vary` headers); default off.
2. Implement an in-memory + optional disk cache (bounded: per-site and global size caps, LRU/TinyLFU, file-backed with `O_NOFOLLOW`, content-addressed names, no path derived from user input), request coalescing (collapsed forwarding), stale-while-revalidate/stale-if-error (bounded), and byte-range support.
3. Implement **cache poisoning defenses**: normalized keys; unkeyed header detection (headers that influence the response without being in `Vary` flagged via differential probing in monitor mode); reject responses with `Content-Type` mismatching extension for executable types; strip hop-by-hop; limit cached object size (default 5 MiB); never cache error pages generated by HDD; respect `Vary: *`; cache-deception protection (path-extension tricks like `/profile.php/x.css` are not cached unless the origin marks them public).
4. Implement **WAF ordering:** cache lookup occurs after inspection and ban checks (a banned IP is never served from cache); cache hits skip origin but still apply outbound policies (header policy; the outbound scanner runs at fill time for cacheable bodies).
5. Implement the **purge API** (`POST D/cache/purge` by URL, prefix, tag (surrogate keys via `Cache-Tag` header), or all) with rate limits, audit and permission; purge propagates to all proxy processes within 2 s.
6. UI: cache settings (patterns, TTL overrides within bounds, query param allowlist), hit ratio charts, purge dialog, and "cache bypass test" tool; metrics for hits/misses/stale/bytes saved.
7. Integrate with the shield (`cache.serve_static` action in ATTACK state, serving stale content when the origin is overloaded).
8. Write tests: key normalization properties, poisoning corpora (unkeyed header attacks, web cache deception patterns), concurrency (coalescing), eviction, disk safety, purge propagation, performance, claims-lint.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, cache module, purge API/UI, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: responses with cookies, private directives or authorization are never cached (test corpus).
- A2: banned IPs never receive cached content.
- A3: web-cache-deception and unkeyed-header corpora do not result in cross-user content exposure.
- A4: purge takes effect ≤ 2 s across proxy workers.
- A5: memory and disk caps are enforced.
**Tests.**
- Unit, property, integration, security corpora.
**Notes.** HDD is not a CDN; the cache is a resilience and cost optimization, off by default.

### T-0545 · Tier 2: antivirus scanning integration for uploads (clamd)
`P32` `[DP][SEC][OPS]` · deps: T-0297, T-0413 · size: M · owner: sec
**Objective.** Add optional malware scanning to multipart uploads on protected sites.
**Steps.**
1. ADR: ClamAV via `clamd` socket (local Unix or loopback TCP) as the first backend; interface trait `UploadScanner` for future engines; scanning happens in a separate sandboxed service (`hdd-avscan`) with its own user, seccomp, no network, memory limits, and size/time limits; HDD does not bundle signatures (operator installs ClamAV and `freshclam`; docs provided).
2. Implement streaming integration: upload parts that match configured paths are teed to the scanner with `INSTREAM` (size cap, default 25 MiB), decisions: `clean` (forward), `infected` (block with a branded response and event `malware_upload`, optional ban per policy), `error/timeout` (policy `fail_open` or `fail_closed` per site; default `fail_closed` for upload paths, with explicit warnings), and `skipped_large`.
3. Preserve fidelity: the original request is forwarded only after a clean verdict (buffer to a bounded temp file with secure permissions and cleanup) or streamed with deferred commit when the origin supports it (documented trade-offs); no scanning of encrypted archives beyond the engine's capability (reported as `unscannable`).
4. Implement events/metrics, signature database age monitoring (alerts when stale > 3 days), and S-097/S-056 settings.
5. Add privacy controls: no file contents retained after scanning; hashes (SHA-256) recorded optionally for correlation (owner opt-in).
6. Implement EICAR-based tests (the standard harmless test string) and benign upload suites, large file behavior, scanner outage behavior, concurrency limits, resource limits and sandbox escape attempts.
7. Document operator setup, performance expectations and limitations (no zero-day guarantees).
8. Update the capability matrix and claims evidence.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-avscan`, integration, settings UI, docs, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: EICAR uploads are blocked and benign uploads pass in `fail_closed` mode.
- A2: scanner outage behaves per configured policy with an alert.
- A3: temporary files are removed and permissions are 0600 (test).
- A4: the scanner service has no network access (sandbox test).
- A5: signature staleness alerts fire.
**Tests.**
- Integration with ClamAV container in the lab (UNVERIFIED if unavailable), unit tests.
**Notes.** Optional integration; documented as best-effort detection.

### T-0546 · Tier 2: alternate ACME CAs and external account binding (EAB)
`P32` `[DP][API][SEC]` · deps: T-0376, T-0377 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Reduce dependence on a single CA and allow operators to use CAs requiring EAB.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on supported directories (Let's Encrypt, ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services, Buypass if available, and private ACME CAs such as step-ca for internal use), differences in rate limits and validation methods, ARI support, and EAB requirements; verify current CA policies at build time (limits, supported challenge types, lifetimes).
2. Extend the ACME client wrapper with EAB (HMAC key id/key stored encrypted), per-account/per-CA settings, CA selection per site/org (`acme.ca_profile`), and automatic fallback order with budgets per CA (failure of the primary CA after N attempts triggers the fallback only if the operator enabled it).
3. Implement budget tracking per CA with provenance of limit values (configurable, verified against CA documentation at build time), CT and CAA interplay (CAA records must allow each CA the operator uses; the CAA wizard lists CA identifiers).
4. Implement private CA mode for internal/lab (`step-ca`), isolated from public CA settings, and clear UI labels ("Private CA: not trusted by browsers").
5. Update the certificate screens (S-050/S-051) to show CA, account and rate-limit state, and the admin certificate inventory (S-112) to show per-CA budgets.
6. Write tests with Pebble (and `step-ca` for private mode), covering EAB success/failure, CA fallback, CAA mismatch, budget exhaustion, ARI-driven renewals on supporting CAs, and key/account rotation.
7. Document operational guidance on choosing CAs and managing accounts.
8. Update claims and capability matrix.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, EAB support, CA profiles, UI changes, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: issuance works through at least two CA profiles in the test environment (Pebble variants) including one with EAB.
- A2: fallback occurs only when enabled and budgets allow.
- A3: CAA wizard lists correct identifiers per CA.
- A4: EAB secrets are encrypted and never logged.
- A5: private CA certificates are clearly labeled.
**Tests.**
- Integration with Pebble/step-ca, unit tests.
**Notes.** Live issuance on alternate CAs requires operator accounts: UNVERIFIED otherwise.

### T-0547 · Tier 5: WebAssembly plugin runtime (`wasmtime`) for custom detectors and transformations
`P32` `[DP][SEC][API]` · deps: T-0245, T-0248, T-0517 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Allow safe extension of the pipeline with sandboxed, resource-limited plugins without risking the data plane.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on the extension model and threat analysis: plugin stages limited to **pure inspection hooks** (`inspect_request(view) -> Findings`, `transform_response_headers`) operating on read-only views; no I/O, no clock, no randomness, no network; deterministic execution; why `wasmtime` (fuel metering, memory limits, WASI-free, component model) versus alternatives (`wasmer`, `wasm3`, native dynamic libraries rejected).
2. Define the **plugin ABI** (WIT/component model): inputs are normalized views (raw/decoded/canonical slices with explicit lengths), outputs are structured findings (category, score, evidence span ranges) validated and capped (max findings, max evidence length); versioned ABI with compatibility rules.
3. Implement the **host runtime:** per-plugin instance pools, fuel limits per invocation (e.g., 2 M instructions), memory cap (e.g., 16 MiB), wall-clock watchdog via epoch interruption, trap handling (a trapping plugin is treated as `no finding` plus a metric and auto-disable after repeated traps, never as fail-open of core rules), compile caching with signature verification, and per-tenant isolation (instances are never shared across tenants).
4. Implement **signing and distribution:** plugins are signed by the platform key (platform plugins) or by tenant keys (tenant plugins in enterprise plans) and uploaded through the API with validation (ABI conformance, size ≤ 2 MiB, static analysis for imports: only allowed host functions), lifecycle states (draft → monitor → enforce → retired) identical to rules, and rollback.
5. Provide an **SDK** (`hdd-plugin-sdk`, Rust) with templates, local test harness (`xtask plugin test`) running fixtures against the same host runtime, benchmarks, and examples (custom header anomaly, app-specific token format validator).
6. Implement **performance and fairness:** plugin budgets added to inspection budgets (T-0256); global fuel accounting per tenant; shed plugin execution before core inspection under load.
7. Security review: plugin escape attempts (malicious wasm: infinite loops, memory growth, out-of-bounds, huge tables), side channels documented, supply chain of plugins, and a lab pentest note.
8. Write tests: ABI conformance, limit enforcement, determinism (same input same output), trap handling, signature enforcement, tenant isolation, load/fairness simulation, and a corpus of hostile wasm modules.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, runtime, ABI, SDK, UI/API for plugin lifecycle, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: hostile modules cannot exceed fuel, memory or time limits and cannot affect other tenants (corpus).
- A2: plugin traps never cause fail-open of core detection.
- A3: unsigned/non-conforming plugins are rejected.
- A4: results are deterministic across runs.
- A5: overhead of a no-op plugin ≤ 20 µs per request.
**Tests.**
- Unit, hostile corpus, performance, integration.
**Notes.** The ADR slot referenced in P00 (`wasmtime`) is settled here.

### T-0548 · Tier 3: online DNSSEC signing (ECDSA P-256) with DS workflow and validation oracles
`P32` `[DP][API][UI][SEC]` · deps: T-0403, T-0388, T-0394 · size: XL · owner: dns
**Objective.** Offer optional per-zone DNSSEC with safe key management and verified correctness, without unsupported claims.
**Steps.**
1. ADR (building on the stub from T-0403): algorithm ECDSAP256SHA256 (13) default, optional Ed25519; NSEC vs NSEC3 (NSEC3 with opt-out disabled, minimal iterations, salt rotation) vs "NSEC with minimal responses/white lies" for online signing, zone enumeration implications, key hierarchy (CSK or KSK/ZSK), key storage in the envelope store, rollover schedules (ZSK 90 days pre-publish; KSK double-DS), signature validity and refresh (RRSIG validity 7 days, refresh at 1/3), clock sensitivity, and per-query signing vs pre-signing in the snapshot (pre-sign at snapshot build for static data; synthesize on-the-fly only for wildcard/NXDOMAIN proofs under policy).
2. Implement signing in the snapshot builder: DNSKEY/RRSIG/NSEC(3)/NSEC3PARAM generation, CDS/CDNSKEY publication (RFC 8078/7344) for automated DS updates where the parent supports it, deterministic signatures for ECDSA only if safe (document nonce handling), and zone size/performance impact controls (cap signed zones per plan).
3. Implement the **DS workflow** in the UI (S-049): enable signing → keys generated → DNSKEY published → UI shows the DS record to add at the registrar → verification (`delv`/in-process validation) → status `signed_and_validated`; disabling signing requires the reverse (remove DS first, wait, then disable) with enforced waiting and blockers to prevent bogus states.
4. Implement **rollover automation** with pre-publication, double signature phases, state machine with persistence, alerts, and manual override; emergency rollover procedures; time-injected tests of the schedule.
5. Handle **TCP/UDP size**: signed responses are larger; enforce TC=1 behavior with EDNS 1,232 cap, RRL tweaks for DNSKEY amplification (DNSKEY queries have bigger ratios: apply stricter limits, minimal-answers, and update the amplification suite thresholds with documented new ratio caps).
6. Update claims-lint (`dnssec_claim`) to allow statements only when the validation oracle passes for that zone; add the validation probe to monitoring (alerts on bogus/expired signatures with high priority).
7. Validate with oracles: `delv`, `dnsviz`, `ldns-verify-zone`, `unbound-host -v`, public validating resolvers (for the operator's own zones), zone transfer to secondary (signed zones via TSIG AXFR/IXFR must carry signatures; secondaries without DNSSEC support documented).
8. Write tests: key lifecycle, signature validity windows, NSEC chain correctness (property tests vs reference), rollovers, DS removal safety, amplification regression, interoperability with BIND/Knot as secondaries.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, signing engine, key manager, UI workflow, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: signed zones validate with `delv`, `dnsviz` and a validating Unbound in the lab.
- A2: rollovers complete without validation failures in simulated resolvers with cache behavior.
- A3: disabling signing cannot leave a DS without keys (state machine blocks).
- A4: amplification ratios stay within updated thresholds.
- A5: DNSSEC claims appear only for validated zones.
**Tests.**
- Lab validation, property tests, time-injected rollover tests.
**Notes.** DNSSEC increases operational risk; the UI recommends it only with a secondary that supports signed zones.

### T-0549 · Tier 3: HTTP/3 (QUIC) support with `quinn`/`h3` — ADR and implementation
`P32` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0354, T-0357, T-0463 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Serve HTTP/3 to clients while preserving all inspection, banning and hardening guarantees.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on the library (`quinn` + `h3`, or alternatives such as `quiche`/`s2n-quic`), maturity and security posture, amplification protections (address validation tokens, retry), 0-RTT policy (disabled by default due to replay risk; if enabled, only for idempotent requests with documented risk), connection migration policy, and interaction with the TLS crypto provider decision (T-0354).
2. Implement UDP/443 listeners (`SO_REUSEPORT`, GRO/GSO where safe), QUIC handshake with certificates from the shared store (SNI-based), ALPN `h3`, `Alt-Svc` advertisement on h1/h2 responses per-site opt-in with `ma` set conservatively, and `HTTPS`/SVCB DNS records with `alpn=h3` generated by the DNS engine when enabled.
3. Map HTTP/3 requests into the same pipeline (stage 0–19) with a shared request model; implement protocol-specific hardening: stream and header limits (QPACK table size caps, max field section size), rapid-reset-style abuse mitigation (stream reset rate limits per connection), concurrent stream caps, flow-control and memory budgets per connection, idle timeouts, connection ID handling and amplification factor limits before address validation (3x rule), and version negotiation handling.
4. Integrate client IP resolution and bans: QUIC source addresses are subject to the L7 jail on handshake (drop initial packets from banned IPs via the XDP/nft UDP/443 rules if available); migration events re-check bans.
5. Extend metrics, events and the visitor pages (HTTP/3 clients receive the same block/challenge pages).
6. Extend the XDP logic and nftables baseline for UDP/443 (already allowed for HTTP/3) with QUIC-aware limits (per-source initial packet rate caps).
7. Testing: interop with `curl --http3`, `quiche` client, browsers via Chrome/Firefox headless in the lab, `h3spec` (if available) conformance, fuzzing of QPACK and frame parsing, flood tests in the closed lab (QUIC initial floods), and performance comparison with h2.
8. Add documentation and the claims evidence ("HTTP/3 supported" only after tests).
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, QUIC listener, pipeline integration, hardening, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the same WAF fixtures produce identical verdicts over h1, h2 and h3 (differential test).
- A2: QUIC initial floods in the lab do not exhaust resources and legitimate h3 clients succeed.
- A3: 0-RTT is disabled by default and replay tests pass when enabled for idempotent requests.
- A4: banned IPs cannot complete QUIC handshakes (L7 jail and kernel).
- A5: interop tests pass with at least two independent clients.
**Tests.**
- Interop, conformance, fuzz, lab floods.
**Notes.** The `quinn`/`h3` ADR slot referenced in P00 is settled here.

### T-0550 · Tier 3: HTTP/2 SETTINGS and advanced TLS fingerprinting (JA4 family) for bot scoring
`P32` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0342, T-0340, T-0357 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Improve bot classification using protocol-level client fingerprints while handling their limits honestly.
**Steps.**
1. Extend the JA4 implementation (T-0342) to the JA4 family (JA4, JA4S optionally, JA4H for HTTP headers order/cookies presence, JA4X not required), with canonical computation tested against published vectors; compute HTTP/2 fingerprints from SETTINGS frame values and order, WINDOW_UPDATE initial values, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order (Akamai-style fingerprint concept).
2. Build and sign a **fingerprint reference database** of known clients (current browsers, popular HTTP libraries, curl, Go, Python requests/httpx, Java, scanners/headless tools) versioned and updated through packs; entries state confidence and date; unknown fingerprints are neutral, never penalized by default.
3. Integrate into **bot scoring:** consistency checks between claimed `User-Agent` and fingerprints (a Chrome UA with a Go TLS fingerprint scores high; a curl UA with curl fingerprint is consistent), rare-fingerprint tracking per site (new fingerprints seen from many IPs), and use as one signal among several with bounded weight (cannot ban alone; only influences challenge decisions and soft scores).
4. Handle **fingerprint randomization** (Chrome extension permutation, GREASE) with normalized forms; document the arms race and false-negative nature.
5. Privacy: fingerprints are stored as hashes with limited retention (30 days) in aggregated form; settings allow opting out per org.
6. Add S-062 views for fingerprint classes (counts, top unknown fingerprints) without raw identifiers beyond hash prefixes.
7. Write tests: vector tests, consistency scoring tables, randomization handling, FP controls with real browser captures (recorded from major browsers on common OSes, including mobile), performance (≤ 20 µs per connection).
8. Update docs and claims ("fingerprints are heuristics").
**Deliverables.**
- JA4 family, H2 fingerprinting, reference DB tooling, scoring integration, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: published JA4 test vectors reproduce exactly.
- A2: no ban is issued from fingerprint signals alone (test).
- A3: real browser captures are classified as consistent with their UAs (≥ 99% on the capture set).
- A4: retention and opt-out controls work.
- A5: overhead target met.
**Tests.**
- Vector tests, capture replay, performance.
**Notes.** Fingerprint evasion is easy for determined attackers; this improves cheap-bot detection only.

### T-0551 · Tier 6: ClickHouse (or alternative) analytics backend ADR and optional implementation

### T-0553 · Tier 4: health-probed automatic edge failover (DNS-level, multi-edge)
`P32` `[DP][OPS]` · deps: T-0478, T-0554, T-0525 · size: L · owner: dns
**Objective.** Automate the manual standby failover of Tier 1 using external health probing and safe decision logic.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on the decision architecture: probes from at least three independent vantage points (self-hosted `hdd-probe` agents on different providers or operator-chosen services), quorum-based decisions (e.g., 2 of 3 vantage points report failure for 3 consecutive intervals), flap protection, minimum dwell, maximum failover frequency, and operator override.
2. Implement probe agents (`hdd-probe`): lightweight Rust binary performing TLS+HTTP checks of canary hostnames through each edge IP, DNS checks, and reporting signed results to the control plane (HMAC/mTLS) with bounded rates; agents are not trusted for security decisions beyond health.
3. Implement the **failover controller** in `hdd-shield`/control plane: evaluates quorum, verifies standby readiness (snapshot parity, certificates, lockdown allowlists), applies the edge address set revision (T-0478), records audit events, and notifies; includes automatic failback with cool-down and verification; honors per-site and platform-level enable switches (default off).
4. Integrate with TTL strategy: dynamic lowering of proxied TTLs when the system detects instability (bounded), and awareness of resolver caching (documented expected delay).
5. Add failure scenarios: partial failures (one edge degraded), network partition between probes and control plane, probe agent compromise (a single malicious agent cannot trigger failover), split-brain avoidance (control plane is the single decision point).
6. UI: S-127 failover panel gains probe status, quorum view, decision history and simulation mode ("what would happen") without acting.
7. Test with the lab (multiple edges, controlled failures), chaos suite additions, time-accelerated decision tests, and security tests on agent authentication.
8. Document risks (false failovers) and recommended settings.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, `hdd-probe`, controller, UI, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a single failed or malicious probe agent cannot trigger failover (quorum tests).
- A2: real edge failure triggers failover within the configured decision time and answers change within 2 s of decision.
- A3: flapping conditions do not cause oscillation (hysteresis tests).
- A4: simulation mode never changes DNS.
- A5: failback requires verification and respects cool-down.
**Tests.**
- Lab multi-edge, chaos, security.
**Notes.** Requires the multi-node data plane (T-0554) or an operator-run replica edge.

### T-0554 · Tier 4: multi-node data plane and highly available control plane
`P32` `[DP][DB][OPS]` · deps: T-0211, T-0524, T-0522 · size: XL · owner: infra
**Objective.** Scale beyond one VPS: several edge nodes serving the same configuration, with the control plane tolerant of node loss.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on topology: N edge nodes (proxy + DNS + agents) sharing configuration snapshots from a primary control plane with a replicated Postgres (streaming replication with automatic failover via Patroni or manual promotion procedure), Redis replication/Sentinel or per-node local Redis with bus federation, shared ban state distribution across nodes (cross-node ban propagation ≤ 2 s), certificate distribution (encrypted store replication; ACME issuance performed by a single leader with distributed locks), and clock/time sync requirements.
2. Implement **node registration and identity:** mTLS with the internal PKI, node roles and capabilities, join tokens (single use, short TTL), node inventory in S-110 with drift detection, and revocation.
3. Implement **snapshot distribution** with per-node acks and monotonic versions; nodes serve the last good snapshot when disconnected; partition behavior documented (nodes continue enforcing local bans and rules; ban propagation resumes on reconnect with reconciliation).
4. Implement **leader election** for singleton jobs (ACME, rollups, webhook scheduling, report scheduling) using Postgres advisory locks or Raft-lite via `etcd`-free approach; verify no duplicate runs (idempotency keys) and no stuck leadership (leases with fencing tokens).
5. Implement **DNS multi-node:** all nodes serve the same zones; NOTIFY/transfers to secondaries from a designated node; consistent SOA serial published by the control plane; anycast not required (multiple NS addresses).
6. Adjust **rate limiting and counters** for multi-node: Redis-shared sliding windows (already Redis-based) with local fallback; per-node fairness; rollups merge node counters idempotently.
7. Implement **rolling upgrades** across nodes using T-0524 orchestration with health gates and canary node, and capacity-aware draining.
8. Test in the lab with 3 edge nodes + 2 control nodes: node loss, partition, leader failover, snapshot lag, ban propagation across nodes, upgrade, restore; update the chaos suite with multi-node experiments; document operational runbooks.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, node registration, distribution, leader election, runbooks, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: killing any single node (edge or control) does not interrupt protection; bans remain enforced on remaining nodes.
- A2: singleton jobs run exactly once under leader changes (fencing tests).
- A3: cross-node ban propagation ≤ 2 s p95 in the lab.
- A4: rolling upgrade across 3 edges has zero failed requests beyond the budget.
- A5: partitioned nodes serve safely and reconcile after healing.
**Tests.**
- Multi-node lab, chaos, upgrade tests.
**Notes.** Tier 1 is explicitly single-VPS; this task generalizes without changing Tier 1 behavior.

### T-0555 · Tier 4: BGP/RTBH and anycast integration guidance and tooling for ASN operators
`P32` `[OPS][DOC][SEC]` · deps: T-0476, T-0474 · size: L · owner: ops
**Objective.** Support operators who own an ASN with remotely triggered blackhole (RTBH) and optional scrubbing diversion, safely and in the lab first.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on scope: HDD does not run a full BGP stack by default; it integrates with the operator's routers via (a) a BGP speaker sidecar (BIRD or GoBGP) controlled by `hdd-shield` through a narrow API, or (b) provider/router APIs; RTBH only for destination prefixes the operator owns (never customer ranges), with community tags documented; guardrails to prevent self-blackholing the HDD edge.
2. Implement the **control interface:** `hddctl shield rtbh announce|withdraw <prefix> [--ttl]` with strict validation (prefix must be in `owned_prefixes`, not the edge's own service addresses unless `--i-understand-self-blackhole` is present for a single /32 attack target in an anycast context), TTLs, audit events, and automatic withdrawal when the attack subsides or at TTL expiry.
3. Integrate with the shield actions registry as an optional action with human approval by default (`rtbh.require_approval: true`) and a dry-run mode that renders the exact BGP announcements.
4. Document **anycast** designs (multiple edges announcing the same prefix, health-gated withdrawal), limits and operational complexity; provide BIRD/GoBGP configuration templates and a lab topology (`xtask lab --scenario bgp`) with FRR/BIRD containers for rehearsal.
5. Implement monitoring: BGP session state, announced prefixes inventory vs expected, unexpected announcements alerts (route leak detection by comparing against the allowlist), and RPKI ROA status checks against public data (read-only, egress allowlisted).
6. Safety: the integration refuses to start without explicit ASN/prefix configuration; all announcements require signed internal commands; state is reconciled on startup (no orphaned blackholes), and a break-glass withdraw-all command exists.
7. Test in the BGP lab: announce/withdraw correctness, TTL expiry, refusal of non-owned prefixes, reconciliation after restart, failure of the speaker, and dry-run output goldens.
8. Update the DDoS-readiness document with the new layer and its prerequisites, keeping claims honest (depends on upstream acceptance of communities).
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, `hddctl shield rtbh`, sidecar integration, lab scenario, docs, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: announcements for non-owned or self-service prefixes are refused (tests).
- A2: dry-run prints exact announcements and performs no changes.
- A3: TTL expiry withdraws routes and reconciliation prevents orphan blackholes.
- A4: unexpected announcement detection triggers alerts in the lab.
- A5: docs state prerequisites and limits and make no capacity claims.
**Tests.**
- BGP lab (BIRD/FRR), unit tests, goldens.
**Notes.** Requires operator ASN and upstream cooperation: otherwise UNVERIFIED(`capability_not_supplied`).

### T-0556 · Tier 6: organization SSO (OIDC and SAML) and SCIM provisioning
`P32` `[API][UI][SEC]` · deps: T-0117, T-0127, T-0128 · size: XL · owner: auth

ADR on protocols and libraries: OIDC (authorization code + PKCE, discovery, JWKS caching, `nonce`/`state`, `iss`/`aud`/`exp` validation, clock skew), SAML 2.0 (SP-initiated and IdP-initiated policy, signed assertions, encryption optional, XML signature wrapping defenses, strict schema validation, no external entity resolution); library choice (`openidconnect`, `samael` or a minimal in-house SAML validator reviewed and fuzzed); decision to support SAML via a vetted component only.

- A2: enforced SSO cannot be bypassed by password login except the documented break-glass path.
- A3: deprovisioning via SCIM revokes sessions within 60 s.
- A4: cross-org issuer/audience confusion fails.
- A5: conformance and interoperability tests pass with Keycloak (OIDC and SAML).

- Lab IdP integration, security corpus, fuzz.

### T-0557 · Tier 6: infrastructure-as-code provider (Terraform/OpenTofu) generated from the API
`P32` `[API][DOC]` · deps: T-0457, T-0458 · size: L · owner: api
**Objective.** Let customers manage HDD resources declaratively.
**Steps.**
1. ADR: build a Terraform provider (Go, using the plugin framework) generated and hand-tuned from the OpenAPI document and the Rust SDK semantics, versus a pure API-driven `hddctl apply` declarative tool; decision criteria include user demand, maintenance burden and language policy (the provider is the only non-Rust component, isolated in `ecosystem/terraform-provider-hdd/` with its own CI and clearly out of the Rust-first share calculation, recorded in DEVIATIONS).
2. Define resources: `hdd_domain`, `hdd_dns_record`, `hdd_dns_zone_settings`, `hdd_origin`, `hdd_tls_settings`, `hdd_waf_policy` (policy document), `hdd_rule`, `hdd_exception`, `hdd_access_list_entry`, `hdd_rate_limit_rule`, `hdd_alert_rule`, `hdd_webhook`, `hdd_api_key` (write-only secrets), `hdd_member`/`hdd_invitation` (limited), and data sources (domains, egress IPs, readiness score); import support for all.
3. Implement plan/apply semantics with ETags (`If-Match`) for optimistic concurrency, drift detection via read-after-write, idempotency keys, rate-limit aware retries, and clear diffs for policy documents (normalized JSON).
4. Handle sensitive values: write-only attributes for secrets, state redaction guidance, and no secret output in logs; support for provider-level API key from environment; permission scoping docs.
5. Safety features: `prevent_destroy` guidance for domains, plan-time validation using the API's dry-run/validation endpoints (policy validation without applying), and warnings when applying changes that reduce protection (WAF mode downgrade).
6. Generate docs and examples (full site example: domain, DNS, origin, TLS, WAF, alerting), registry-ready metadata (publishing is an operator decision), acceptance tests using `terraform-plugin-testing` against the local stack in CI.
7. Verify compatibility with OpenTofu.
8. Update docs, capability matrix and claims.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, provider code, docs/examples, acceptance tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the full-site example applies, re-plans with no diff, and destroys cleanly against the local stack.
- A2: import works for every resource type.
- A3: secrets never appear in plan output or logs.
- A4: policy downgrade changes produce warnings at plan time.
- A5: the provider passes tests with both Terraform and OpenTofu binaries.
**Tests.**
- Acceptance tests (provider framework), CI.
**Notes.** The provider is the only non-Rust deliverable; it is isolated and optional.

### T-0558 · Tier 6: billing and subscription integration (optional)
`P32` `[API][UI][DB][SEC]` · deps: T-0429, T-0146 · size: XL · owner: api
**Objective.** If the operator runs HDD as a paid service, integrate with a payment provider without storing card data.
**Steps.**
1. ADR on provider (Stripe-class) with PCI scope minimization: hosted checkout/portal only, no card data ever touching HDD servers, webhook-driven state, idempotent handlers, signature verification, and replay protection; choose the provider based on the operator's jurisdiction; support for "invoice/manual billing" mode for B2B.
2. Data model: customers, subscriptions, invoices (references only), plan mappings (`external_price_id`), proration policies, dunning states, trial periods, coupons; usage-based add-ons (extra domains, retention) via metered usage reporting from analytics (idempotent usage records).
3. Flows: upgrade/downgrade, trial, cancellation, payment failure (grace period with banners, no abrupt protection removal: protection continues during the grace period; policy documented), invoice history, receipts, tax handling delegated to the provider (tax ID collection fields), billing role permissions (`billing` role has plan/usage only).
4. Webhook receiver for provider events with HMAC verification, replay window, idempotency table, and strict state machine transitions; reconciliation job comparing provider state with local state daily.
5. Safety: billing failures never disable the data plane abruptly; downgrade enforcement uses the quota semantics of T-0429 (no data deletion); fraud/abuse signals feed the abuse queue.
6. UI: S-085 plan & usage screens with upgrade flows, invoices list, payment method link to hosted portal; admin tools for refunds/credits delegated to provider dashboard (links), manual overrides for support (audited).
7. Tests with the provider's test mode and fake servers: lifecycle scenarios, webhook replay/forgery, race conditions, currency/rounding, proration, dunning, reconciliation, plus security tests (signature bypass, parameter tampering of price ids, IDOR on invoices).
8. Legal/compliance notes (terms, refund policy templates) as operator-reviewed documents; claims-lint for pricing statements.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, billing module, UI, webhook receiver, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: no card data reaches HDD servers (network capture test against hosted flows).
- A2: webhook forgery and replay are rejected.
- A3: payment failure never drops protection abruptly (grace period tests).
- A4: reconciliation detects and reports divergences in the lab scenarios.
- A5: billing role cannot access security data (permission tests).
**Tests.**
- Provider test mode, fakes, security tests.
**Notes.** Disabled in `owner_only` mode; billing integration is explicitly optional.

### T-0559 · Tier 6: explainable ML-assisted anomaly scoring (offline-trained, bounded influence)
`P32` `[DP][SEC][QA]` · deps: T-0349, T-0340, T-0451 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Add an optional statistical layer that surfaces novel anomalies without becoming an opaque blocker.
**Steps.**
1. ADR defining the philosophy: ML never makes a ban decision alone; it produces an **advisory anomaly score** feeding soft scores and owner-facing insights, with caps on influence, full explainability (top contributing features), per-site baselines, and an off switch; training is **offline** on synthetic and opt-in anonymized aggregated features (no raw payloads), models are small (gradient-boosted trees or isolation forests/logistic regression), exported to a deterministic Rust inference implementation (no runtime dependency on Python).
2. Define the **feature set** (privacy-safe): request rate patterns, path-template entropy and novelty, parameter count/length distributions per template, character class ratios, header order/set deviations, method/content-type combos, response status patterns, session-level sequences (bounded), time-of-day features, error ratios; no raw strings are stored in features beyond hashed tokens.
3. Build the **training pipeline** (`xtask ml train`): data from the Vuln-Lab runs, benign corpora, and synthetic traffic generators; cross-validation, calibration, evaluation on held-out sets, false-positive analysis at fixed operating points, drift detection, model cards (`docs/ml/MODEL-CARD.md`) with intended use, limits and bias considerations, and reproducible builds of model artifacts (hash-pinned, signed with pack signing).
4. Implement **inference** in `hdd-waf-core` as an optional detector with strict budgets (≤ 50 µs per request, no allocation in the hot path), deterministic outputs, per-site calibration of thresholds using local baselines (EWMA), and shadow mode by default (records scores without influence) for at least 14 days before enabling influence.
5. UI: anomaly insights panel (S-072 extension) showing flagged requests/path templates with explanations ("unusually long parameter for this endpoint; rare character mix"), an owner feedback loop (mark as normal) feeding local baselines (not global training without opt-in), and clear labeling "advisory".
6. Safety: model files are signed; invalid models are rejected; a model fault falls back to disabled with an alert; adversarial robustness tests (evasion by mimicry, poisoning attempts via crafted benign-looking requests to shift baselines): baseline updates are rate limited and bounded.
7. Evaluate on AC-06 (no increase in false positives with influence enabled) and AC-39 (no reduction in detection); document that ML does not replace signatures.
8. Governance: opt-in data sharing policy for model improvement (off by default), privacy impact notes, and claims-lint for ML statements ("advisory anomaly detection", never "AI-powered protection" without evidence).
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, feature extractor, training pipeline, inference, UI insights, model card, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: inference meets the latency and allocation budgets.
- A2: enabling influence causes zero additional false positives on the benign corpora and no reduction in AC-39 detections.
- A3: poisoning attempts cannot shift baselines beyond the configured bound (adversarial tests).
- A4: models are signed and invalid models are rejected.
- A5: the UI shows explanations for every flagged item.
**Tests.**
- Evaluation harness, adversarial tests, performance benchmarks.
**Notes.** If evaluation does not show a clear benefit at acceptable risk, the task closes with the ADR documenting "not adopted".

### T-0560 · Backlog governance: tier index, prioritization process and re-planning for later revisions
`P32` `[DOC][QA]` · deps: T-0540 · size: S · owner: pm
**Objective.** Keep the backlog healthy, ordered and linked to evidence so future work starts from facts.
**Steps.**
1. Maintain `docs/BACKLOG.md` as the single index of Tier 2 to Tier 6 items with: task id, tier, theme, value hypothesis, dependency on operator inputs, estimated size, risk class, status (`not_started|in_progress|done|deferred|dropped`), and links to ADRs and gate notes.
2. Define the **prioritization process**: inputs are operator feedback, support tickets, abuse trends, attack matrix gaps (from AC-07/AC-49 results), exposure/advisory events, performance limits (capacity model triggers), cost and complexity; scoring (value × urgency × confidence ÷ effort) recorded per item; quarterly review with the operator.
3. Define **triggers** that pull items forward: for example ClickHouse when sustained ingestion exceeds 60% of the measured Postgres limit; multi-node when availability SLO requires; HTTP/3 when client share exceeds a threshold in analytics; DNSSEC on customer demand with a secondary that supports it; WASM plugins when ≥ 3 customers request custom detectors that cannot be expressed as rules; cache when origin load or attack resilience needs it.
4. Define **entry criteria** for any backlog task: operator approval for architecture-changing items, STRIDE delta started, test plan, acceptance criteria, and rollback plan; and **exit criteria**: gate report, claims updates, docs, and evidence in the acceptance catalog (new AC ids appended after AC-54 without renumbering).
5. Provide a **re-planning template** for later spec revisions: process for adding new tasks beyond T-0560 while keeping `INDEX.md` consistent (new ids T-0579+ in new phases P34+), and for deprecating tasks.
6. Review the **attack matrix gaps** (ATK ids with status not PASS) and add backlog items with links to the failing fixtures; review the capability matrix for `planned` entries.
7. Review **DEVIATIONS.md** for deviations that should be reversed when the underlying constraint disappears (for example UI stack choice, PDF path, plugin-language policy) and schedule decisions.
8. Present the backlog summary to the operator at the end of the project and record the operator's priorities.
**Deliverables.**
- `docs/BACKLOG.md`, prioritization process doc, triggers list, v5.1 re-planning template
**Acceptance.**
- A1: every backlog item has all required fields and no orphan dependencies.
- A2: triggers are measurable and tied to metrics that exist.
- A3: attack-matrix gaps are represented as backlog items or accepted limits.
- A4: the operator's priorities are recorded.
- A5: `INDEX.md` includes the backlog tasks with correct statuses.
**Tests.**
- Index consistency checks (`xtask tasks index --check`).
**Notes.** This is the closing task of the specification; execution of backlog items continues under the same rules.

## PHASE P33: Runtime profiles, local mode, 24/7 hosting and defense completeness (T-0561 to T-0578) · milestone M13 · gate G33

Requirement prefix `RTM`. Goal: one product that runs in two ways. **Local:** on an operator's computer (Windows, macOS or Linux, no Docker required), live only while it runs. **Hosted:** on a server, running 24/7 under a supervisor with backups, upgrades and runbooks. Plus the controls that make coverage as complete as can honestly be shown: an access gate for sensitive paths, API discovery with positive security, business-flow protection, and a coverage map with a "does not cover" list. Read Part C, C18 and C19 and rules R-31 and R-32 first.

Design rules for this phase:
- One code path (R-31). Profile-dependent code lives only in `hdd-local`, `hdd-common::kv`, `hdd-common::profile` and the `Enforcer` factory; `xtask profile-lint` enforces it. Wherever another task says "Redis" for runtime state it means the `KvStore`, `Bus` and `Limiter` traits, and only `hdd-common::kv` talks to Redis (`xtask kv-lint`). Tests that say "real Redis" or "testcontainers" run against both backends, and on a builder without Docker (Track L) against the embedded PostgreSQL and in-process stores.
- Nothing weakens security to be convenient locally. There is no `DEV_MODE`.
- Honest availability: local protection exists only while HDD runs; hosted availability is measured, not promised (section 4).

**Execution order within P33 (the numbering is not the order).** T-0561 to T-0563 run immediately after gate G00 (delivery slice R0, section 0.8) because later phases build on the profile model, the store traits and the embedded database. T-0564 to T-0570 run as soon as their dependencies exist (slice R1, the local walking skeleton, and R2). T-0571 to T-0574 run with the deployment phases (slice R3). T-0575 to T-0577 run after P15 and P17 (slice R4). T-0578 and gate G33 close the phase.

Gate G33 passes when: AC-55 (local runtime, including `profile-parity` with zero verdict differences), AC-56 (24/7 hosting readiness), AC-57 (access gate, API discovery and business flows) and AC-58 (coverage map integrity and absolute-wording lint) pass; the local suite is green on Windows, macOS and Linux CI runners; the hosting check passes on the pilot server with a successful reboot test and a restore drill; and the coverage map lists every mapped category with a status and the "does not cover" section.

### T-0561 · Runtime profile model, capability matrix and the parity contract
`P33` `[OPS][SEC][DOC]` · deps: T-0004, T-0006, T-0009 · size: L · owner: infra
**Objective.** Make `local` and `hosted` first-class, validated profiles that share one code path, and make "same behavior in both" a tested contract.
**Steps.**
1. Write the ADR "One code path, two runtime profiles" recording R-31, the list of things a profile may change, and the enforcement mechanisms below.
2. Add `runtime:` to the live-profile schema (section 8) and the environment variables of B10 (`HDD_RUNTIME_PROFILE`, `HDD_DATA_DIR`, `HDD_LOCAL_*`, `HDD_KV_BACKEND`, `HDD_HOSTING_PROFILE`) in `hdd-common::profile`, with typed validation and JSON Schema output.
3. Encode the capability matrix of C18.2 as code (`Profile::capabilities()`): for each capability (authoritative DNS on 53, kernel enforcement, ACME, `saas`, open signup, `full_ns`, LAN exposure, embedded database, memory store) the result is `allowed`, `allowed_with_ack`, or `unavailable(ERR-LOCAL-001, reason)`. Every refusal path in the API and UI goes through this function.
4. Implement `xtask profile-lint`: fails if `runtime.profile`, `Profile::` or profile `cfg` checks appear in the detection, pipeline, authentication or tenancy crates, or if any crate other than `hdd-common::kv` uses the Redis client (`xtask kv-lint`).
5. Implement `xtask profile-parity`: runs the core SQLi set (M1 to M6 plus variants), the benign corpus, the BOLA suite and a ban lifecycle scenario under both profiles with the same fixtures and compares the decision fields (action, category, subtype, rule_id, hardness, score, threshold, vector, field, evidence) and the ban intent (reason, scope, TTL step), excluding identity key, enforcement backend, `config_revision` and timestamps; any other difference fails (AC-55).
6. Extend `hddctl preflight` with a "what can run here" section: for the detected platform and profile, which acceptance checks can run and which are UNVERIFIED(`environment_unsupported`) with the reason, so a Windows builder without Docker gets an honest plan instead of an error.
7. Extend the first-response protocol output (section 9) with the build-track decision (Track H or Track L) computed from discovery results.
8. Write `docs/LOCAL.md` and `docs/HOSTING.md` skeletons with the comparison table of C18.2.
**Deliverables.**
- profile schema and validation, capability matrix, `profile-lint`, `kv-lint`, `profile-parity` skeleton, preflight section, ADR, docs skeletons
**Acceptance.**
- A1: `local` with `deployment_mode: saas`, open signup or `full_ns` is refused with `ERR-LOCAL-001` at config load and in the API.
- A2: `xtask profile-lint` fails when a profile check is added to `hdd-waf-core` (injected-violation test) and passes on the clean tree.
- A3: `xtask kv-lint` fails when a Redis client call appears outside `hdd-common::kv`.
- A4: `profile-parity` runs on the available backends and reports zero differences on the seed corpus.
- A5: on a machine without Docker, Postgres, Redis, `nft` and `dig`, `hddctl preflight` prints Track L and a correct list of runnable and UNVERIFIED checks, and exits 0 for the build track.
**Tests.**
- Unit: matrix table tests; config validation; integration: parity harness; xtask lint tests with injected violations.
**Notes.** The matrix is the single place that decides what a profile may do. Adding a capability without adding it to the matrix fails `xtask profile-lint`.

### T-0562 · `KvStore`, `Bus` and `Limiter` traits with Redis and in-process backends, and the conformance suite
`P33` `[DP][SEC][QA]` · deps: T-0561 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Let every runtime-state feature work against Redis (hosted) or in-process memory (local) with identical semantics, proven by one shared suite.
**Steps.**
1. Define the traits in `hdd-common::kv` exactly as C18.3: `KvStore` operations, the named atomic operations (`rate_window_check`, `challenge_nonce_consume`, `offence_incr_with_decay`, `flow_signal_update`), `Bus` with revisioned messages and gap detection, `Limiter` with `counter`, `exact` and `gcra` algorithms. Keys follow B5.12.
2. Implement `RedisKv` on `fred` with Lua scripts for the named operations (`EVALSHA`, `NOSCRIPT` recovery), pipelining, a circuit breaker with half-open probes, and TLS/auth required.
3. Implement `MemoryKv`: sharded maps with per-key TTL (hierarchical timing wheel or lazy expiry plus a sweeper), named operations under shard locks, a bounded `Bus` on `tokio::sync::broadcast` with revision counters and drop counters, size caps with eviction by TTL then LRU, and **pinned namespaces** (bans, sessions) that are never evicted but are capped with a clear error.
4. Implement the restart contract of C18.3: a `rehydrate(ctx)` step that loads bans, offences and sessions from Postgres into `MemoryKv` before listeners open, with a metric for rows loaded and time taken.
5. Write the conformance suite `kv_conformance` (TTL accuracy ±50 ms, atomicity under 64 concurrent tasks, bus ordering, gap detection and resync, eviction rules, pinned namespaces, large-value limits, key-length limits) and run it against both backends in CI; the Redis run uses testcontainers on Track H and is `UNVERIFIED(environment_unsupported)` on Track L.
6. Publish the usage contract for the tasks that consume the traits: ban store (T-0316), rate limiter (T-0333, including the exact algorithm for auth endpoints and the counter bound), challenge nonces (T-0108, T-0337), session cache (T-0113), config bus (T-0211), live event feed (T-0446), credential-stuffing counters (T-0343), campaign detection (T-0325) and the gate and flow engines (T-0575, T-0577). Those tasks use the traits from the start (section 0.9; `xtask kv-lint` fails any direct Redis use), so there is no later port; this task provides the traits, both backends, the helpers and the suite.
7. Add `MET-hdd_kv_ops_total` and `MET-hdd_kv_latency_seconds`, and a startup refusal: `HDD_KV_BACKEND=memory` with `runtime.profile: hosted` and more than one registered service process.
8. Benchmark both backends (criterion): `MemoryKv` limiter check ≤ 5 µs p99, `RedisKv` ≤ 1 ms p99 in-datacenter.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-common::kv` (traits, two backends), conformance suite, ports, metrics, benchmarks
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the conformance suite passes on `MemoryKv` and, where Redis is available, on `RedisKv` with identical results.
- A2: `rate_window_check` agrees with a reference model on 10,000 random request sequences for the counter algorithm (within its documented bound) and exactly for the exact algorithm, on both backends.
- A3: the `rehydrate` contract is tested against a fixture durable source (bans, offences, sessions); the end-to-end restart test with real tables is acceptance A6 of T-0564.
- A4: the bus delivers revisions in order and signals a resync on a forced gap.
- A5: memory use is bounded under a key flood (cap and eviction counters verified); pinned namespaces never evict.
**Tests.**
- Conformance, property tests of TTL and eviction, loom or shuttle tests on the shard-lock logic, chaos (kill Redis), benchmarks.
**Notes.** This task changes how existing tasks store state; it must not change what they decide. The differential check is `profile-parity`.

### T-0563 · Embedded PostgreSQL manager and `cargo xtask db up`
`P33` `[OPS][SEC][DB]` · deps: T-0561, T-0009 · size: L · owner: infra
**Objective.** Give a machine without Docker or a database server a real, private PostgreSQL that HDD manages, so the build, the tests and the local profile all run against real Postgres.
**Steps.**
1. Spike and ADR: choose between the `postgresql_embedded` crate and an equivalent (own downloader over a pinned binary distribution); require SHA-256 and signature verification against the distributor's published checksums, a pinned download host that must be in `egress_allowlist`, an offline bundle path (`--bundle <file>`), and per-OS binaries (Windows x64, macOS arm64 and x64, Linux x64 and arm64).
2. Implement `hdd-local::pg`: install into the data directory, `initdb` with a generated superuser password (not echoed), `scram-sha-256` only, `listen_addresses` loopback (or a Unix socket where available), a restrictive `pg_hba.conf`, `fsync` on, data checksums on, memory settings sized from the host, and a unique port chosen from a configured range.
3. Implement lifecycle: start, wait for readiness, fast shutdown on exit, crash recovery messages, stale `postmaster.pid` handling, and a version marker so a future major-version upgrade runs through dump and restore (never an in-place guess).
4. Create the database and the `hdd_owner` role with a generated password stored in the data directory (0600); the migrations of T-0105 create the other roles, whose generated passwords the manager stores the same way; expose connection URLs to the services through files, not command lines or environment variables.
5. Implement `cargo xtask db up|down|reset|status` for builders (default data directory under `target/` or a configured path), used by tests when Docker is absent, and `hdd-local backup|restore` (logical dump with `pg_dump -Fc --no-unlogged-table-data` via the bundled tools, as `hdd_backup` once T-0105 creates it and as the embedded superuser before that, encrypted at rest with a key from the data directory).
6. Implement ports-in-use detection and clear errors (`ERR-LOCAL-004` guidance), disk-space preflight (at least 2 GiB free), and antivirus-friendly behavior notes for Windows.
7. Add `MET-hdd_embedded_db_up` and `AUD-runtime.embedded_db` events; add the supply-chain record (versions, digests) to the SBOM.
8. Add the embedded server to CI on all three operating systems with a sample migration; when T-0105 and T-0128 land, their migration, RLS and BOLA suites are added to the same jobs and run unchanged (they depend on this task, not the reverse).
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-local::pg`, xtask commands, ADR, backup and restore, CI jobs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: on a clean Windows runner with no Docker and no Postgres, `cargo xtask db up` produces a working database that accepts a sample migration as `hdd_owner`.
- A2: a binary with a wrong checksum is refused and nothing is started (negative test).
- A3: from another local user account or a LAN address, the database accepts no connection (listener and `pg_hba` tests).
- A4: backup then restore into a fresh data directory reproduces the schema and data (hash comparison).
- A5: once T-0105 and T-0128 exist, their migrations and the RLS cross-tenant tests pass unchanged against the embedded server (a CI job those tasks add).
**Tests.**
- Integration on three OS runners; negative checksum test; listener scan; restore test.
**Notes.** Embedded does not mean weaker: same migrations, same roles, same RLS (R-31). If the embedded route proves unreliable on an OS, the ADR records the substitute (an external server or Compose) and `hdd-local doctor` says so.

### T-0564 · `hdd-local` supervisor: lifecycle, readiness, crash policy, first run, doctor and self-test
`P33` `[OPS][SEC][DP]` · deps: T-0562, T-0563, T-0073, T-0134, T-0208, T-0211 · size: XL · owner: infra
**Objective.** One command that starts, supervises and stops the whole product on a personal computer, safely, with honest status.
**Steps.**
1. Create the `hdd-local` binary with the commands of C18.4 and the in-process service runner: each service crate exposes `run(ctx)`; the supervisor owns the shared `MemoryKv`, the configuration, the data directory and the embedded database handle.
2. Implement the start order and readiness gates of C18.4 (lock, light doctor, database, migrations, rehydrate, snapshot compile and cache, api/web/worker, listeners, DNS), with a 60 s database timeout and precise error messages.
3. Implement task supervision: panic isolation per task (R-09), exponential backoff restarts (1 s to 30 s), the five-in-ten-minutes stop rule with a UI banner and `AUD-` event, and `MET-hdd_watchdog_restarts_total`.
4. Implement graceful shutdown (signal and console-close handling per OS, 10 s drain, database fast shutdown, lock release; on Windows the abbreviated path and a Job Object, C18.4) and the single-instance lock with stale-lock detection.
5. Implement first run: secret generation into the data directory, one-time bootstrap token file (hash stored, 15-minute expiry), printing only the setup URL and the token file path, and `hdd-local token show` for interactive terminals.
6. Implement sleep and wake detection (OS power events with the late-ticker fallback), re-validation of listeners and database, correct expiry of time-bound state, and `resumed_after_seconds` in the runtime page.
7. Implement `hdd-local doctor` (ports, disk, permissions, clock, antivirus or firewall hints, database, certificates, listeners) and `hdd-local selftest` (starts a temporary instance, runs the six mandated payloads through the inspect API and a sandbox route, verifies loopback-only binding of the control plane, verifies backup and restore of a scratch database, and prints PASS/FAIL per item with evidence).
8. Implement `status` with real values only (profile, stores, uptime, listeners, last restarts, snapshot age) and `logs --follow`, with JSON logs rotating at 10 MiB × 5.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-local` binary and library, supervisor, doctor, self-test, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: from an empty data directory, `hdd-local run` reaches "ready" and `selftest` passes on Windows, macOS and Linux CI runners without Docker.
- A2: killing any single service task results in a restart within 5 s and no outage of the other services (fault injection).
- A3: `Ctrl+C`, SIGINT and SIGTERM produce a clean shutdown within 15 s; on Windows console-close, logoff and shutdown produce the abbreviated shutdown within 5 s; in every case no database process is orphaned, and a stale one is stopped at the next start.
- A4: a second `hdd-local run` against the same data directory refuses to start with a clear message.
- A5: a simulated 10-minute sleep triggers the resume path, and bans that expired during the sleep are treated as expired.
- A6: after a restart of `hdd-local`, bans and sessions created earlier are enforced before the first request is accepted (restart test with the real tables).
**Tests.**
- Integration with real processes; fault injection; clock-jump test; per-OS signal tests.
**Notes.** The supervisor never needs administrator rights for its default configuration.

### T-0565 · Loopback client identity, local ban semantics and the tunnel listener
`P33` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0564, T-0315, T-0316, T-0318, T-0327 · size: M · owner: dp
**Objective.** Make bans, rate limits and reputation work when every local client is `127.0.0.1`, without banning the operator's own browser.
**Steps.**
1. Extend client-IP resolution (T-0315) with the local identity rules of C18.5: keyed `lo:` identities from a user-agent and accept-language HMAC, `X-HDD-Test-Client` labels, bounded registry (4,096 entries, LRU), and the per-listener trust rule (provider headers trusted only on the dedicated tunnel listener).
2. Implement the dedicated `tunnel_http` listener (default loopback port 8081) with provider header mappings (`CF-Connecting-IP`, `X-Forwarded-For`, configurable header) and strict header parsing (single value, valid address, no private ranges accepted as client addresses from the internet side).
3. Scope `lo:` bans to the protected site and make sure the platform surfaces (served directly by `hdd-web` and `hdd-api` in the local profile, or through the proxy when `dogfood` is on) never consult them (R-19); implement one-click unban in S-067 and `hdd-local unban --all-loopback`.
4. Implement the `loopback_client_identity: single` guard (allowed only when every site is in `monitor` or `log` mode, otherwise `ERR-LOCAL-001`).
5. Make the never-ban rules (T-0318) profile-aware: in `local`, loopback is not never-banned, platform addresses and the operator's configured LAN addresses are.

Write tests: sqlmap-like user agent banned while the browser identity is unaffected; same user agent from two tools shares an identity (documented); registry flood stays bounded; header spoofing on the normal listener is ignored; spoofing on the tunnel listener uses the header only when the provider is configured; label rotation through the tunnel listener creates no new identities; a tunnel-listener request without the provider header gets 421.

### T-0567 · Local control-plane hardening: rebinding, CSRF, Private Network Access, bootstrap and loopback-only proof
`P33` `[UI][SEC]` · deps: T-0564, T-0075, T-0080, T-0134 · size: L · owner: sec
**Objective.** Make a browser-reachable control plane safe against hostile web pages and rebinding.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the exact `Host` allowlist (`HDD_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, derived from the surface names only) as the first middleware on every control-plane listener, answering `ERR-LOCAL-003` without routing or detail, plus the loopback-alias behavior of C18.7 item 1 (308 to the surface name, no cookies, `/healthz` only).
2. Implement the `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` checks of C18.7 item 2 for cookie-authenticated requests only (bearer-only requests are exempt), with the separate rules for WebSocket upgrades, SSE and other GET requests (browsers send no `Origin` on same-origin GET) and mutations, including browsers that omit `Sec-Fetch-*` (fall back to a strict `Origin`/`Referer` rule; missing both on a cookie-authenticated mutation is refused).
3. Ensure no CORS headers are ever emitted by the control plane and that Private Network Access preflights (`Access-Control-Request-Private-Network`) are answered without an allow header; add tests for each.
4. Implement the `/setup` flow (S-136 local): bootstrap token verification (constant time, hash compare, single use, 15-minute expiry, rate limit), disappearance after the first platform owner exists, and MFA enrollment before the first admin session is usable.
5. Implement the loopback-only verification used by `hdd-local selftest`: enumerate own listeners, then from a non-loopback local address try to connect to each control-plane port and fail on any success.
6. Ensure secrets never appear on command lines or child-process environments (inspect the process table in a test).
7. Build a **hostile-page test fixture**: a page served from another origin (and a DNS rebinding server in the lab) that tries fetch, form POST, EventSource, WebSocket and image-beacon CSRF against the local control plane; every attempt must fail.
8. Document the shared-machine limitation and the residual risks in `docs/LOCAL.md`.
**Deliverables.**
- middleware, `/setup` flow, verification routines, hostile-page fixture, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: requests with a rebinding `Host` header receive `ERR-LOCAL-003` before any handler runs (test with 50 shapes: case, trailing dot, port variants, IDN, IPv6 literal).
- A2: the hostile-page fixture cannot read or mutate anything through fetch, form, SSE or WebSocket (browser test).
- A3: the bootstrap token works once, expires after 15 minutes, and `/setup` returns 404 after the first owner exists.
- A4: the self-test fails when a control-plane port is deliberately bound to `0.0.0.0` (injected-fault test).
- A5: no secret appears in the process table or `/proc`-equivalent listings during a run.
**Tests.**
- Browser tests; lab rebinding server; fault injection; process-listing test.
**Notes.** This is AC-55's security core; a failure here blocks the local profile from release.

### T-0572 · 24/7 supervision: systemd watchdog, restart policy, last-known-good snapshot autonomy, disk guard
`P33` `[DP][OPS]` · deps: T-0522, T-0364, T-0211, T-0375, T-0388 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Make the data plane survive crashes, reboots and control-plane outages without human action, and say so only as far as it is tested.
**Steps.**
1. Generate systemd units with the settings of C18.11 item 1 (`Type=notify`, restart policy with `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` in `[Unit]`, `WatchdogSec`, `OnFailure=hdd-alert@%n` plus a restart-rate alert, `RestartSteps` only where systemd is 254 or newer, `MemoryMax`, `OOMScoreAdjust`, `Wants=` not `Requires=` on stores) and Compose equivalents (restart policy, healthchecks).
2. Implement `sd_notify` watchdog pings from every service main loop in a way that stops pinging when the event loop is blocked (test with an injected stall).
3. Implement the last-known-good snapshot: atomic write after each swap to `HDD_SNAPSHOT_CACHE_DIR` (write temp, fsync, rename), integrity hash, schema version, and startup loading in proxy and DNS when Postgres or Redis is unavailable, with the degraded banner, disabled config changes, and `MET-hdd_snapshot_lkg_age_seconds`.
4. Implement the bounded disk spool for events during store outages (256 MiB, oldest dropped with counters) and replay on recovery with deduplication by `(ray_id, ts)`.
5. Implement the disk guard of C18.11 item 4 (`HDD_DISK_GUARD_PCT`) with `MET-hdd_disk_guard_active`, alerts, and the rule that bans, audit rows and the database are never auto-deleted.
6. Add chaos tests: kill each service, kill Postgres, kill Redis, fill the disk, stall an event loop, reboot the VM; assert enforcement continues from the snapshot and local ban cache, inspection never fails open (R-26), and recovery needs no manual step.
7. Add the metrics and alert rules (T-0525 family) for restarts, watchdog misses, snapshot age and spool depth.
8. Document the exact degraded-mode behavior table in `docs/HOSTING.md`.
**Deliverables.**
- unit generators, watchdog integration, snapshot cache, spool, disk guard, chaos tests, alerts
**Acceptance.**
- A1: with Postgres and Redis stopped, restarting proxy and DNS yields correct answers and enforcement from the cached snapshot within 10 s.
- A2: an injected event-loop stall makes systemd restart the service within `WatchdogSec` plus 5 s.
- A3: during a 10-minute store outage no request is passed uninspected (differential test), and events spooled during it appear after recovery without duplicates.
- A4: at 90% simulated disk usage events are sampled and exports refused; bans still write.
- A5: a VM reboot returns all services to ready with no manual step (HC-19 evidence).
**Tests.**
- Chaos suite on a VM; unit tests on snapshot atomicity (power-cut simulation); spool replay tests.
**Notes.** This task proves resilience of the single-node design; it does not make one node highly available.

### T-0575 · Access gate (S-131): protect sensitive paths before they reach the origin
`P33` `[UI][API][DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0355, T-0362, T-0343, T-0232, T-0242, T-0337, T-0562, T-0106, T-0114 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Let an owner put an HDD-enforced barrier in front of administration areas, database tools and debug endpoints of an origin that may itself be vulnerable.
**Steps.**
1. Add `access_gate_rules` and `access_gate_credentials` (B5.6) with migrations, RLS and indexes; add `PERM-gate.*`, `AUD-gate.*`, `ERR-GATE-*` and `MET-hdd_gate_decisions_total` (B4.2, B7, B8, B9).
2. Implement stage 8a: a compiled path trie per site with both raw and canonical match, priority and `allow_paths`, executed before rate limiting and inspection with a 20 µs budget; build the canonicalization (decode, dot-segments, repeated slashes, path parameters, optional case folding) on the WAF canonicalizer (T-0242) so both agree.

Implement the policies: `ip_allowlist`; `hdd_login` (gate login page, HDD-generated secrets stored as HMAC-SHA-256 and operator-chosen passwords through the password library of T-0106 behind the hashing semaphore, optional TOTP via T-0114, server-side session in `KvStore`, `__Host-hdd_gate` cookie, binding to user-agent hash and IP bucket, CSRF, proof of work when under attack); `basic` (consume and strip `Authorization`, cache a successful verification for at most 60 s, warn on origin challenge conflict); `signed_link` (secret in the URL fragment, nonce-protected confirm page then POST, single-use server state, path-scoped `__Secure-hdd_gate_p` cookie, 24 hours default and 7 days maximum, revocable); `mtls` rejected with `ERR-VAL-005`.
4. Implement failure behavior (`deny`, `challenge`, `redirect_login`) and identical responses for unknown user and wrong secret; the cost controls of C19.2 (per-address token bucket and the global hashing semaphore with `ERR-GATE-005` before any hash); throttling on (username, address bucket) pairs (5 failures per 10 minutes) where a per-username global counter above a threshold escalates to proof of work and an alert and never hard-locks the account (R-19), and recognised devices (a valid gate cookie, an earlier success from the same address bucket) are exempt; feeding credential-stuffing detection (T-0343) and the ban policy.
