Implement the templates (WordPress admin with `admin-ajax.php` allowed and `xmlrpc.php` denied, phpMyAdmin and Adminer, Spring actuator, `/admin`, `/manager`, `/server-status`, `/.env`, `/.git`, `/debug`, API docs pages) and the self-lockout preview (`ERR-GATE-004`, R-19) in API and UI, plus `hddctl gate disable --site`.
6. Build S-131 (rule list, editor, template picker, credentials with one-time reveal, link generator) and the API of B6.7 with OpenAPI entries and the permission matrix tests.
7. Write the **bypass suite**: at least 200 path shapes (encoding layers, dot segments, double slashes, case, path parameters, trailing characters, h2 `:path` forms, absolute-form request targets, `Host` tricks, method override headers) against gated prefixes, each of which must be gated.

- migrations, stage 8a, policies, templates, S-131, API, bypass and abuse suites
**Acceptance.**
- A1: all 200+ bypass shapes against a gated `/wp-admin/` receive the gate decision, none reaches the origin (origin access log check on `hdd-canary`).
- A2: unknown user and wrong secret are indistinguishable in status, body and timing (statistical test).
- A3: a gate cookie replayed from a different IP bucket or user agent requires re-authentication.
- A4: a rule that would block the acting user's current address returns `ERR-GATE-004` until acknowledged.
- A5: gate decisions add at most 20 µs p99 on non-gated paths and 100 µs on gated paths (benchmark; session lookups served from the in-process cache, paths up to 2 KiB).
- A6: 10,000 unauthenticated requests per second carrying Basic credentials to a gated path never run more concurrent password hashes than the semaphore allows, and a distributed wrong-password flood against `admin` does not lock the real operator out.
**Tests.**
- Unit and property tests for matching; integration with proxy and canary; abuse suite; browser tests for S-131 and the login page.
**Notes.** The gate narrows exposure; it does not replace the WAF, which still inspects authenticated traffic.

### T-0576 · API discovery, inventory and enforcement preview (S-132)
`P33` `[UI][API][DP]` · deps: T-0302, T-0303, T-0304, T-0250, T-0368 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Know the API surface a site really exposes, flag shadow and zombie endpoints, and let the owner enforce schemas safely.

Implement the learner as an asynchronous consumer of the event pipeline (T-0368) so the hot path only emits compact observations: path templating by the rules of C19.3 (typed shape patterns become `{param}` immediately, before counting; otherwise literal segments stay unless at least 50 distinct values appear at that position under the same parent template with no value above 20% of requests), parameter type and bound statistics, JSON property names (collapsed beyond 64 distinct per object), credential presence, and no values except enumerations of at most 20 short values for parameters whose names are not on the sensitive-name list.
3. Implement the states of C19.3 (`discovered`, `approved`, `shadow`, `deprecated`, `blocked`) with the 30-day zombie rule and the proposal rule (200 requests over 24 hours).

7. Build S-132 (tiles, table, drawer, enforcement panel, spec import) per B12.2 and the API of B6.7 with OpenAPI entries.
8. Write tests with a real sample API (the `hdd-canary` API fixtures and the Vuln-Lab API apps in the lab): shadow endpoint detection, mass-assignment rejection, type confusion, GraphQL depth and alias limits, spec import round trips, and a privacy test proving no request value appears in the stores.

- learner, inventory, import, preview, S-132, API, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: after 200 mixed requests, the inventory lists every exercised endpoint with correct templates (no more than 2% wrong templates on the fixture API).
- A2: an endpoint absent from an imported spec but present in traffic is marked `shadow` within one learner cycle.
- A3: an approved schema with `additionalProperties: false` rejects a mass-assignment request in `block` mode and only logs in `monitor` mode.
- A4: no request or response value is present in the inventory tables or logs except enumerations of non-sensitive parameters (privacy test with canary values in sensitive-named parameters, free-text fields, JSON keys and path segments).
- A5: a malicious 5 MiB OpenAPI document (deep nesting, remote `$ref`, entity-like expansion) is rejected within limits without memory growth.
**Tests.**
- Integration with fixture APIs; fuzz targets for importers; privacy test; browser tests for S-132.

### T-0577 · Business-flow protection (S-133)
`P33` `[UI][API][DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0312, T-0333, T-0337, T-0343, T-0345, T-0350 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Detect and limit abuse of legitimate business functions (credential stuffing, fake signups, OTP/SMS pumping, carding, scraping, coupon guessing, form spam) with explainable signals.
**Steps.**
1. Add `business_flows` (B5.6), `PERM-flow.*`, `AUD-flow.*`, `ERR-FLOW-001`, `MET-hdd_flow_events_total`, the Redis/kv keys of B5.12 and the migrations with RLS.
2. Implement the flow engine in three phases (C19.4): Phase A at stages 9 and 10 (request-line and header signals, template match, lookups), Phase B at the new stage 12a (declared-field signals after extraction), Phase C at the new stage 18a (outcome recording from status, redirect or declared body marker, with asynchronous counter updates); all signal computation goes through `KvStore.flow_signal_update`; a combined score and the action ladder (`monitor`, `challenge`, `block`, `ban` for high-confidence classes only) integrate with the ban policy (C6.4) and rate limiter (T-0333). Phase C actions apply to subsequent requests.
3. Implement the signal library of C19.4 by flow kind: velocity and distinct-credential ratios, time-to-complete, honey fields (site-declared hidden field populated), sequence integrity, per-destination OTP caps, declined-to-approved ratios using declared card-hint fields restricted to the last four digits or the first six plus last four (Luhn-valid 13-to-19-digit values are dropped unhashed with a misconfiguration alert; hints are HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 32 bits under a per-site key, held in `KvStore` only, never persisted or logged), scraping breadth and timing regularity, coupon guess rates, duplicate-content hashes.
4. Implement templates for login, signup, reset, OTP, checkout, search, contact, coupon and gift card with sensible defaults, shipped in `monitor`.
5. Implement guards against false positives: clearance cookies relax limits, verified bots and allowlisted addresses bypass flow signals, per-flow allowlists, and a maximum action per signal class until the owner raises it.
6. Implement **Simulate** (replays recent event summaries against a definition and reports would-be actions) and the S-133 screen and API of B6.7.
7. Add explainability: every flow event stores the signals and values that fired (counts, ratios, durations), never request values, and the event drawer shows them in plain language.
8. Write lab tests with synthetic traffic generators: credential stuffing from rotating IPs, signup flood with disposable domains, OTP pumping to many destinations, carding-shaped checkout bursts, price scraping with realistic timing, coupon enumeration, and a benign replay that must produce zero blocks.
**Deliverables.**
- flow engine, signal library, templates, simulate, S-133, API, lab tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: each synthetic abuse scenario triggers its intended signal and, in `block` mode, its intended action; the benign replay produces zero challenges and zero blocks.
- A2: flows in `monitor` never change a response (differential test).
- A3: the OAT items marked covered in E15 each map to at least one passing scenario.
- A4: no card hint, credential or form value appears in events or logs (privacy test with canary values).
- A5: flow evaluation adds at most 50 µs p99 CPU time per matched request with the in-process store; Redis-backed counters are pipelined asynchronously and never delay the response (benchmark).
**Tests.**
- Lab generators; benign replay; privacy test; benchmark; browser tests for S-133.
**Notes.** Business-flow controls reduce abuse; they cannot know an application's intent, and E15 says so.

<!-- PHASE:P34 -->
## PHASE P34: Learned detection, Bypass Guard and known-vulnerability coverage (T-0579 to T-0599) · milestone M14 · gate G34

Requirement prefix `HRD`. Goal: close the three gaps that remain after the deterministic engine: (1) **unusual techniques** that no signature knows, with bounded and explainable machine-learning assistance (Sentinel, C20); (2) **bypass**: after a domain and its requirements are set, no request reaches the origin except through HDD, enforced structurally where possible and verified continuously everywhere else (Bypass Guard, C21, rule R-34); (3) **well-known vulnerabilities**: a knowledge base and pipeline that turn named CVEs and vulnerability classes into tested, signed, staged rules, plus the hardening measures of C22.5. Read C20, C21, C22 and rules R-33 and R-34 first.

Design rules for this phase:
- The deterministic engine stays authoritative. Learned components are advisory-first, bounded, explainable, signed, shadow-tested and never the only reason to ban (R-33).
- Nothing in this phase claims that attacks cannot succeed or that bypass is impossible. Claims cite measurements and verification dates (section 4).
- The analyst (a language model) is optional, off by default, never on the request path and never applies anything by itself.
- Where a task needs the runtime state, it uses the `KvStore`, `Bus` and `Limiter` traits (R-31).

**Execution order within P34 (the numbering is not the order).** T-0579 to T-0587 run after P13 and P14 (the engine and the SQLi shield) and P17 (behavior). T-0588 to T-0592 run after P21 (origin protection) and should be scheduled early in delivery slice DS3, because they decide whether a site may be called protected. T-0593, T-0597 and T-0598 run after P15. T-0594 and T-0595 run after P27; T-0596 runs after T-0595, T-0597 and T-0598. T-0599 and gate G34 close the phase.

Gate G34 passes when (each criterion PASS, or UNVERIFIED only with the enumerated reasons the operator has accepted in writing): AC-59 (Sentinel safety, robustness and shadow evidence), AC-60 (Bypass Guard: signed authentication, tunnel, firewall generators, continuous verification and the go-live gate), AC-61 (known-vulnerability coverage: VKB pipeline and ATK-301 to ATK-390) and AC-62 (additional hardening: parser differentials, inspection-window evasion, cache guard, deception, AI-endpoint protections) pass; no learned component can ban alone (tested); a site cannot enter `block` mode while its lockdown is not verified (tested); the held-out evaluation, including leave-one-family-out runs, is published with its limits; and the coverage map (E15) is regenerated with the new rows.

### T-0579 · Sentinel doctrine, threat model and runtime decision (ADR)
`P34` `[SEC][DOC][DP]` · deps: T-0246, T-0252, T-0253, T-0254, T-0255 · size: M · owner: sec
**Objective.** Fix what learned components may and may not do before any model is written, and choose the inference runtime.
**Steps.**
1. Write the ADR "Learned detection under a deterministic core" recording R-33, the layers and the modes of C20.2 and C20.5, and the explicit non-goals: no opaque blocking, no training on tenant raw data, no model on the request path that cannot be skipped within budget.
2. Write the ML threat model (C20.7) into `docs/STRIDE.md` as abuse cases: evasion, poisoning, extraction, prompt injection into the analyst, drift, resource exhaustion; each with a planned test (T-0585).
3. Spike the inference runtime: an inference-only Rust path (`tract`, ONNX Runtime bindings, or a hand-written tree-ensemble evaluator), comparing p99 latency, memory, binary size, supply-chain surface and `unsafe` exposure; prefer a pure-Rust evaluator for tree models; record the choice and the FFI justification if any (R-08).
4. Define the model artifact format (versioned, hash-pinned, signed with the release key, with a model card reference) and the verification rules at load (reject unsigned, wrong schema version, oversize).
5. Define the evaluation protocol: fixed splits, the leave-one-family-out procedure, operating-point selection at a false-positive budget, and which numbers appear in public statements.
6. Define the claims language (approved patterns in section 4.3) and add the forbidden forms to claims-lint (T-0005 rules).
7. Define the data-governance policy: what is stored for a finding (feature classes only, redacted snippet through T-0253), retention (30 days; sequence-model state 24 hours), and the opt-in aggregate-feature sharing rule (default off, minimum population of 50 distinct clients per cell, noise added).
8. Record the decisions in `ARCHITECTURE.md` and seed the capability-matrix rows.
**Deliverables.**
- ADR, STRIDE additions, runtime spike report, artifact format, evaluation protocol, claims rules
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the ADR states the bounds of C20.5 and a reviewer can derive from it that no learned component bans alone.
- A2: the runtime choice has measured p99 numbers on the reference hardware named in `docs/ml/BENCH.md` (fixed CPU model, input cap of 8 KiB per vector) for a 200-tree ensemble and a small convolutional model; tree ensembles are the default and a convolutional model is shipped only if its measured p99 fits the budget.
- A3: the artifact verification rules reject an unsigned and a tampered artifact in a test.
- A4: claims-lint fails on "AI-powered protection" and passes on the approved phrasing.
- A5: the evaluation protocol document defines leave-one-family-out for at least five attack families.
**Tests.**
- Unit tests for artifact verification; claims-lint tests; documentation review.
**Notes.** If the spike shows a model cannot meet the 200 µs budget, the ADR records which layers run only in `shadow` or asynchronously.

### T-0580 · Structural features and the privacy-safe feature extractor
`P34` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0240, T-0241, T-0242, T-0253, T-0263, T-0579 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Turn a normalized request into a small, privacy-safe feature vector that models can score cheaply.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the feature extractor in `hdd-waf-core::features` (pure, no I/O) over the three views and the SQL, HTML and shell tokenizers: hashed token n-grams (2^18 buckets), token-class sequences, character-class ratios, entropy, nesting depth, encoding-layer count, view-disagreement measures, keyword density, header order and set, content-type versus body-shape agreement. Per-site terms (shape novelty, length z-scores per template) are computed by T-0582 and plugged into the prefilter there; here they are stubbed to neutral.
2. Implement the cheap prefilter (entropy, view mismatch, token-class anomaly, with the per-site novelty hook) that decides whether the models run, with a target of under 5 µs for 95% of requests.
3. Guarantee privacy: features are computed in memory and dropped; the only retained artifacts are the top contributing feature classes (never hashed n-gram buckets) and the redacted evidence snippet; add a test that no feature vector or raw value reaches storage or logs.
4. Keep feature definitions versioned (`feature_schema_version`) so models refuse to load against a different schema.
5. Bound memory and time: per-request feature budget, caps on tokens per vector, behavior on oversized input (skip with a counter).
6. Add deterministic property tests (arbitrary Unicode never panics, features are stable across runs) and a fuzz target.
7. Benchmark (criterion) the extractor on the benign corpora and the attack fixtures.
8. Document the features in `docs/ml/FEATURES.md`.
**Deliverables.**
- feature extractor, prefilter, schema version, tests, benchmarks, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the extractor is deterministic and panic-free on the fuzz corpus.
- A2: the prefilter lets at most 10% of the benign corpus reach the models while passing at least 98% of the attack fixtures of AG-01 to AG-07.
- A3: p99 extraction plus prefilter time is at most 50 µs on the reference hardware of `docs/ml/BENCH.md` for requests up to the input cap, and the combined p99 of extraction, prefilter and inference stays within 200 µs.
- A4: the privacy test finds no raw value or feature vector in any store or log after a 100,000-request run.
- A5: a model built against another schema version is refused at load.
**Tests.**
- Unit, property and fuzz tests; benchmarks; privacy grep over a run.
**Notes.** Features describe *shape*, not content; the same feature vector is produced for the same shape regardless of tenant.

### T-0581 · `hdd-sentinel` runtime: bounded inference, model registry, hot swap and fail-safe behavior
`P34` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0579, T-0580, T-0261, T-0256 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Run models inside the pipeline at stage 13b without ever hurting latency or correctness.
**Steps.**
1. Create the `hdd-sentinel` crate (forbid unsafe) with a model registry, a loader that verifies signatures and schema, and a typed `Detector` interface returning `(score, calibrated_probability, top_features)`.
2. Integrate as pipeline stage 13b (C2): runs after the deterministic detection, only when the prefilter passes, under a hard 200 µs p99 budget per request and a global concurrency cap.
3. Implement fail-safe behavior: any error, timeout, oversize input or missing model skips Sentinel with `MET-hdd_sentinel_fallback_total{reason}`; the deterministic verdict is never altered by a failure; there is no panic path (R-09).
4. Implement atomic hot swap of models (`ArcSwap`) with canary versions per site, instant rollback, and version recorded in each finding.
5. Implement the mode state machine (`off`, `shadow`, `assist`, `block`) per site with the promotion rules of C20.5 enforced in code (not only in UI) and audit events.
6. Implement metrics (`MET-hdd_sentinel_score`, `MET-hdd_sentinel_findings_total`, `MET-hdd_sentinel_fallback_total`, `MET-hdd_sentinel_inference_seconds`), audit events `AUD-sentinel.mode_changed`, `AUD-sentinel.auto_demoted`, `AUD-sentinel.model_loaded` and `AUD-sentinel.model_rejected`, the findings table writer (`sentinel_findings`, batched through the event pipeline T-0368), and the retention job (30 days).
7. Add `hddctl sentinel off|status` break-glass commands working without the API.
8. Add chaos tests: corrupt model file, slow model, memory pressure, thousands of concurrent requests.
**Deliverables.**
- `hdd-sentinel` crate, stage 13b, registry, mode machine, metrics, `hddctl` commands, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: with Sentinel enabled the proxy-added p99 stays within the budget of E4 (functional profile benchmark).
- A2: a corrupt, slow (simulated with an injected clock, so the test is deterministic) or missing model leaves every deterministic verdict byte-identical (differential test over 10,000 requests).
- A3: `shadow` mode never changes a response (differential test with models returning maximal scores).
- A4: promotion to `assist` or `block` is refused in code when its prerequisites are missing (`ERR-SENT-002`), a model that fails signature or schema checks is refused (`ERR-SENT-001`), and each refusal names the unmet prerequisite.
- A5: `hddctl sentinel off` takes effect within 2 s without the database.
**Tests.**
- Integration, differential, chaos and benchmark tests.
**Notes.** The Sentinel crate depends on `hdd-waf-core` but nothing in `hdd-waf-core` depends on it, preserving the purity rule.

### T-0582 · Per-site baselines and poisoning-resistant learning
`P34` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0580, T-0581, T-0272, T-0349 · size: L · owner: dp
**Objective.** Learn what normal looks like for each site, without letting an attacker teach the model that attacks are normal.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the bounded per-(template, parameter) profile of C20.4: t-digest lengths, character-class histograms, token-class bigram count-min sketch, plus the site-wide isolation forest over aggregated features, with fixed memory per template and a global cap per site.
2. Implement the **learning eligibility rule**: only requests that the deterministic engine allowed with no soft score, from cleared clients or established sessions, with a 2xx or 3xx outcome, update the baseline; flagged, challenged, banned and low-reputation requests never do.
3. Implement poisoning controls: trimmed updates, a per-identity contribution cap per hour, an **aggregate cap on movement per template** (so many identities cannot add up to a large shift), a requirement that learning events be spread over time and come from established sessions, a global rate cap on baseline movement, and a drift alarm when a baseline shifts faster than a bound.
4. Implement cold start (no influence before 10,000 requests and 7 days) and the "mark as normal" feedback path with owner confirmation (rate limited, audited).
5. Persist baselines compactly (sketch snapshots every 10 minutes to Postgres, loaded at start; in the local profile also to the data directory) with versioning and a reset command.
6. Implement the novelty score and length z-scores and plug them into the T-0580 prefilter; calibrate against the benign replay of the site.
6a. Implement the session-sequence layer (Layer D of C20.2): a bounded first-order model of path-template transitions with a 24-hour state limit, advisory only, with its own tests and privacy check (no values, only template ids).
7. Test with realistic traffic generators and with an adversary generator that tries to drift the baseline.
8. Document the privacy properties (no values, only distributions) in `docs/ml/BASELINES.md`.
**Deliverables.**
- baseline engine, eligibility and poisoning controls, persistence, calibration, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: an adversary sending 100,000 crafted requests from 500 identities over 24 hours moves any template's length median and token-class histogram by less than 5% (the stated bound) and does not make a held-out attack unflagged.
- A6: the sequence layer flags a scripted login-to-export sequence at machine speed in the fixtures, never alters a verdict, and stores no request value.
- A2: flagged and challenged requests never alter the baseline (property test).
- A3: memory per site stays within the cap for 10,000 templates.
- A4: restart restores baselines within 5 s and scoring resumes without a cold start.
- A5: no stored sketch can be inverted to a raw value in the privacy test (canary values never appear).
**Tests.**
- Unit, property, adversary-generator and persistence tests.
**Notes.** The baseline is advisory input; it never blocks on its own.

### T-0583 · Global attack-shape classifier and the reproducible training pipeline
`P34` `[QA][SEC][DP]` · deps: T-0579, T-0580, T-0254, T-0255, T-0278, T-0496 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Train, evaluate and ship an attack-shape classifier whose claims about unseen techniques are measured honestly.
**Steps.**
1. Assemble training data: public corpora (licenses recorded in `lab/LICENSES.md`), HDD fixtures of all attack groups, benign corpora, Vuln-Lab captures, and the synthetic mutation generator (case, whitespace, comments, encodings, homoglyphs, splitting, padding); keep the held-out sets of E1.9 strictly out of training and freeze them with hashes in `tests/fixtures/heldout/MANIFEST.sha256` (at least 200 SQLi, 100 XSS, 60 traversal, 60 command-injection and 60 SSTI items), together with the benign replay sets; `xtask verify` fails if a frozen file changes, a training run that opens one fails in a sandbox test, and every published metric cites the manifest hash it came from.
2. Implement `cargo xtask ml train|eval|export` with pinned data hashes, fixed seeds, recorded toolchain, and reproducible artifacts; training may use Rust (`linfa`, `smartcore`, `xgboost` bindings by ADR) or an offline tool whose output is exported to the supported runtime; the trainer is never shipped to production.
3. Implement the evaluation protocol: per-family metrics, calibration, operating point at a false-positive budget of at most 0.01% on the benign corpora, and **leave-one-family-out** runs for at least five families (SQLi, XSS, command injection, traversal, SSTI) reporting detection of the unseen family.
4. Implement adversarial augmentation (mimicry with benign text, homoglyph and padding mutations) and report robustness (T-0585 consumes it).
5. Produce the model card (`docs/ml/MODEL-CARD.md`): intended use, data, metrics with confidence intervals, known failure modes, fairness-style bias checks across languages and character sets (non-Latin text must not look anomalous), and the explicit statement of what the model cannot do.
6. Sign and package the artifact; store metrics in `sentinel_models`.
7. Add a regression gate: a candidate model that raises the benign false-positive count, or lowers held-out detection, is rejected. Because repeated use of one frozen set leaks it into model selection, each release round adds a fresh held-out slice (kept sealed until the round) and the report states which slice each number came from.
8. Document how to retrain and how to add an attack family.
**Deliverables.**
- training pipeline, evaluation reports, model card, signed artifact, regression gate, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: the pipeline rebuilds a bit-identical **unsigned** artifact from pinned inputs and single-threaded fixed seeds (reproducibility test; signing is a separate step and signatures are not compared).
- A2: on benign replays of at least 100,000 requests each (`benign-general`, `benign-sql-prose`), the observed false-positive rate at the operating point is at most 0.01% and the 95% upper confidence bound is stated next to it.
- A3: leave-one-family-out detection is published for five families; whatever it is, it is stated (the task fails if it is not measured or not published).
- A4: non-Latin benign text (at least 10 scripts) does not exceed the false-positive budget.
- A5: the regression gate rejects a deliberately degraded model in a test.
- A6: modifying a frozen evaluation file fails `xtask verify`, and the model card cites a manifest hash for every metric.
**Tests.**
- Reproducibility test; evaluation harness tests; regression-gate test.
**Notes.** The unseen-family number is expected to be modest; it is reported as measured and never rounded up.

### T-0584 · Score integration, influence caps, corroboration and explainable findings
`P34` `[DP][SEC][API]` · deps: T-0581, T-0582, T-0583, T-0317, T-0273, T-0246 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Make the influence policy of C20.5 real: bounded, corroborated and explainable.
**Steps.**
1. Integrate Sentinel scores into the scoring engine (T-0246) as a separate, capped component (maximum 3 points, and clamped so that the total with the deterministic score never reaches the block threshold: Sentinel can raise a request to a challenge but cannot turn a deterministic `pass` into a `block` in `assist`) that appears separately in `Verdict` and events.
2. Implement the mode semantics exactly as C20.5: `shadow` has no effect; `assist` adds capped soft score and may escalate to proof of work on non-authentication GET requests; `block` may block alone only at probability 0.99 or higher in a mature field kind with the false-positive budget met.
3. Implement ban rules: no ban from Sentinel alone, ever; a ban needs a deterministic signal in the same request, and repeated high-confidence findings only raise that identity's challenge level and review priority; never in cross-site subresource context, never for password fields (hooks into the ban policy engine T-0317).
4. Generate the plain-language explanation from the top five features with a message catalog (i18n keys), shown in event detail and appeals.
5. Implement the feedback loop: owner labels (`attack`, `normal`), appeal outcomes, and automatic demotion triggers (appeal spike, label spike, drift; appeals counted only from distinct cleared or verified clients with capped weight; re-promotion needs owner confirmation) with audit events.
6. Implement the promotion checklist API and UI hooks (14 days in shadow, review of the top 100 findings, replay false-positive rate, held-out uplift).
7. Add the replay tool: run any model against a site's recorded event summaries and report what it would have done.
8. Test that every combination of mode, field kind and context follows the policy table (generated matrix test).
**Deliverables.**
- scoring integration, policy engine, explanations, feedback and demotion logic, replay tool, matrix tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: no combination in the generated matrix (every mode, field kind, context and score) produces a ban from Sentinel alone, and no `assist` combination turns a deterministic `pass` into a `block`.
- A2: `assist` mode never changes the response to an authentication POST.
- A3: every Sentinel-influenced block or challenge event carries at least three human-readable feature explanations.
- A4: an injected appeal spike demotes the site to `shadow` and raises an alert within 5 minutes.
- A5: the replay tool reproduces the live findings for a recorded hour (differential test).
**Tests.**
- Matrix and property tests; integration with the ban engine; demotion tests.
**Notes.** The policy table lives in `docs/ml/POLICY.md` and is generated from the code that enforces it.

### T-0585 · Adversarial robustness suite for learned components (AC-59)
`P34` `[QA][SEC][LAB]` · deps: T-0583, T-0584, T-0586, T-0496 · size: L · owner: qa
**Objective.** Attack the learned components the way an attacker would, and publish what happens.
**Steps.**
1. Build the evasion harness: mimicry (benign prefix/suffix), padding, homoglyphs, token insertion, case and whitespace mutation, encoding layers, splitting across vectors; measure the share of malicious requests that drop below the operating point and whether the deterministic layer still catches them.
2. Build the poisoning harness: drift attempts against baselines from rotating identities, from cleared clients, and through the feedback path (forged "mark as normal").
3. Build the extraction harness: probing to infer thresholds through response differences; verify scores never appear in responses and timing differences stay below a bound.
4. Build the resource harness: inputs designed to maximize inference time and memory.
5. Build the prompt-injection harness for the analyst (T-0586): payloads in evidence fields that instruct the model to ignore rules, reveal context, or propose permissive rules.
6. Run each campaign in the lab with the Vuln-Lab, record results as `lab-proven` with limits, and add every successful evasion to the fixtures for the next training round.
7. Define thresholds: across the enumerated campaigns and the stated number of runs, no campaign may cause a ban, a response change in `shadow`, or a latency violation; evasion rates are published, not hidden.
8. Wire the suite into the nightly lab run and the AC-59 acceptance check.
**Deliverables.**
- five harnesses, campaign reports, fixtures from found evasions, acceptance wiring
**Acceptance.**
- A1: no poisoning campaign moves a baseline beyond the T-0582 bound.
- A2: no extraction probe obtains a score or a threshold from a response; timing differences stay below the stated bound.
- A3: the worst-case inference time stays within budget (skip counter increments instead of delay).
- A4: prompt-injection payloads never change an analyst output into an applied rule or reveal other-tenant data (T-0586 tests).
- A5: the evasion report lists measured evasion rates per technique, with the deterministic layer's coverage of the evaded set.
**Tests.**
- The campaigns themselves; nightly runs; fixture round-trip.
**Notes.** A published evasion rate is a success of the suite: it tells owners where not to rely on Sentinel.

`P34` `[SEC][API][DP]` · deps: T-0584, T-0229, T-0009, T-0368 · size: L · owner: sec
**Objective.** Give owners a helpful assistant that can never act on its own and cannot be steered by attackers.

- A2: a drafted rule always shows its replay results before the approve button is enabled.
- A3: no secret, cookie or other-tenant datum appears in any prompt (privacy test with canary values).
- A4: disabling the analyst changes nothing else in the product (differential test).
- A5: the egress allowlist rejects a non-configured endpoint (egress test).
**Tests.**
- Injection suite; privacy test; integration with the dry-run harness.
**Notes.** The analyst is a convenience. Everything it can do can also be done by a human without it.

### T-0588 · Signed origin authentication and generated origin verifiers
`P34` `[SEC][DP][API]` · deps: T-0405, T-0361, T-0365, T-0384, T-0210 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Make a direct request to the origin useless: only HDD can produce a request the origin will accept.
**Steps.**
1. Define the `HDD-Origin-Auth` v1 format of C21.3 and the canonical string to sign (newline-terminated, length-prefixed fields exactly as in C21.3: version, kid, method, host, port, raw request-target, body hash or `nobody`, timestamp, nonce, Ray ID, `via` marker), with byte-level test vectors in `docs/ORIGIN-AUTH.md`.
2. Implement signing in the origin client (stage 16): per-site keys in `origin_auth_keys` (envelope encrypted), key ids, rotation with overlap, strip of any inbound `HDD-Origin-*` header, and guarantees that keys and signatures never appear in logs, events or responses.
3. Implement the **verifier reference** in Rust (`hdd-origin-guard` library and a small standalone sidecar) with replay protection (nonce retention of at least twice the skew window, fail closed when full, a shared store option for multi-instance origins), skew window of 30 s, clock requirement and reason code, constant-time comparison, generic 403 responses and rejection of the static header of T-0361 in signed mode.
4. Generate **verifier modules** from templates for nginx (njs or Lua), Apache, Caddy, HAProxy, Express and Fastify, WSGI and ASGI, PHP `auto_prepend_file`, Java servlet filter and .NET middleware; every template ships with tests that run against a real instance of that server in the lab.
5. Extend the lockdown wizard (T-0406) with the verifier choice, the key download (shown once, `PERM-bypass.key_view`, audited), a copy-ready snippet and a verification probe that sends a valid, an expired, a replayed and a forged request and checks the four outcomes.
6. Implement rotation: new key, both accepted, switch after every verifier instance acknowledges or a rolling probe confirms every origin target, retire the old only then; reminders and audit (`AUD-origin_auth.key_viewed`, `key_rotated`, `key_retired`).
7. Report rejected requests (attempts, aggregated by rate) and confirmed bypasses (site content served without a valid signature) from verifiers to HDD in a heartbeat signed with its own key, to be consumed by T-0591, and expose `MET-hdd_origin_unsigned_total`.
8. Keep the static secret header (T-0361) as a documented weaker mode and show it as such in readiness.
**Deliverables.**
- signing, key management, `hdd-origin-guard`, verifier templates with tests, wizard changes, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: for every verifier template, a valid request passes and expired, replayed, forged and unsigned requests are rejected (lab matrix per server).
- A2: the signature covers every field of the canonical string: changing the method, host, port, request-target, body or `Content-Length` invalidates it (property test), and field-boundary shifting does not produce a valid signature.
- A3: key rotation completes with no failed legitimate request (traffic test).
- A4: keys never appear in logs, events, errors or responses (grep over a 10,000-request corpus).
- A5: a captured signed request replayed after 30 s, or twice, including across two verifier workers and after a verifier restart within the window, is rejected.
**Tests.**
- Cross-implementation test vectors; lab matrix against real servers; rotation test; log grep.
**Notes.** A stolen key lets an attacker forge requests until rotation (C21.5); keys are stored with web-server-only permissions and rotated on suspicion.

### T-0589 · `hdd-tunnel`: outbound-only connector so the origin has no inbound exposure
`P34` `[SEC][DP][OPS]` · deps: T-0384, T-0365, T-0405, T-0355 · size: XL · owner: dp
**Objective.** Offer the strongest lockdown available: no inbound listener on the origin once the closure is verified.
**Steps.**
1. Specify the tunnel protocol: the connector on the origin host opens an outbound mutually authenticated TLS connection (HTTP/2 or QUIC-free multiplexing over TCP) to the HDD tunnel endpoint; HDD sends origin requests down existing streams; the connector forwards to a local address.
2. Implement the HDD side (`hdd-proxy::tunnel`): connector registration with single-use enrollment tokens (15-minute lifetime, bound to the site, fingerprint confirmed on both sides), client certificates from the internal PKI (T-0384), stream limits, health, backpressure and per-site isolation (a connector can serve only its own site).
3. Implement the connector binary `hdd-tunnel` (Rust, static, small): reconnect with jittered backoff, the target pinned to one configured `host:port` (no ranges), preferably a Unix socket or a dedicated address so that origin apps that trust loopback peers do not see tunnel traffic as local, no listening ports, resource limits, signed self-update through the release process (T-0518).
4. Integrate with the origin client: a site in tunnel mode routes through its connector, with failover to a second connector, and with signed authentication (T-0588) still applied inside the tunnel.
5. Extend the lockdown wizard: enrollment command, systemd/launchd/Windows service templates, and the firewall guidance to close all inbound web ports; verification probe confirms that direct connections fail.
6. Implement connector revocation, rotation and the `tunnels` table, with metrics (`MET-hdd_tunnel_connected`) and alerts for disconnects.
7. Test with a real origin in the lab: restart storms, network partitions, slow connectors, many connectors, hostile connector (tries other sites), enrollment-token race and replay, and a loopback-only admin path on the origin.
8. Document limits (latency added, single connector as a failure point without a second).
**Deliverables.**
- tunnel endpoint, `hdd-tunnel` connector, enrollment and revocation, wizard flow, tests, docs
**Acceptance.**
- A1: with the origin's inbound web ports closed, the site works end to end through the tunnel and every direct probe in the lab matrix fails.
- A2: a connector cannot receive or send traffic for any other site (isolation test).
- A3: a revoked connector is disconnected within 5 s.
- A4: killing the network for 60 s and restoring it resumes service without manual action.
- A5: the connector exposes no listening socket in the port-scan test.
**Tests.**
- Lab integration; chaos tests; isolation and revocation tests; port scan.
**Notes.** Tunnel mode removes the direct network path only if the origin host's inbound ports are closed; the probe checks it.

### T-0591 · Continuous bypass verification, origin tripwire and the Bypass Guard screen (S-138)
`P34` `[SEC][OPS][UI][API]` · deps: T-0588, T-0590, T-0165, T-0192, T-0201, T-0063 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Prove, repeatedly and from outside, that no direct path exists, and say so only with evidence.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the verification engine in `hdd-scan` (read-only, own addresses only): from at least two vantage points outside HDD's network (operator runner, operator-configured probes, bring-your-own-probe token page) attempt direct connections to the origin address, after proving ownership of each probed address and name (DNS or HTTP challenge), resolving once and pinning, and refusing private, loopback, link-local and cloud-metadata ranges, on the common web ports, configured ports and the top-100 web ports (rate-limited), over IPv4, IPv6 and UDP 443, with and without SNI and with varied `Host` values, plus every historic and certificate-transparency name and every sibling hostname found.
2. Classify results: `blocked`, `site_content` (matched by the echo canary token or content hash: bypass), `exposed_service` (any non-HDD service that answers: also fails verification), `inconclusive`, `unverified` (vantage unavailable); first run the origin-address check (a unique token must be seen on both the proxied and the direct path), record evidence hashes in `bypass_probes`, and write every probe target to the audit log. At least one vantage is HDD-operated with rotating unpublished addresses; owner probes sign results with a per-probe key and nonce.
3. Implement the origin tripwire ingestion: verifier heartbeats (T-0588) and the canary echo (T-0210) create `bypass_events` only for confirmed bypasses (served without a valid signature); rejected attempts are aggregated as informational counters and never change the state (health checkers are allowlisted by the owner).
4. Implement the state machine of C21.4 (`unprotected` to `bypass_detected`), transitions with evidence, two clean runs to leave `bypass_detected`, and the effects: critical alert, one-click key rotation, readiness penalty, block-mode promotion hold; a site already in `block` keeps blocking; `degraded` starts only after 24 hours without a valid verification.
5. Implement DNS and exposure checks: unproxied records sharing the origin address, wildcard policy, dangling names (T-0192), certificate-transparency names that resolve to the origin (T-0201), mail-header leaks.
6. Build S-138: state, evidence timeline, per-vantage results, open bypass paths with remediation links, probe schedule, and the exact wording rule ("no direct path found from N vantage points on <date>").
7. Implement the API of B6.7 (`/origin/bypass-guard*`), `PERM-bypass.read`, `PERM-bypass.verify`, `PERM-bypass.key_view` and `PERM-bypass.accept_risk`, the audit events `AUD-bypass.state_changed`, `AUD-bypass.risk_accepted`, `AUD-bypass.probe_run` and `AUD-bypass.event`, the metrics of B9 and notifications.
8. Test with lab origins in four configurations: open, header-only, signed, tunnel with closed inbound; plus injected faults (an open alternate port, an IPv6 side door, a leaked sibling hostname).
**Deliverables.**
- verification engine, tripwire ingestion, state machine, S-138, API, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: each injected bypass (open alternate port, IPv6 side door, leaked sibling hostname, direct IP with Host header) is detected within one probe interval.
- A2: a site whose origin is open is never shown as `verified`; the surfaces show "bypassable".
- A3: a probe from HDD's own network is never accepted as evidence, a probe target without ownership proof or in a private or metadata range is refused, and an owner probe that always reports `blocked` is flagged (tests).
- A6: a lab origin that answers on an alternate port with a non-site service is classified `exposed_service` and fails verification, and a header-only origin never exceeds `applied_unverified`.
- A4: a request served without a valid signature creates a `bypass_events` row within 60 s and an alert, while a rejected unsigned request only increments the attempt counter.
- A5: zero serious or critical axe findings on S-138, and no copy says bypass is impossible.
**Tests.**
- Lab matrix of origin configurations; injected-fault tests; browser tests; claims-lint.
**Notes.** The probe set is deliberately limited to the owner's own address and rate-limited; it never scans third parties (section 2.1).

`P34` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0241, T-0242, T-0299, T-0358, T-0486 · size: L · owner: waf

- VKB schema, importers, classification, matching, S-139, API, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: importing the recorded KEV fixture creates entries with correct fields and flags request-visible ones for review.
- A2: an entry with an unreviewed license is rejected with `ERR-VKB-001` and a logged reason.
- A3: a site with a matching inventory component sees the entry on S-139 with the correct rule state.
- A4: S-139 never shows "protected" for an entry; it shows the rule state and the R-11 banner.
- A5: malformed and oversize feed items are rejected with `ERR-VKB-001` without affecting other entries.
**Tests.**
- Importer fixtures; matching tests; browser and API contract tests.
**Notes.** The VKB tracks, it does not promise; its coverage numbers cite the date of the last feed run.

### T-0595 · Exploit-signature ingestion, staged rollout and the emergency channel
`P34` `[SEC][DP][OPS]` · deps: T-0594, T-0310, T-0255, T-0425, T-0496, T-0497 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Turn request-visible exploit shapes into tested, signed rules quickly and safely.
**Steps.**
1. Implement the converter from community templates and advisory-derived patterns to the HDD rule format (match on method, path, headers, parameters, body shape), rejecting constructs HDD cannot evaluate safely and recording what was dropped.
2. Implement the lint (ReDoS check, cost budget, specificity score) and the automatic false-positive gate against `benign-general`, `benign-sql-prose` and **full-request replay corpora** (method, path, headers, cookies and body, in HAR style) per product, so that rules on paths, headers and cookies are exercised and not only string lists; a minimum corpus size and a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on the false-positive rate are stated with every result; a rule that matches benign traffic is rejected or narrowed to a product and path scope, which is the defined outcome for false-positive-prone rows. Every converted rule needs a human reviewer's approval before it can leave `candidate`.
3. Implement lab proof where a vulnerable container exists (T-0496): the exploit succeeds directly and is blocked through HDD; results recorded `lab-proven` with the container digest.
4. Implement signing and the staged rollout on the ring ladder of T-0425 (internal canary, 5%, 25%, 100% of opted-in sites, with dwell times) with `monitor` before `block` and a stated promotion criterion (no rule hit-rate spike, ban-rate or 4xx/5xx change on matched requests beyond stated bounds for the dwell time). Auto-rollback triggers on those quantitative signals, and a rollback also bulk-unbans every ban attributed to the rolled-back rule id.
5. Implement the **emergency channel**: a signed single-rule push that shortens the staging calendar (the lint and false-positive gate still apply) for KEV entries with confirmed active exploitation. Controls: two-person approval (`PERM-vkb.emergency`), a signing key held offline or in an HSM, emergency rules start in `monitor` or `B` (never a ban) for the first 60 minutes, expire after 24 hours unless confirmed, are limited in count per day and in path breadth, have a per-rule kill switch, and are recorded with notification to operators; the key-compromise and revocation procedure is documented.
6. Implement offline mode: `hddctl vkb apply <bundle>` for air-gapped installs, verified by signature, with a monotonic serial number and an expiry in every bundle (an older serial is refused), and a signer revocation list.
7. Implement the time-to-rule tracker: candidate within 24 hours and monitor rule within 72 hours for request-visible KEV entries, reported as measured, with misses explained.
8. Add tests with synthetic entries, hostile templates (ReDoS, huge patterns), signature failures and rollback.
**Deliverables.**
- converter, lint and gate, lab proof harness, staged rollout, emergency channel, offline bundles, tracker, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: a template using unsupported constructs (back-references, lookaround, unbounded nested repetition) is rejected and logged by the lint, and the engine's linear-time guarantee is tested with a worst-case input.
- A2: a candidate rule that matches 1 item of the replay corpus is rejected or narrowed, and the report states the corpus size and the upper confidence bound.
- A3: an emergency push reaches 95% of a 20-node test fleet within 10 minutes, starts in `monitor`, expires after 24 hours and is logged; a single approver cannot publish it.
- A4: an unsigned, tampered, expired or older-serial bundle, and one from a revoked signer, is rejected by `hddctl vkb apply`.
- A5: a rolled-back rule's bans are removed (bulk-unban test), and the tracker report lists, for the recorded KEV fixture, the time-to-rule per entry and flags misses.
**Tests.**
- Converter and lint tests; lab proofs; rollout and rollback tests; signature tests.
**Notes.** The emergency channel never skips the false-positive gate and never starts with a ban; a fast wrong rule is worse than a slow right one.

`P34` `[DP][SEC][QA]` · deps: T-0595, T-0597, T-0598, T-0496, T-0497, T-0313, T-0289, T-0290, T-0296, T-0308, T-0310, T-0495 · size: XL · owner: waf

### T-0597 · Parser-differential rejection and inspection-evasion defenses
`P34` `[DP][SEC]` · deps: T-0249, T-0257, T-0360, T-0302 · size: L · owner: waf
**Objective.** Reduce the effect of representation tricks and padding on inspection, for the variants listed in the matrix.
**Steps.**
1. Implement strict-parse policies with explicit outcomes: duplicate JSON keys, comments, trailing commas, BOM, lone surrogates and numbers beyond safe ranges (reject, canonicalize or pass as a string, by per-field site policy, so large identifiers above 2^53 are not broken), multipart edge cases (duplicate part names, malformed boundaries, `filename*`, LF-only lines, nested multiparts), and re-serialize-and-compare used for comparison only (forwarded bytes are never changed unless the owner opts in, so signed webhooks keep verifying). Every strict policy ships in `monitor` first with a would-have-rejected counter; LF-only multipart and duplicate keys are allowed per site where observed legitimate clients need them.
2. Implement charset and encoding confusion defenses: a per-site charset allowlist seeded from the charsets observed in passive data (T-0486; `utf-8`, `iso-8859-1`, `windows-1252` as the minimum, with Shift_JIS, GBK, EUC-KR, Windows-1251 and ISO-8859-2 available as presets), rejection of UTF-7, UTF-16 without BOM agreement, `ibm037`, `ibm500` and other EBCDIC charsets, and decode-compare between declared and detected encoding.
3. Implement content-type switching defenses: per-endpoint content-type policy from learned or declared schemas (T-0302, T-0576) and rejection of a body whose shape contradicts its type.
4. Extend the tail-window and field-wise inspection of T-0257 with **rolling-window inspection** beyond the inspect prefix for suspicious shapes (padding detection by entropy and repeated-junk ratio) with a bounded budget, which narrows the room to hide a payload behind padding; `over_limit_policy` remains the backstop and, under the default `inspect_prefix`, the verdict is tagged `truncated`.
5. Implement reassembly before detection for payloads split across chunks, multipart parts, parameters and cookies (ATK-353), with bounds.
6. Implement HTTP/2 pseudo-header, CRLF-in-field and authority consistency checks (ATK-343, ATK-354) and WebSocket upgrade validation (ATK-355) if not already complete.
7. Add differential fuzzing between HDD's parsers and reference parsers of popular stacks for each format.
8. Add metrics, events and documentation of every rejection reason.
**Deliverables.**
- strict parsers, charset and type defenses, rolling-window inspection, reassembly, differential fuzzing, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: every row ATK-348 to ATK-355 has fixtures that are rejected or neutralized, with no false positive on the benign corpora and on legitimate-client fixtures (non-UTF-8 charsets, large identifiers, signed webhook bodies, LF-only clients).
- A2: a 1 MiB padded request hiding a Class A SQLi shape after the inspect prefix is detected in `block` mode with the rolling window, is blocked under `over_limit_policy=block`, and is tagged `truncated` under the default policy.
- A3: payloads split across chunks, parts and parameters are detected after reassembly (matrix test).
- A4: the differential fuzzer runs 10 minutes per format in `verify` without a disagreement that is not listed as a documented policy.
- A5: the added work stays within the E4 inspection budgets (benchmark).
**Tests.**
- Fixture matrix; differential fuzz; benchmarks.
**Notes.** Rejecting ambiguous input is the safest answer to a parser differential; policies can allow canonicalization where an owner needs it.

### T-0598 · Deception, cache guard, origin integrity, script integrity and AI-endpoint protections
`P34` `[DP][SEC][API]` · deps: T-0309, T-0409, T-0412, T-0311, T-0302 · size: XL · owner: sec
**Objective.** Address further gaps that are not injection or bypass: stolen data, cache abuse, post-exploitation, client-side tampering and AI-backed endpoints.
**Steps.**
1. **Honeytokens:** generate decoy credentials, API keys, tokens and records, place them in responses to known-bad probes, decoy files and optional page comments; tokens are issued per session or per client and never placed in globally public comments; a token seen in a request raises a critical event and a high score, and it causes a ban only when the request is same-site or first-party and the token was issued to a different client (never in cross-site context, never behind a shared address without other signals; crawlers and archivers do not trigger bans) (`honeytokens` table, hashed values, rotation).
2. **Cache guard** (ATK-155, 156, 345, 346): applies to HDD-owned caching and to a declared cache topology (it warns when a CDN fronts HDD, where HDD sees neither key nor cache): strip a configured set of unkeyed headers only, enforce `Vary`, normalize path delimiters for cache eligibility only (never in the forwarded path, so matrix parameters and encoded slashes keep working), refuse caching of responses with credentials or with dynamic markers (a documented list: `Set-Cookie`, `Authorization`, `Cache-Control: private`, per-user content types), and detect cache-poisoned-DoS shapes.
3. **Webshell interaction detection** (ATK-127): request-side parameter and command shapes of common web shells, response-side output signatures (directory listings, command output), and file-hash watch of static public files.
4. **Origin integrity watch:** the verifier or canary reports hashes of an owner-chosen set of public files (scripts, templates, entry points); a changed hash raises an alert and, if the file is a served script, feeds the script-integrity monitor.
5. **Script-integrity monitor and generated CSP / Trusted Types:** inventory of scripts served to visitors (from the crawler and reports), change alerts, SRI suggestions, and a generated CSP in report-only mode first (extends T-0412); skimmer-shape detection (ATK-267).
6. **AI-endpoint protections** (ATK-361 to ATK-369): declared AI endpoints get prompt-size caps, per-identity token budgets, invisible-Unicode and instruction-marker signals (signal only), model-artifact upload checks, access-gate templates for model-serving and MCP paths, and outbound checks for secrets in model responses.
7. **Response hardening:** response-splitting and header-injection re-checks on origin responses, and `Content-Type` sniffing protection defaults.
8. Add tests for each measure with fixtures and a benign replay, and add S-132 and S-131 template entries for the new endpoint families.
**Deliverables.**
- honeytokens, cache guard, webshell and integrity detectors, script monitor and CSP generator, AI-endpoint protections, tests
**Acceptance.**
- A1: use of a honeytoken in the first-party case results in a critical event and a ban within 2 s, use in a cross-site or crawler context results in a critical event without a ban, and a benign replay never trips one.
- A2: the cache-deception and cache-poisoning fixtures (ATK-155, 156, 345, 346) do not poison or leak through the cache in the lab (differential test against named lab caches: Varnish, nginx proxy cache and a CDN emulator, with stated TTLs and cases).
- A3: a changed watched file raises an alert within one check interval.
- A4: a declared AI endpoint rejects an over-budget prompt and a per-identity token overrun with the right status and no origin traffic.
- A5: the generated report-only CSP runs on the canary site with zero violations of first-party assets.
**Tests.**
- Lab integration; cache differential tests; integrity tests; browser CSP test.
**Notes.** Prompt-injection signals on AI endpoints are advisory; HDD cannot make an LLM-backed application immune to prompt injection and says so.

`P34` `[QA][DOC][OPS]` · deps: T-0585, T-0587, T-0592, T-0593, T-0595, T-0596, T-0597, T-0598, T-0578 · size: L · owner: qa

## E0. How to use the appendices

The appendices are normative data for the tasks in Part D. Where a task says "the fixture set", "the benign corpus", "the acceptance matrix", "the thresholds", "the gate report" or "the canonical names", it means the corresponding appendix section here. Appendix values may be **tightened** freely by the agent; **loosening** any value requires the operator's approval in chat and an entry in `docs/DEVIATIONS.md` (rule R-15). Every fixture in these appendices is data for tests: the agent writes it into `tests/fixtures/` with the metadata header defined in E1.0, never inlines it into production code, and never sends it anywhere the payload class does not allow (section 2.2).

## E1. Fixtures and payload seeds

### E1.0 Fixture file format and rules

Every fixture file under `tests/fixtures/` starts with a header block of `#`-prefixed metadata lines, followed by one payload per line (lines are literal; leading/trailing spaces are significant and are shown with `␠` in this document only, the real files contain actual spaces). A blank line or a line starting with `#` is metadata. Multi-line payloads use the escape `\n` and are decoded by the loader. Encoded payloads are stored in their encoded form exactly as they appear on the wire. Invisible or control characters are written in this document as `⟦U+XXXX⟧` (for example `⟦U+0000⟧` is a NUL byte); the fixture generator expands each marker to the literal code point, so the committed fixture files contain the real characters. Visible non-ASCII quote lookalikes are shown literally.

```text
# class: A                      # A | B | C (section 2.2); loader rejects files without a class
# category: sqli                # matrix group slug: sqli, xss, traversal, rce, ssti, xxe, ssrf, crlf, redirect, nosql, ldap, jndi, deser, upload, protocol, scanner, honeypot, cms
# subtype: tautology            # optional; see C4 families H1..H8 for sqli
# hardness: hard                # hard | soft | none (benign)
# vectors: query,form,json,xml,multipart,cookie,header,path   # allowed placements
# expect: would_block           # would_block | allow | challenge | would_ban | gated | not_gated | rejected_early | gated_or_rejected
# field_kinds: any              # any | username | password | search | numeric_id | free_text | email
# dialects: mysql,postgres,mssql,oracle,sqlite   # optional
# source: authored | operator | public-corpus   # provenance; public corpora keep their license in lab/LICENSES.md
# heldout: false                # true => never used for tuning (E1.9)
' OR 1=1--
```

Rules: (1) hosts inside payloads use `.invalid` or reserved example names, never a resolvable name; (2) Class C content (resource exhaustion, billion-laughs, zip bombs, heavy queries) is generated at test time by builders in the test crate and is never committed as a file; (3) fixtures are append-only within a gate, a removed line needs a reason in `tests/fixtures/CHANGELOG.md`; (4) `heldout/` files are listed in `.heldout-manifest` with SHA-256 and the loader refuses to include them in tuning runs; (5) every fixture line gets a stable id `fx_<file>_<line-hash>` used in evidence.

### E1.1 The mandated SQL injection set (M1 to M6)

The operator supplied these six payloads. v4.1 referred to "7 required payloads"; the operator's message lists six, so v5 treats the six below as the authoritative mandated set and keeps the seventh v4.1 item (the `#`-terminated tautology) inside the variant family E1.2 where it is covered 100% anyway (`DEV-V5-003`).

| ID | Payload (literal) | Intent | Families (C4) | Dialect validity | Expected verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | `' OR 1=1--` | Quote breakout, always-true predicate, comment truncation | H1 + H2 | MySQL requires a space or control char after `--`; PostgreSQL, MSSQL, Oracle, SQLite accept `--` | hard, `sqli`, would_block, would_ban |
| M2 | `' OR '1'='1` | Quote breakout, string tautology, relies on the application's closing quote | H1 | All dialects | hard, `sqli` |
| M3 | `admin' --` | Authentication bypass by comment truncation after a known username | H2 + H7 | All dialects (MySQL needs trailing space, present) | hard in username and free-text; soft 4 in password field (Balanced), hard in Paranoid |
| M4 | `admin' #` | MySQL-style comment truncation | H2 + H7 | MySQL/MariaDB only; still hard everywhere (intent) | hard, `sqli` |
| M5 | `admin'/*` | Block-comment truncation | H2 + H7 | MySQL, PostgreSQL (nested), MSSQL, Oracle, SQLite | hard, `sqli` |
| M6 | `' or 1=1 LIMIT 1 --` | Lowercase tautology plus row limiter to defeat single-row checks | H1 + H2 | MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite; MSSQL uses TOP | hard, `sqli` |

**Matrix obligations (AC-39):** each of M1 to M6 must be a hard hit in every vector of C4.2, in every field kind except the documented password-field softening, after each transformation in E1.2, with the same verdict under the three views (raw, decoded, canonical). The expected ban is created once per source (TTL ladder step 1 = 1 h; test bans 60 s), outside cross-site subresource context.

**Placement templates** (the loader substitutes `{P}` with the payload, URL-encoding it only when the vector requires):

```text
query:        GET /search?q={P}
query-multi:  GET /search?q=a&q={P}
path:         GET /items/{P}
path-param:   GET /items;id={P}/view
form:         POST /login  application/x-www-form-urlencoded  username={P}&password=x
form-pass:    POST /login  application/x-www-form-urlencoded  username=alice&password={P}
json:         POST /api/login  application/json  {"username":"{P}","password":"x"}
json-nested:  POST /api/profile  application/json  {"user":{"profile":{"bio":"{P}"}}}
json-array:   POST /api/batch  application/json  {"ids":["1","{P}"]}
xml:          POST /soap  text/xml  <login><user>{P}</user></login>
multipart:    POST /upload  multipart/form-data  name="comment"; value={P}
multipart-fn: POST /upload  multipart/form-data  filename="{P}.txt"
cookie:       GET /  Cookie: session={P}
header-ua:    GET /  User-Agent: {P}
header-xff:   GET /  X-Forwarded-For: {P}
header-ref:   GET /  Referer: https://example.invalid/?q={P}
header-custom:GET /  X-Api-Key: {P}
fragment-ref: GET /  Referer: https://example.invalid/#{P}
param-name:   GET /search?{P}=1
basic-auth:   GET /admin  Authorization: Basic base64("{P}:x")
```

### E1.2 Variant families for the mandated set (generated and listed)

The generator `xtask fixtures sqli` produces `tests/fixtures/sqli/core.txt` deterministically from the transformations below (seed `0x5eed`), de-duplicates, and checks that at least 300 distinct variants exist. The list in this section is the **committed minimum**; the generator may emit more. Class A unless noted.

#### Transformation catalog

| ID | Transformation | Example on M1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T01 | Case permutations of keywords | `' oR 1=1--` |
| T02 | Whitespace substitutes (`%09 %0a %0b %0c %0d %a0`, `+`) | `'%09OR%091=1--` |
| T03 | Inline comments as whitespace | `'/**/OR/**/1=1--` |
| T04 | Versioned comments (MySQL) | `'/*!50000OR*/1=1--` |
| T05 | Comment terminator swaps (`-- `, `--+`, `--%20`, `#`, `%23`, `/*`, `;%00`) | `' OR 1=1#` |
| T06 | Quote forms (`'`, `%27`, `%2527`, `\u0027`, `%u0027`, `&#39;`, `&#x27;`, fullwidth `＇`, modifier apostrophe `ʼ`, curly `‘`) | `%27%20OR%201=1--` |
| T07 | Tautology substitutes (listed under T07 in E1.2.1) | `' OR 2>1--` |
| T08 | Parenthesis wrapping | `') OR (1)=(1)--` |
| T09 | Numeric context (no quote) | `1 OR 1=1` |
| T10 | Double URL encoding | `%2527%2520OR%25201%253D1--` |
| T11 | Mixed encodings per character | `%27 OR 1%3D1--` |
| T12 | Null-byte insertion | `'%00 OR 1=1--` |
| T13 | Concatenation/obfuscation of operands | `' OR CHAR(49)=CHAR(49)--` |
| T14 | Hex/octal/scientific numerals | `' OR 0x31=0x31--`, `' OR 1e0=1--` |
| T15 | Unicode normalization (NFKC) tricks | `' ＯＲ 1=1--` |
| T16 | Duplicated parameters (HPP) | `id=1&id=' OR 1=1--` |
| T17 | Line-break splitting | `'%0aOR%0a1=1--` |
| T18 | Trailing junk after terminator | `' OR 1=1-- -` |
| T19 | JSON string escaping | `\u0027 OR 1=1--` |
| T20 | Multipart charset/filename placement | filename=`' OR 1=1--.txt` |

#### E1.2.1 Systematic variants of M1 to M6 (committed list)

admin' --

' Or '1'='1

ADMIN' --
Admin' --

' Or 1=1 Limit 1 --
' oR 1=1 lImIt 1 --

### E1.7 Protocol anomalies, scanners, honeypots, CMS probes and host confusion

Raw-socket and h2 protocol fixtures are **builders in `hdd-acceptance`**, not text files (they must produce exact bytes). Their catalog (ids PRO-001..PRO-060) is used by AC-14 against `sandbox_hostname` only under the `protocol-abuse` profile:

| ID | Case | Expected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PRO-001 | `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` together (CL.TE) | 400, connection closed |
| PRO-002 | `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` plus conflicting `Content-Length` values (TE.CL) | 400 |
| PRO-003 | Two `Content-Length` headers with different values | 400 |
| PRO-004 | Duplicate `Host` headers | 400 |
| PRO-005 | `Transfer-Encoding: xchunked` / `chunked , identity` / tab-separated variants | 400 |
| PRO-006 | Obsolete line folding (obs-fold) in headers | 400 |
| PRO-007 | Absolute-form request target mismatching `Host` | 400 or normalized per policy |
| PRO-008 | Bare LF line endings | 400 |
| PRO-009 | CR in header value | 400 |
| PRO-010 | Null byte in header or path | 400 |
| PRO-011 | Request line over 8 KiB | 414 |
| PRO-012 | Header block over 32 KiB | 431 |
| PRO-013 | Body over cap | 413 |
| PRO-014 | Slowloris (1 byte/s headers) | cut at 10 s header timeout |
| PRO-015 | Slow POST (RUDY) | cut at idle timeout |
| PRO-016 | Chunk size overflow / negative / huge hex | 400 |
| PRO-017 | Chunk extension flood | 400 or limit |
| PRO-018 | Trailer abuse | ignored or 400 |
| PRO-019 | `Expect: 100-continue` abuse with large bodies | limits respected |
| PRO-020 | HTTP/0.9 / unknown version | 400/505 |
| PRO-021 | `GET` with body and `Content-Length` | per policy |
| PRO-022 | `TRACE`/`TRACK`/`CONNECT` methods | 405/501 |
| PRO-023 | Header names with spaces or invalid tokens | 400 |
| PRO-024 | `Range` overlapping flood | 200 full or 416, bounded work |
| PRO-025 | gzip bomb request body (generated, Class C builder, inspect/unit only) | rejected by ratio cap |
| PRO-026 | h2 Rapid Reset (HEADERS+RST_STREAM loop) | GOAWAY after limit, process healthy |
| PRO-027 | h2 CONTINUATION flood | connection closed, memory bounded |
| PRO-028 | h2 HPACK bomb | connection closed |
| PRO-029 | h2 SETTINGS flood | GOAWAY |
| PRO-030 | h2 PING flood | GOAWAY |
| PRO-031 | h2 empty DATA frame flood | GOAWAY |
| PRO-032 | h2 priority tree abuse | ignored/limited |
| PRO-033 | h2 pseudo-header misuse (`:authority` vs `Host`) | 421/400 |
| PRO-034 | h2 request with uppercase header names | PROTOCOL_ERROR |
| PRO-035 | h2 `connection`-specific headers | PROTOCOL_ERROR |
| PRO-036 | h2 to h1 smuggling via header values with CRLF | rejected |

### E1.9 Held-out, public-corpus and evasion sets

1. `heldout/sqli/*` (at least 200 payloads), `heldout/xss/*` (100), `heldout/lfi/*` (60), `heldout/rce/*` (60): authored **after** the detectors by a separate role (the "red" role of T-0533) or sourced from public corpora with recorded licenses; never used for tuning; hashes recorded in `.heldout-manifest`. Results are reported separately from the core set (AC-07, AC-39).
2. Public corpora (sourced into `lab/corpora/`, licenses in `lab/LICENSES.md`, never shipped): OWASP CRS regression tests, PayloadsAllTheThings subsets, SecLists fuzzing lists, sqlmap tamper outputs generated in the lab, `libinjection` test corpora (for tokenizer comparison only), FuzzDB. Detection rate on public corpora must be at least 95% for hard families (E4) and false-positive rate at most 0.1% on the public benign corpora.
3. Evasion catalog (C4.8) lives at `tests/fixtures/sqli/evasion.txt`; the matrix runner applies every transformation T01..T20 to every base payload in `core.txt` and to the first 100 lines of `heldout/sqli` to measure transformation robustness; misses are tracked as diagnosis tasks, never silently ignored.
4. Dialect files `tests/fixtures/sqli/by-dialect/{mysql,postgres,mssql,oracle,sqlite,db2}.txt` hold at least 40 payloads each using that dialect's distinctive functions, comments and string/identifier quoting, tagged with `dialects:`.

### E1.10 Expected-verdict table for the mandated set (field-kind policy)

| Field kind | M1 | M2 | M3 | M4 | M5 | M6 | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| username | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Auth endpoint strict mode |
| password (Balanced) | hard | hard | soft(4) | soft(4) | soft(4) | hard | H2 comment-breakout alone is soft in password fields; tautology parts remain hard |
| password (Paranoid) | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | All hard |
| email | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Email syntax rarely contains quotes plus SQL words |
| search | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Free text, apostrophes allowed but not with SQL structure |
| numeric_id | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Any quote in numeric context is already suspicious |
| free_text (comments, bios) | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Prose with apostrophes is benign (E2) |
| header (UA, Referer, XFF) | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Cross-site subresource context rules apply to bans |
| cookie | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | hard | Session lookups are classic SQLi sinks |

### E1.12 Access-gate bypass shapes (`tests/fixtures/gate/bypass.txt`, Class A, new in v5.1)

Used by T-0575 and AC-57 against a rule gating the prefix `/admin` (canonicalization and matching rules of C19.2). `HOST` stands for the site's hostname. Lines of the form `GET / with header H: V` add a header; lines starting with `h2` are HTTP/2 frames sent by the raw-socket client; other lines are the path. Invisible characters are written as `\uXXXX` escapes that the loader expands.

**How they are run (section 2.2 applies).** GET and HEAD path shapes may target the gated test site whose origin is `hdd-canary`; every shape that uses another method, or a request body, runs only against the sandbox route configured with an identical gate rule (a gate miss then yields the sandbox's 404 or 405, never the canary) or in lab mode. The inspect-first step for `category: gate` calls `POST /api/v1/waf/inspect` and requires `gate_decision` to be `gated` (or `rejected_early` for the early-reject list); anything else fails the test and nothing is sent.

### E1.13 Business-flow scenario seeds (`tests/fixtures/flows/*.yaml`, new in v5.1)

Each scenario is a generator description for the lab traffic tool (`hdd-loadgen` lab mode against the Vuln-Lab or the canary, `lab`/`functional` profile caps), with the signal it must trigger and the action expected in `block` mode. The benign replay must produce zero challenges and zero blocks.

| Scenario | Generator | Expected signal | Expected action in `block` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `stuffing-rotating` | 5,000 distinct synthetic usernames, each tried once or twice, from 50 source identities | distinct-username ratio, failure ratio | challenge then ban of the identities past threshold |
| `stuffing-slow` | 1 attempt per minute per username across 200 identities for 30 minutes | per-username HMAC counter across identities | challenge |
| `takeover-shape` | 40 failures then one success for the same username from a new ASN label | success after failures, new network | notify; challenge on the next attempt from that identity (the success itself cannot be undone) |
| `signup-flood` | 300 signups in 5 minutes, disposable domains, 0.5 s form time | velocity, disposable domain, time-to-complete, honey field | challenge then block |
| `signup-honey` | one signup with the hidden field filled | honey field | block (no ban unless repeated) |
| `otp-pumping` | 200 OTP requests to 200 distinct destinations from 3 identities | per-destination and per-identity send caps | block |
| `reset-spray` | 100 reset requests for 100 accounts from one identity | per-identity reset velocity | challenge then block |
| `carding-shape` | 80 checkout attempts, 70 declined, 60 distinct card hints, 10 sessions | decline ratio, distinct card hints per session | challenge then block |
| `scrape-sequence` | sequential product pages 1 to 5,000, no asset fetches, 100 ms jitter-free | breadth, sequential pagination, missing assets, timing regularity | challenge then block |
| `scrape-slow` | the same walk at 1 request per 5 s with random jitter | breadth over time (long window) | monitor event only (documented limit) |
| `coupon-guess` | 2,000 coupon codes against one endpoint | guess rate, distinct-code ratio | block |
| `contact-spam` | 100 identical bodies from 30 identities with links | duplicate content hash, link count | challenge |
| `benign-replay` | the AC-06 baseline replay including a burst of legitimate logins and a checkout | none | none (zero challenges, zero blocks) |

## E2. Benign corpus specification

### E2.1 Principles

1. A false positive is a defect in a rule, never in the corpus (R-23). The corpus is **append-only**; entries are removed only with a written reason in `tests/fixtures/CHANGELOG.md`.
2. Every benign file carries the header of E1.0 with `# class: A`, `# hardness: none`, `# expect: allow` (or `# expect: soft_only(max=N)` for documented ambiguous entries; the gate fails on any hard match or block regardless).
3. Entries are original material written for this project or taken from public-domain/permissively licensed sources with provenance recorded. Real traffic captured for baselines (HAR, access logs) is scrubbed by the redaction library (cookies, tokens, emails, IPs) before it touches a file.
4. Each entry is exercised in **every vector** its metadata allows (query, form, JSON, XML, multipart, cookie, headers, path), in **every field kind** it is plausible for, under presets Balanced, Strict and Shield Balanced at paranoia levels 1 and 2 (Shield Paranoid and paranoia 3 report soft hits but still must not produce hard hits except in the documented password-field exception list).
5. Soft scores are measured and reported (near-miss report); tuning may adjust soft weights but never the hard families, and never to hide a benign hit.

### E2.2 Files, minimum sizes and gate usage

| File | Minimum entries | Content | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `benign-general.txt` | 500 | Everyday web input: names, addresses, comments, search terms, product titles, URLs, emails, phone numbers, dates, markdown | AC-06, every detector change |
| `benign-sql-prose.txt` | 600 | Natural language about databases and SQL keywords used innocently, tutorial sentences, forum questions, error messages quoted by users | AC-06, T-0279 |
| `benign-apostrophes.txt` | 200 | Names and phrases with `'`, `"`, backticks, smart quotes and elisions in many languages | AC-06, AC-39 |
| `benign-code.txt` | 150 | Code samples pasted into comments/forums (SQL in fenced code, JSON, shell, HTML) that are not injection (no quote breakout, no tautology, no comment truncation) | T-0279 (soft_only allowed) |
| `benign-structured.txt` | 200 | JSON/XML/form/multipart bodies with SQL-ish keys (`order`, `group`, `select`, `limit`, `where`) | T-0279, T-0302 |
| `benign-passwords.txt` | 150 | Passphrases and symbol-heavy passwords (including `P@ss'word#1`), ambiguous cases listed with expected soft outcomes | C4.6, T-0272 |
| `benign-i18n.txt` | 150 | Multilingual text (Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, CJK, Devanagari, Thai, emoji), RTL marks, combining characters | T-0241, T-0242 |
| `benign-urls-headers.txt` | 200 | URLs, query strings, cookies, `User-Agent`, `Accept-*`, `Referer`, `Content-Disposition`, JWT-looking tokens, base64 blobs | T-0240, T-0298 |
| `benign-html.txt` | 120 | Rich text from editors (allowed tags, entities, inline styles) for sites that accept HTML by policy; sites that do not accept HTML expect soft only | T-0285 |
| `benign-api.txt` | 150 | REST/GraphQL requests of well-behaved clients (pagination, filters, mutations) | T-0302, T-0304 |
| `benign-outbound.txt` | 500 pages | Documentation, tutorials and security blog pages discussing SQL errors, stack traces and secrets; must not be blocked by the outbound filter | T-0408, T-0409, T-0415 |
| `benign-dns-names.txt` | 200 | Hostnames and records for DNS protocol tests (IDN, underscores, long labels) | T-0389 |
| `har-scrubbed/*.har` | operator supplied | Scrubbed real traffic (GET/HEAD replay unless allowlisted) | AC-06 baseline |

The total committed benign line count must be at least **2,500** across the text files (excluding HAR and outbound pages); `xtask fixtures benign --check` enforces the minimums and the header format.
